Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 4, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Before a restart
questions.question: A Cayman Islands fund administrator's investor chatbot began quoting wrong redemption prices; an engineer wants to restart it at once, which would clear its session logs. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Restart it now, then rebuild its logs by rerunning prompts
options.B: Disengage the chatbot and save its logs before restarting
options.C: Retrain the chatbot on the correct redemption prices
options.D: Post a notice that the chatbot's prices may be wrong

questions.key_concept: Containing an AI incident means disengaging it without destroying evidence: preserve logs, inputs and version before restarting or fixing.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the restart would erase, and who needs it later.
questions.correct_explanation: The chatbot must stop quoting prices, so it is disengaged first. A restart may not even stop the errors, since their cause is unknown, and it wipes the session logs; a generative chatbot's answers cannot be reliably regenerated from prompts later. Saving the logs first preserves who was quoted which wrong price, and why, for root cause work and for correcting investors' redemptions.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is quick. But rerun prompts produce new answers, not the ones investors saw, so who was quoted what is lost.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it targets the wrong prices. But retraining is an untested change made before the cause is known, which may not be the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it warns investors. But wrong prices keep going out while the notice stands, and no evidence is preserved.

tips: Eliminate: C retrains before the cause is known, an untested change, and D warns investors while wrong prices keep going out.
Final two: B beats A because rerunning prompts on a generative chatbot gives new answers; only logs saved before the restart show who was quoted what.
Exam cue: in an AI incident, stop the harm in a way that keeps the evidence; capture logs, inputs and version before any restart or fix.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. An agent still acting
questions.question: A Solomon Islands hospital's supply agent placed duplicate medicine orders; staff closed its chat window, but its scheduled order jobs keep running under its service account. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Roll back the model behind the service account's scheduled jobs
options.B: Cancel the duplicate orders with each medicine supplier
options.C: Suspend the agent's service account and scheduled jobs
options.D: Add a prompt rule forbidding repeat orders to one supplier

questions.key_concept: Disengaging an AI agent means suspending its credentials, tools and scheduled jobs; hiding its interface leaves it able to act.
questions.pre_read: Ask what still lets the agent act after its chat window closed.
questions.correct_explanation: Closing the chat window hid the agent from staff but left it acting: its scheduled jobs still place orders with its own credentials. Suspending the service account and jobs stops every action path while keeping them intact as evidence. Canceling duplicate orders is needed, but done first it chases a growing list, because new orders keep arriving until the agent's ability to act is cut off.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because rollback is a standard containment step. But nothing shows an update caused this, and an older model would still act through the same jobs and account.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because suppliers need correcting. But new orders keep arriving while the jobs run; stop the source first, then cancel.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it targets the behavior. But a prompt rule is an instruction, not a block, and scheduled jobs may never consult it.

tips: Eliminate: A changes the model version but leaves the same jobs and account acting, and D adds a prompt rule, which enforces nothing.
Final two: C beats B because orders keep coming until the agent's access is cut; canceling first chases a growing list.
Exam cue: disengaging an AI agent means cutting its credentials and scheduled actions, not just closing its user interface.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Repeats after refreshes
questions.question: An Aruban hotel group's guest chatbot gave wrong check-out times after four of the last five weekly index refreshes; each was closed as a separate incident. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Open a problem record on how refreshes rebuild the index
options.B: Roll back the index after any refresh that gives wrong times
options.C: Open a problem record and retrain the model on correct times
options.D: Pause index refreshes until the hotels confirm their times

questions.key_concept: Recurring AI incidents need a problem record aimed at the failing component; when faults follow index refreshes, look at retrieval content, not the model.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the four incidents have in common.
questions.correct_explanation: Four failures after refreshes is a pattern, not four unrelated incidents: something in how the index is rebuilt, such as an old policy file or a parsing step, keeps reintroducing wrong times. A problem record on the refresh process links the incidents and finds that cause. Retraining the model targets the wrong component: the chatbot answers from what the index retrieves, so new weights leave the faulty content in place.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because rollback restores correct answers. But it repeats a workaround every week; nothing finds why refreshes keep bringing the wrong times back.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it opens a problem record and targets the wrong answers. But the faults follow index refreshes; the chatbot answers from retrieved content, so retraining leaves the cause.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because refreshes trigger the fault. But pausing them leaves other content stale and still finds no cause.

tips: Eliminate: B rolls back after every bad refresh, a weekly workaround that never finds the cause, and D pauses refreshes, leaving content stale with no cause found.
Final two: A beats C because the faults track index refreshes, so the cause lies in retrieval content; retraining the model changes a component that is not failing.
Exam cue: when AI incidents repeat with a common trigger, expect a problem record aimed at the component the trigger points to: data, index, prompt or model.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A cause in the vendor's model
questions.question: A Congolese cobalt mining company's safety assistant gives wrong unit conversions, traced to the vendor's base model; the vendor's fix is five months away. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Close the problem record, since the vendor owns the cause
options.B: Switch to another vendor's model before the five months end
options.C: Log a known error; add a tested prompt rule to recheck sums
options.D: Log a known error; send conversions to a tested calculator

questions.key_concept: A vendor-side AI root cause stays open as a known error, with a workaround outside the model protecting people until the fix is verified.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens to workers' safety figures during the five months.
questions.correct_explanation: When the root cause sits in a vendor's model and the fix is months away, the problem stays open as a known error, with a workaround that protects workers meanwhile. Sending conversions to a separate, tested calculator takes the arithmetic away from the model. A prompt rule to recheck sums, even a tested one, is still an instruction to the model that makes the errors, so wrong safety figures can still reach workers.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor must fix it. But the company still owns the risk to its workers; a problem closes when the cause is removed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it avoids the faulty model. But a rushed switch is a major untested change, and the new model brings its own flaws.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it logs the known error and the rule passed tests. But the model that miscalculates would do the rechecking; a prompt instruction is not an enforced workaround.

tips: Eliminate: A closes a problem whose cause remains, though the company still owns the risk, and B rushes a major untested change.
Final two: D beats C because a workaround must take the faulty step away from the model; a prompt rule asks the same model to check its own sums.
Exam cue: when an AI fault sits with a vendor, expect a known error record and a tested workaround outside the model until the vendor's fix is verified.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Cleaning steps in a notebook
questions.question: A Dominican baseball academy's player-injury model was trained on data an analyst cleaned in a personal code notebook, since edited; only the raw files remain. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the analyst write up the cleaning steps from memory
options.B: Rebuild the cleaning as versioned code linked to each training set
options.C: Archive the raw files with hashes so training can be repeated
options.D: Retrain the model on the raw files without the cleaning steps

questions.key_concept: Lineage must be executable: cleaning steps kept as versioned pipeline code tied to each training set, not a description or the raw files alone.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the model actually learned from: the raw files, or the cleaned set.
questions.correct_explanation: The model learned from the cleaned data, not the raw files, so lineage must show how one became the other. Rebuilding the cleaning as versioned pipeline code linked to each training set makes future training traceable and repeatable; the current model then needs retraining and validation through change control. Archiving the raw files with hashes protects the inputs, but without the exact steps no one can recreate what the model learned from.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it recovers some history quickly. But recollection is not evidence of what the edited code actually did, and it cannot be tested or rerun.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because hashes prove the raw files are unchanged. But the model learned from cleaned data, and without the steps that training set cannot be recreated.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the raw files are the only trusted data left. But cleaning may have removed real errors, and an unplanned retrain on uncleaned data is an untested change.

tips: Eliminate: A rests on memory, which cannot show what the edited code did, and D retrains on uncleaned data, which may bring errors back through an untested change.
Final two: B beats C because lineage must cover every step from raw files to training set; intact raw files cannot recreate what the cleaning produced.
Exam cue: when a model's training data was shaped by unrecorded steps, look for versioned pipeline code tying each training set to its sources and transformations.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Chatbot drafts in its own sources
questions.question: A Ugandan solar-kit distributor's chatbot now drafts many help-center articles, unmarked; those articles feed both its retrieval index and its quarterly fine-tuning. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Tag chatbot drafts so unreviewed ones stay out of its data
options.B: Have editors review a random sample of new articles each month
options.C: Fine-tune monthly instead, so the chatbot learns newer articles sooner
options.D: Add a reader notice that some articles may be AI-written

questions.key_concept: Provenance should mark AI-generated content so unreviewed model output does not flow back into the same model's retrieval or training data.
questions.pre_read: Trace where the chatbot's own drafts end up after they are published.
questions.correct_explanation: When a model's own drafts flow back into its retrieval index and tuning data, its errors become sources it repeats and learns from. Tagging which articles the chatbot drafted lets the model owner keep unreviewed ones out of both. A monthly editor sample finds some errors, but unsampled drafts still feed the index and the next tuning round, and nothing marks which articles came from the model.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because review catches errors. But a sample leaves most drafts unchecked, and without provenance tags nobody can keep them out of training and retrieval.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fresher content seems better. But tuning more often on unreviewed output repeats the chatbot's own errors sooner.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is honest with readers. But a notice changes nothing about what the chatbot retrieves or learns from its own drafts.

tips: Eliminate: C tunes more often on unreviewed output, which repeats its errors sooner, and D informs readers without changing what the chatbot retrieves or learns.
Final two: A beats B because provenance tags let the model owner keep every unreviewed draft out of training and retrieval; a sample leaves most drafts flowing back in.
Exam cue: when AI output can become AI input, look for provenance that marks generated content and a gate that keeps unreviewed content out.

Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Tripling a skewed image archive
questions.question: A Saint Lucian hospital's burn model, trained mostly on lighter-skin photos, misses more deep burns on darker skin; staff will triple the data from that archive. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Triple the training set as planned, then retest on darker skin
options.B: Lower every patient's alert threshold so fewer deep burns are missed
options.C: Add images of darker skin, then report misses by skin tone
options.D: Have burn specialists relabel the archive images to cut label errors

questions.key_concept: More data with the same skew repeats a representativeness gap; fix the mix with targeted data and measure results by group.
questions.pre_read: Ask who is in the image archive and who the hospital's patients are.
questions.correct_explanation: The gap comes from who is in the data: an archive with few darker-skin images teaches the model little about them, and tripling it repeats the same mix. Adding darker-skin images targets the gap, and reporting misses by skin tone shows whether it closed. Relabeling the archive improves label quality, but it adds no darker-skin images, so the model still learns from the same population.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it adds data and tests the group. But more images from the same archive repeat the skew, so the retest would show the same gap.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it catches more deep burns quickly. But it raises false alarms for every patient and does not fix what the model failed to learn.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because clean labels matter. But the problem is who is missing from the archive, not how its images were labeled.

tips: Eliminate: A adds more images from the same skewed archive, which repeats the gap, and B lowers the alert threshold for everyone, trading false alarms for an unfixed gap.
Final two: C beats D because the archive lacks darker-skin images; better labels on the same images teach the model nothing new about the missing group.
Exam cue: when one group is missed more often, look for targeted data for that group and results reported by group, not more of the same data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Labels confirmed from suggestions
questions.question: A Slovenian hospital's clinical coders confirm diagnosis codes its model pre-fills, accepting 98%; the next model version will be tested against these confirmed codes. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Coders may not keep pace with the volume the model codes
options.B: The test set may hold too few rare diagnoses to judge them
options.C: Confirmed codes may expose patient data to the model's testers
options.D: Test labels may repeat the model's own errors and inflate scores

questions.key_concept: Labels confirmed from a model's pre-filled suggestion can echo its errors, so testing a successor against them overstates its accuracy.
questions.pre_read: Ask who really chose each code: the coder, or the model the coder agreed with.
questions.correct_explanation: Coders shown a pre-filled code tend to accept it, so a 98% acceptance rate may reflect anchoring rather than independent judgment. If those confirmations become test labels, the next version is graded against its predecessor's choices, and shared errors look like correct answers. Too few rare diagnoses is a common test weakness, but nothing in the facts points to it, while the label source is stated.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because throughput matters to coding teams. But pace is an operations issue; it says nothing about whether the test labels are valid.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because rare cases often lack test data. But nothing here points to it; the stated problem is where the labels came from.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because test teams handle patient records. But normal access controls cover that, and it does not affect whether the scores mean anything.

tips: Eliminate: A is a staffing and pace question, and C is an access question that normal data controls handle; neither affects whether the test is valid.
Final two: D beats B because the stem says the test labels are pre-filled codes the coders confirmed; rare-case coverage is a real risk the facts never raise.
Exam cue: labels people confirmed from a model's suggestion can carry the model's errors; ask whether ground truth was formed independently of the model.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.1 (Test sets, metrics and TEVV tools documented); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration)

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Selling the model to new farms
questions.question: An Irish farm-software firm's mastitis-alert model, built from 40 client farms' records split randomly into training and test sets, will now be sold to new farms. Which test should the IS auditor request FIRST?

options.A: A test on whole farms whose records the model never saw
options.B: A rerun of the same test with a larger random sample
options.C: A test on the latest months from the same 40 farms
options.D: A review of the code that splits records into the two sets

questions.key_concept: The test split must match deployment: a model for new sites needs whole sites held out, since random splits let it learn each site.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the farms buying the model look like any farm in the test set.
questions.correct_explanation: A random split puts records from every farm in both sets, so the test shows how well the model knows farms it has seen; the holdout must match how the model will be used. The buyers are new farms, so the test must hold out whole farms. Testing the latest months is a sound out-of-time check, but the model has already learned every test farm, so it would overstate results on new farms.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more test records narrow the error range. But a random split still places each farm in both sets, so it cannot show results on unseen farms.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because newer data shows drift. But the model has already learned these 40 farms, so the test overstates results on farms it never saw.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a flawed split causes leakage. But reading the code shows how the split was made, not how the model performs on new farms.

tips: Eliminate: B enlarges a random split that still mixes each farm into both sets, and D reviews split code, which gives no evidence of performance on new farms.
Final two: A beats C because the new use is new farms; a later time window still tests farms the model already learned.
Exam cue: match the holdout to the deployment. New sites, customers or regions need test data from sites the model never trained on.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A.3 Training, Validation and Test Separation (the holdout must match deployment, so new sites need whole sites held out). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Monthly retraining of a tower-fault model
questions.question: A Haitian mobile operator retrains its tower-fault model monthly on all labeled records, including the fixed test set on which it reports each release's score. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Monthly releases may be too frequent for proper change review
options.B: The fixed test set may no longer match current tower faults
options.C: Each release is scored on records it was trained on
options.D: Field crews may distrust a model that changes every month

questions.key_concept: A retraining pipeline that folds the test set into training turns every later score into a memory test.
questions.pre_read: Follow the test records through each monthly retraining run.
questions.correct_explanation: Once test records are folded into training, the model has seen the answers, so each release's score measures memory, not performance on new faults. That makes every reported score unreliable from the first retrain on. A fixed test set can also grow stale as faults change, which matters, but a stale yet unseen set still tests the model; a set it trained on tests nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because frequent changes strain review. But automated gates can test monthly releases; frequency is not what makes these scores unreliable.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because fault patterns change. But even an up-to-date test set gives no unseen test once the model has trained on it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because crews must trust alerts. But trust is an adoption issue; the question is whether the reported scores mean anything.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about release frequency, which automated gates handle, and D is a user-adoption concern; neither touches whether the scores are valid.
Final two: C beats B because a test set the model trained on measures memory; staleness weakens a test, leakage voids it.
Exam cue: in retraining pipelines, check that the holdout stays out of every later training run, not just the first one.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.1 (Test sets, metrics and TEVV tools documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A.3 Training, Validation and Test Separation (a holdout folded into retraining stops being an unseen test). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A prompt-built assistant
questions.question: A Rwandan examinations council built its assistant for students from a system prompt on a hosted model; as no model was trained, it skipped the validation gate. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have staff review the system prompt's wording before it goes live
options.B: Test how it answers as deployed before students rely on it
options.C: Rely on the vendor's safety testing of its base model
options.D: Launch it, then fix problems that students report

questions.key_concept: A prompt-built assistant on a hosted model is still an AI system that needs the organization's own validation gate before use.
questions.pre_read: Ask what was actually built here, and whose tests cover it.
questions.correct_explanation: A system prompt on a hosted model creates a new AI system whose answers depend on the prompt, the model and the questions people ask. Skipping validation because nothing was trained treats it like ordinary content. The vendor's safety testing covers its general model, not the council's prompt, exam rules or students, so it cannot stand in for validating the assistant as deployed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the council wrote only the prompt. But the assistant generates a new answer to each question; reading the prompt cannot show what those answers say.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor tests its model thoroughly. But that testing covers general behavior, not this prompt, these exam rules or these students.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because student reports find real problems. But students may act on wrong exam advice before reporting it; testing must come before launch.

tips: Eliminate: A reviews the prompt's text, which cannot show what generated answers say, and D tests only after launch, once people may have acted on wrong advice.
Final two: B beats C because the vendor's testing covers its base model, not the council's prompt and use; the lifecycle gates apply to the system as built.
Exam cue: building with prompts instead of training does not exempt an AI system from the lifecycle; validate what the organization deployed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.12 (Value Chain and Component Integration)

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Features computed two ways
questions.question: An Omani airline's fuel-load model passed validation on features the data team computed in batch; in production, a separately coded live service will compute them. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST before go-live?

options.A: Load-test the live service at peak flight-planning volumes
options.B: Review the live service's code against the coding standard
options.C: Revalidate the model on a fresh, batch-computed holdout set
options.D: Compare live and batch features for the same flights

questions.key_concept: Training-serving skew: features computed differently in production than in validation make validation results unreliable for the live model.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the numbers the model sees in production come from the same code it was validated on.
questions.correct_explanation: The model was validated on features from one piece of code and will run on features from another. Small differences in rounding, time windows or missing-value handling can shift fuel recommendations without any error message. Comparing batch and live features for the same flights exposes this skew before go-live. A fresh batch holdout retests the model, but on batch features again, so the live service's numbers stay untested.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because live services must handle peak loads. But speed testing shows capacity, not whether live features match those the model was validated on.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because standards reduce defects. But compliant code can still compute a feature differently, such as a different time window or rounding rule.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fresh data gives a clean retest. But it uses batch features again, so differences in the live service's calculations stay hidden.

tips: Eliminate: A tests speed and B tests coding style; neither shows whether the live service computes the same feature values that validation used.
Final two: D beats C because a new batch holdout repeats the batch calculation; only comparing both pipelines on the same flights reveals training-serving skew.
Exam cue: when features are computed one way for validation and another way in production, ask for evidence that both produce the same values.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-11 (Developer Testing and Evaluation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B.1 The AI Lifecycle and Stage Gates (validation evidence holds only if production computes the same features). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A spice exporter's buyer assistant
questions.question: A Grenadian spice exporter's buyer assistant adds a system prompt, retrieval index and output filter to a vendor model; the vendor's model card is its sole record. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Document the whole assistant, including what the exporter added
options.B: Ask the vendor for a fuller model card with known limits
options.C: Rely on the vendor's card until buyers report a problem
options.D: Keep the assistant's system prompt in the code repository

questions.key_concept: An AI system's documentation covers what the organization added, such as prompts, retrieval sources and filters, not just the vendor's model card.
questions.pre_read: List what shapes the assistant's answers, then ask which of those parts any document describes.
questions.correct_explanation: The assistant's behavior comes from the vendor model plus everything the exporter added: the prompt that steers it, the index it answers from and the filter that shapes its replies. Documentation must cover that whole system, its intended use and limits. A fuller vendor card helps with the base model's limits, but it still says nothing about the parts the exporter built, which no one has documented.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because base-model limits matter. But the vendor cannot document the exporter's prompt, index and filter, which shape what buyers are told.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor's card exists today. But documentation is needed before use, and waiting for buyer problems leaves the added parts unrecorded.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because versioned prompts help change control. But a stored prompt records one component; it describes no purpose, data source, filter or limit.

tips: Eliminate: C waits for buyer problems, though documentation must exist before use, and D stores one component's text, which records no purpose, sources or limits.
Final two: A beats B because the gap is the exporter's own additions; no vendor card, however full, describes a prompt, index and filter it never saw.
Exam cue: document the AI system as deployed, not just the model inside it; prompts, retrieval sources and filters change what users get.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.12 (Value Chain and Component Integration)

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Tuning on restricted candidate files
questions.question: An Estonian executive-search firm's recruiters all use a language model fine-tuned on every candidate file, though many files are restricted to named recruiters. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Add an output filter hiding restricted candidates' names from recruiters
options.B: Remove every restricted file from the model's tuning dataset
options.C: Limit use of the model to recruiters cleared for every file
options.D: Retrain the model without restricted files at the next cycle

questions.key_concept: A tuned model can reveal details of any file it learned to any user, so limit its use as tightly as its most restricted data.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can query the model today and what it learned from.
questions.correct_explanation: A tuned model can reveal details from any file it learned to anyone who queries it, so it is as sensitive as its most restricted training file. Until restricted content is removed, only recruiters cleared for every file should use it. Retraining without the restricted files is the lasting fix, but until the next cycle ends every recruiter can still draw out restricted candidates' details.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because names are the obvious leak. But reworded questions can draw out a restricted candidate's salary or situation without a name, so exposure continues.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it removes the restricted source. But the model has already learned from those files, so removing them from the tuning set changes nothing until a retrain.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it removes restricted content for good. But every recruiter can draw it out until the next cycle ends; use must be limited now.

tips: Eliminate: A filters names only, but reworded questions still draw out restricted details, and B cleans a tuning set the model has already learned from.
Final two: C beats D because the model already holds every file's content; retraining is the lasting fix, but exposure continues until it is done.
Exam cue: a tuned model is as sensitive as the most restricted data it learned; limit who uses it until that content is removed by rebuilding.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Retiring a scheduling agent
questions.question: A Chilean architecture firm retired its meeting-scheduling agent by deleting its service account; staff had each authorized the agent's app to read their mailbox. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Confirm the account deletion in the next access review
options.B: Revoke the access users delegated to the agent
options.C: Revoke the agent's API key with its model vendor
options.D: Update the AI inventory to show the agent as retired

questions.key_concept: AI agents often act through access users delegated to them; retirement must revoke those grants, not just the agent's own account.
questions.pre_read: List every way the agent could reach a mailbox, not just its own account.
questions.correct_explanation: Deleting the service account removed the agent's own identity, but its mailbox access came from grants each staff member gave it, and those grants stay valid until revoked. Anything still holding them, such as a leftover copy of the agent, can keep reading mail. Revoking each grant ends that access. Revoking the agent's model API key seems to shut it down, but the grants open mailboxes without the model.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because access reviews catch leftover accounts. But the account is already gone; the live access sits in delegated grants the review may not list.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because without model access the agent cannot act. But the delegated grants work without the model; anything holding them can still read staff mail.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retirement needs an inventory update. But recording the agent as retired does not end the access its delegated grants still give.

tips: Eliminate: A rechecks an account that is already deleted, and D updates the inventory, which records retirement but leaves the delegated grants working.
Final two: B beats C because the delegated grants open the mailboxes without the model; revoking its API key stops the agent's model calls, not access through the grants.
Exam cue: retiring an AI agent means removing every route it acts through: its own accounts, its keys and the access users delegated to it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.7 (Decommissioning AI systems safely); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Archived models and a platform license
questions.question: A Trinidadian vehicle-inspection agency keeps its retired roadworthiness models to rescore appeals with corrected readings, but they run only on a platform whose license ends soon. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Delete the archived models when the platform license ends
options.B: Ask the platform vendor to confirm the models are archived safely
options.C: Document how each model scored so staff can explain appeals
options.D: Keep a way to run the archived models until appeals close

questions.key_concept: Retired models kept for appeals must stay runnable; a model that only a retired platform can load cannot reproduce or explain decisions.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an appeal reviewer would need to do with the archived model.
questions.correct_explanation: An archived model that nothing can load is a file, not evidence. Appeals here need the exact model rerun on corrected readings, so the agency must keep a working way to run it until appeals close, such as a supported export or a retained environment. Documenting how each model scored helps staff explain past decisions, but it cannot produce a new score from corrected readings.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the platform is being retired. But open appeals may need the exact model to rerun or explain decisions, so deletion removes the evidence.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor holds the files. But safe storage does not make the models runnable once the license ends.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because documentation supports explanations. But it cannot rescore a case with corrected readings; only the exact model, still runnable, can.

tips: Eliminate: A deletes models that open appeals may need, and B confirms storage, which does not keep the models runnable after the license ends.
Final two: D beats C because documentation explains past scores but cannot produce new ones; rescoring appeals needs the exact model running.
Exam cue: archived AI is evidence only if it can still be run or explained; check whether it depends on a platform being retired.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.7 (Decommissioning AI systems safely); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-12 (Information Management and Retention)

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Retraining as a standard change
questions.question: A Bolivian mining cooperative wants its ore-price model's weekly retraining, same code and data sources each time, classed as a pre-approved standard change. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Allow it only if each run passes independently approved tests
options.B: Refuse it; send each retrain to the change advisory board
options.C: Allow it, as the code and data sources do not change
options.D: Allow it if the data scientist who ran it signs off

questions.key_concept: Routine retraining can be pre-approved as a standard change only when every run must pass release tests approved in advance, independently of the builders.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each weekly run produces, and what stops a bad one from going live.
questions.correct_explanation: Each weekly run produces a new model from new data, so it is a change, even with identical code. A standard change can still fit, but only if every run must pass performance and data checks approved in advance by someone other than the builders, with rollback ready. Sending every run to the change advisory board is safe but adds a weekly delay without adding evidence the approved tests could not give.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because change advisory board review feels safest. But it adds a weekly delay, and preset, independently approved tests can give stronger evidence for each run.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because nothing in the pipeline changed. But new data makes a new model each week, which can behave differently.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the data scientist knows the model. But a builder approving their own release breaks segregation of duties; it is not an independent check.

tips: Eliminate: C treats unchanged code as an unchanged model, though new data makes a new one, and D lets the builder approve their own release.
Final two: A beats B because a retrain can be pre-approved when independently approved tests gate each run; change advisory board review of every run adds delay, not evidence.
Exam cue: a repeated change such as routine retraining can be pre-approved only when every run passes preset, independently approved gates; one-off edits, such as new prompt wording, cannot.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control); COBIT 2019 BAI06 (Managed IT Changes)

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Cutting the human review step
questions.question: To cut costs, a Burundian public university reduced staff review of its model's fee-waiver rejections from every rejection to a 10% sample; the model itself is unchanged. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept it as a staffing decision, since the model did not change
options.B: Treat it as an AI change, assessed and approved before use
options.C: Watch rejection error rates after the cut and restore if they rise
options.D: Have the model owner raise the model's rejection threshold instead

questions.key_concept: Human review is part of an AI system's controls; reducing it is an AI change needing assessment and approval before use.
questions.pre_read: Ask what caught the model's wrong rejections before the cut, and what catches them now.
questions.correct_explanation: Human review is part of how the AI system controls its errors, so cutting it from every rejection to a 10% sample changes the system even though the model is untouched. It needs an impact assessment and approval before use, like any AI change. Watching error rates afterward is useful monitoring, but it finds problems only after students have been wrongly rejected.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model and its code are untouched. But review is part of the AI system's controls, so changing it changes the risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it measures real effects. But it detects harm after students are rejected; the change needs assessment before it takes effect.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fewer rejections need less review. But a threshold edit is itself an untested change and does not replace the lost review.

tips: Eliminate: A treats oversight as staffing outside the AI system, and D swaps in an untested threshold edit, which is a change of its own.
Final two: B beats C because changes to the human-AI setup need assessment and approval before use; monitoring afterward finds wrongful rejections only once students bear them.
Exam cue: an AI change is not only to the model; changes to human review, thresholds or prompts change the system's risk too.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A rollback target with a known flaw
questions.question: A New Zealand tribunal service's documented rollback target for its transcription model is version 5, which was replaced because it misheard Māori names far more often. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Record the known name errors in the rollback runbook
options.B: Drop the rollback plan, since no older version is safe
options.C: Choose and test a rollback target that meets current criteria
options.D: Keep version 5, since its overall error rate meets target

questions.key_concept: A rollback target runs in production, so it must meet current criteria by group; an overall error rate can hide the harm it brings back.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the tribunal's transcripts would contain if the rollback were used tomorrow.
questions.correct_explanation: A rollback target is a version the tribunal would run in production, so it must meet today's acceptance criteria, including the fix for misheard Māori names. Choosing and testing a target that does, or a manual fallback if none does, keeps recovery from reintroducing a known harm. Version 5 meeting the overall error-rate target settles nothing: an overall rate can hide far higher errors on Māori names.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because documenting a known flaw looks like control. But a note in the runbook does not stop a rollback putting the misheard Māori names back into tribunal records.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it avoids the flawed version. But it leaves no recovery path if the current version fails.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the overall error rate is within target. But an overall rate can hide far higher errors for one group, here the Māori names a rollback would bring back.

tips: Eliminate: A only documents the known errors, which a rollback would still put into tribunal records, and B removes the only recovery path, leaving nothing to fall back to.
Final two: C beats D because an overall error rate can hide a group's much higher errors; a rollback target runs in production and must meet today's criteria, Māori names included.
Exam cue: test rollback targets against today's criteria; rolling back can reintroduce a fixed fairness or accuracy problem.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A ship registry's tuned adapters
questions.question: A Marshall Islands ship registry's document checker runs a tuned adapter on an open-weight base model; its model registry versions each adapter but not its base model. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep every adapter version so any one can be restored quickly
options.B: Retune the adapter each time a new base model is released
options.C: Ask the base model's publisher to announce each new release
options.D: Record each adapter's base model and test rollbacks as a pair

questions.key_concept: A tuned adapter works only with the exact base model it was tuned on, so the version baseline and any rollback must pair the two.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an adapter needs underneath it to behave as it did in testing.
questions.correct_explanation: An adapter holds only the changes learned in tuning; its behavior depends on the exact base model underneath. If the registry cannot say which base each adapter was tuned on, restoring an older adapter on a newer base gives untested behavior, so no rollback is really known. Recording each adapter's base model and testing rollbacks as a pair closes that gap. Keeping every adapter alone restores only half the system.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because every adapter is kept. But an adapter restored on a different base model behaves in untested ways, so half the pair is missing.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it keeps the adapter current. But each retune is a change of its own, and the registry still cannot say which pair ran before.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because notice of new releases helps planning. But it records nothing about which base each past adapter needs.

tips: Eliminate: B retunes on every release without recording the pair, and C collects release notices, which record nothing about past adapters.
Final two: D beats A because an adapter reproduces its behavior only on the base it was tuned on; storing adapters alone restores half the system.
Exam cue: for tuned models, the version baseline must name the base model too; a rollback restores the pair, not just the tuned part.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A vendor update that shifts scores
questions.question: A Nicaraguan crowdfunding platform pauses campaigns scoring above 0.7 on a vendor's scam-detection model; the vendor says next month's version gives lower scores overall. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Reset the cutoff on the new version's scores, then retest
options.B: Keep 0.7, since the vendor says the new version is better
options.C: Lower the cutoff by the vendor's stated average score drop
options.D: Have staff review every campaign for the first month

questions.key_concept: A decision threshold is calibrated to one model version's scores; a vendor update that shifts scores needs the threshold re-derived and retested.
questions.pre_read: Ask what 0.7 means on the new version's scale.
questions.correct_explanation: A cutoff is tuned to one model's score scale. If the new version scores lower, 0.7 will pause fewer scam campaigns, though nothing in the platform's code changed. The model owner should reset the cutoff on the new version's scores, using labeled campaigns, and retest before the switch. Subtracting the vendor's average drop assumes every score moved equally, which rarely holds near the cutoff, where it matters.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor expects better results. But better is measured on its own tests, and lower scores mean 0.7 pauses fewer scams.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it adjusts by a stated figure. But an average shift hides uneven changes near the cutoff, so pausing could still drift.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because people catch what the model misses. But reviewing every campaign cannot last and leaves the cutoff misaligned.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps a cutoff set on old scores because the vendor says the update is better, and D adds full manual review, which cannot last and leaves the cutoff misaligned.
Final two: A beats C because a new version's scores must be calibrated on labeled data; an average shift misses uneven changes near the cutoff.
Exam cue: thresholds belong to a model version; when a vendor's scores change, re-derive and retest the threshold before relying on it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-4 (Impact Analyses)

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Changes behind a pinned version
questions.question: A Latvian timber exporter pins the vendor model version behind its contract-translation assistant, yet more passages return untranslated; the vendor says only its server-side safety filter changed. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rely on the pin, as the model version did not change
options.B: Require the vendor to give notice of every filter change
options.C: Run fixed regression tests on a schedule, pinned or not
options.D: Move to a self-hosted open model to avoid vendor changes

questions.key_concept: Pinning a hosted model's version does not freeze the service; vendor-side filters and settings can still change results, so regression testing continues.
questions.pre_read: List what besides the model weights sits between the contract and the translation.
questions.correct_explanation: A version pin fixes the model's weights, but a hosted service also includes filters, system instructions and settings the vendor can change on its side. Here a filter change left more passages untranslated with the pinned version untouched. Scheduled regression tests on the exporter's own contracts detect such shifts whatever their source. Notice of filter changes helps, but it says what changed, not whether contracts are still translated correctly.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because pinning is the standard control. But it fixes the model's weights only; the vendor's filters and settings around it can still change.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because notice is a sound contract term. But notice says a change happened, not how it affects translations, and some changes arrive unannounced.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it removes the vendor. But self-hosting is a major untested change that brings new security and support risks.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts a pin that covers the model's weights alone, and D trades the vendor for a major, untested move to self-hosting.
Final two: C beats B because only tests on the exporter's own contracts show whether a change hurt results; notice tells you something changed, not its effect.
Exam cue: version pinning does not freeze a hosted AI service; keep running regression tests on your own cases.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.2 (Pre-trained models monitored as part of regular maintenance); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-07 (Supplier risks assessed and monitored over the relationship)

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. When the model's flag appears
questions.question: Georgian hospital radiologists' agreement with an unchanged fracture model's flags rose from 70% to 96% once the flags began appearing before the X-ray image. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Remove the radiologists' step, since they agree with the model anyway
options.B: Have radiologists record their own reading before the flag appears
options.C: Remind radiologists in training that the model's flags can be wrong
options.D: Retrain the model on radiologists' readings to align them further

questions.key_concept: Showing a model's output before reviewers judge anchors them; recording an independent judgment first counters automation bias.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changed: the model, or what the radiologists see first.
questions.correct_explanation: The model did not change; only when its flag appears did. A jump from 70% to 96% agreement then suggests radiologists anchor on the flag rather than read each image afresh. Having them record their own reading before seeing the flag keeps their judgment independent and lets the owner measure real disagreement. A training reminder raises awareness, but it does not change the screen that pulls radiologists toward the flag.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because high agreement suggests the review adds little. But the jump came from the display change, so it signals anchoring, not a model fit to run alone.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because awareness is part of oversight. But knowing flags can be wrong does little against anchoring when the flag is the first thing shown.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because aligned labels look consistent. But anchored readings would carry the model's own flags back into its training.

tips: Eliminate: A removes oversight because of agreement that the display change produced, and D trains the model on readings anchored to its own flags.
Final two: B beats C because anchoring is countered by design at the moment of judgment; a training reminder leaves the anchor in place.
Exam cue: when agreement with a model jumps after a screen or workflow change, suspect automation bias and look for design fixes, not just training.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.1 Human Oversight and Automation Bias (showing the model's output first anchors reviewers). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Reviewers who cannot check citations
questions.question: A Lithuanian consumer-protection agency's clerks approve AI-drafted replies that cite consumer law; reviews show they rarely question citations, which they cannot check without legal training. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add a notice telling consumers that replies are AI-assisted
options.B: Stop the model from citing consumer law in replies
options.C: Show clerks the model's confidence score for each citation
options.D: Route replies citing law to staff able to verify them

questions.key_concept: Human oversight needs reviewers competent to judge the output; approval by staff who cannot verify it is a rubber stamp.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the person approving each reply could spot a wrong citation.
questions.correct_explanation: Oversight is real only if the reviewer can judge what they approve. Clerks without legal training cannot tell a wrong or invented citation from a right one, so their approval adds little. Routing replies that cite law to staff who can verify them puts competent judgment where the risk is. Showing clerks the model's confidence in each citation seems helpful, but models can be confidently wrong, and clerks still cannot check the law.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because transparency is good practice. But a notice does not make the legal advice right; consumers may still act on wrong citations.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it removes the error source. But replies then lose their legal basis, and the advice itself stays unchecked.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a score seems to flag weak citations. But a model can be confidently wrong, and clerks still cannot check the law behind a high score.

tips: Eliminate: A informs consumers without checking the advice, and B strips the legal basis from replies while leaving the advice itself unverified.
Final two: D beats C because the model's own confidence is not verification; only staff who know the law can check a citation.
Exam cue: a human reviewer is real oversight only with the skill, time and authority to judge the output; check competence, not just presence.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.4 (Operator and practitioner proficiency defined and assessed); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 3.2 (Roles defined for human-AI configurations and oversight)

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. A visitor chatbot's quality measure
questions.question: An Antiguan tourism authority tracks its generative visitor chatbot by thumbs-up ratings, steady at 92%; its answers on entry rules sound equally confident when wrong. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have staff check sampled answers against current entry rules
options.B: Add a rating question asking if entry-rule answers were accurate
options.C: Retrain the chatbot monthly so its answers stay current
options.D: Report the 92% rating to the board as the quality measure

questions.key_concept: User satisfaction ratings do not measure the correctness of generative AI answers; monitoring needs sampled checks against authoritative sources.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the people giving the ratings could tell a confident wrong answer from a right one.
questions.correct_explanation: Thumbs-up ratings measure whether visitors liked an answer, not whether it was right. A generative chatbot states wrong entry rules as confidently as right ones, so a wrong answer can still earn a thumbs-up. Having staff check sampled answers against the current rules measures accuracy directly. Asking visitors whether an answer was accurate looks like an accuracy measure, but visitors cannot see through a confident wrong answer either.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it asks about accuracy directly. But a confident wrong answer misleads visitors too, so their rating measures belief, not correctness.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fresh training seems to keep answers current. But scheduled retraining gives no evidence that answers are right and is itself a change.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the figure is steady and high. But it measures satisfaction, so reporting it as quality would mislead the board.

tips: Eliminate: C retrains on a schedule, which gives no evidence of correct answers, and D reports a satisfaction score to the board as if it measured quality.
Final two: A beats B because visitors misled by a confident wrong answer cannot rate its accuracy; expert checks against the source measure it.
Exam cue: user ratings show satisfaction, not correctness; monitoring generative AI quality needs checks against authoritative sources.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.2 Monitoring Drift, Performance and Impacts (satisfaction ratings do not measure correctness). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. A drift check with a rolling baseline
questions.question: A Tuvaluan coastal-works agency's drift check compares each month's erosion-model inputs with the prior month's and never trips, though sea levels edged up steadily for two years. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Tighten the month-to-month drift limit so smaller shifts trip it
options.B: Compare inputs with the data the model was trained on
options.C: Retrain the model monthly so drift cannot build up
options.D: Drop sea level as an input, since it keeps changing

questions.key_concept: Drift measured against a rolling baseline can hide slow, steady change; a fixed reference such as the training data shows total drift.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each month's inputs are being compared with.
questions.correct_explanation: Comparing each month with the one before measures only the latest step, so a slow, steady shift never looks large. Over two years the inputs can move far from the conditions the model learned, unnoticed. Comparing inputs with the training data gives a fixed reference that shows the total drift. A tighter month-to-month limit trips more often, including on normal variation, but still never measures the distance from training.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it makes the check more sensitive. But it still compares against a baseline that moves, so it never measures the total shift since training.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because frequent retraining follows the data. But scheduled retraining is no substitute for monitoring and can bake in bad data unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the input is unstable. But removing a key input is an untested model change that may weaken the forecasts.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on scheduled retraining instead of measurement, and D removes a key input, which is an untested change to the model.
Final two: B beats A because a baseline that moves each month hides slow drift; only a fixed reference such as the training data shows the total shift.
Exam cue: check what a drift monitor compares against; a rolling baseline can hide gradual drift.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Declaration risk-score logs
questions.question: A Ghanaian customs service's officers decide the declarations its risk model flags; importers dispute decisions using its log of model version, inputs, score and final status. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add the flagging threshold in force for each score to the log
options.B: Have officers sign a monthly statement that they reviewed declarations
options.C: Log each officer's action and reason beside the model's output
options.D: Store the existing log in write-once storage for disputes

questions.key_concept: Decision logs for human-reviewed AI must record each reviewer's action and reason, or oversight and appeals cannot be tested.
questions.pre_read: Ask how anyone would tell, from this log, who actually decided a declaration.
questions.correct_explanation: Without the officer's action in the log, no one can tell whether a declaration was decided by the model alone or by an officer who agreed with it or overrode it. That gap blocks importers' disputes, override analysis and any test of whether oversight works. Logging each officer's action and reason beside the model's output closes it. Adding the flagging threshold shows why a declaration was flagged, but still hides the human decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the threshold shows why a declaration was flagged. But the log would still not show whether an officer or the model made each final call.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it records accountability. But a monthly statement is not evidence of what happened to any one declaration.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tamper-proof logs strengthen evidence. But protecting the log does not add the missing record of who decided.

tips: Eliminate: B gives a general monthly attestation, not per-declaration evidence, and D protects a log that still lacks the human step.
Final two: C beats A because oversight and disputes turn on who made the final call; the threshold explains the flag, not the decision.
Exam cue: decision logs for human-reviewed AI should show the model's output, the reviewer's action and the reason, for each case.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.1 (Post-deployment monitoring including appeal, override, incident response and change management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-2 (Event Logging)

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Appeal outcomes as training labels
questions.question: A Scottish council retrains its council-tax reduction model on appeal outcomes as corrected labels; most successful appeals come from applicants helped by welfare-rights advisers. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The model learns fixes mainly from applicants who had advisers
options.B: Appeal outcomes may take months to reach the training data
options.C: Advisers may learn how to game the model's decisions
options.D: Corrected labels may lower the model's overall accuracy

questions.key_concept: Appeal outcomes used as labels correct errors only for people who appeal, so the model may keep its errors against those who cannot.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose wrong decisions ever reach the appeal process.
questions.correct_explanation: Appeal outcomes are an incomplete label source: they correct errors only for people who appeal and win, and here those are mostly applicants with advisers. The model learns to fix the cases they bring, while similar errors against applicants without advisers stay labeled as correct. Delay in appeal outcomes slows learning, but the corrections still arrive; the skew decides whose errors are ever corrected.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because late labels slow retraining. But delay only postpones corrections; the skew decides whose errors are ever corrected.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because feedback can be gamed. But nothing suggests manipulation; advisers helping applicants appeal is the process working.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because label changes can shift scores. But correcting wrong labels should improve accuracy; the issue is whose labels get corrected.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes manipulation the facts never suggest, and D misreads corrected labels, which should improve accuracy rather than lower it.
Final two: A beats B because the skew decides whose errors the model ever unlearns; delay only slows corrections that still arrive.
Exam cue: feedback used as training labels carries the bias of who gives it; ask who is missing from the feedback.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.3 (Feedback and appeal processes for end users and affected communities); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Testing answers that vary
questions.question: A Japanese city's step-free-route assistant for wheelchair users passed acceptance testing, each of 200 test questions asked once; its answers vary run to run. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add 200 more test questions, each asked once
options.B: Accept the results, since the 200 answers each passed
options.C: Set the model's temperature to zero and close testing
options.D: Ask each question several times and judge pass rates

questions.key_concept: Generated output varies run to run, so acceptance tests should repeat each case and judge pass rates, not single answers.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a single passing answer shows when the next answer may differ.
questions.correct_explanation: When answers vary run to run, one pass per question shows only that a single draw was acceptable, not how often wrong routes appear. Asking each question several times and setting pass rates on all runs measures the error rate wheelchair users will meet. More questions asked once widen coverage, which helps, but each still gets a single draw, so occasional unsafe routes can stay hidden.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because broader coverage finds more problems. But each question still gets one draw, so answers that fail only sometimes stay hidden.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because every answer passed. But each was a single draw from varying output; a repeat could give a wrong route.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because lower randomness cuts variation. But it is an untested setting change, and hosted models can still vary, so testing must measure it.

tips: Eliminate: B treats one pass as proof though answers vary, and C changes a setting without testing, while hosted models can still vary.
Final two: D beats A because repeated runs measure how often an answer fails; more questions asked once still sample each answer once.
Exam cue: for generative AI, acceptance tests should repeat each case and judge pass rates, because one run is one sample.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.1 (Test sets, metrics and TEVV tools documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.1 TEVV and Acceptance Criteria (varying output needs repeated test runs). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Testing the nurse with the tool
questions.question: A Bermudian hospital's emergency-triage model met its acceptance criteria when tested alone; in use, nurses will see its suggested level and decide. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST before go-live?

options.A: Retest the model alone on a larger set of past cases
options.B: Trial nurses deciding with the tool on realistic cases
options.C: Raise the pass mark to allow for nurses' own errors
options.D: Have nurses confirm in training that they understand the levels

questions.key_concept: When people decide with AI suggestions, testing should measure the combined human-AI decision, since deference can make it worse than either alone.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose decision reaches the patient, and whether that decision was ever tested.
questions.correct_explanation: What patients receive is the nurse's decision with the model's suggestion in view, and that pairing can be worse than either alone if nurses defer to wrong suggestions. Trialing nurses deciding with the tool on realistic cases measures the system that will run. Training nurses on what the levels mean is useful, but it is not evidence of how they decide when the suggestion is wrong.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because larger tests are more reliable. But they still test the model alone, not the decisions nurses make with it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it builds in a margin. But a stricter model test says nothing about how nurses respond to its suggestions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because understanding supports oversight. But a training sign-off does not show how nurses decide when a suggestion is wrong.

tips: Eliminate: A enlarges a model-only test, and C tightens the model's pass mark; neither measures decisions nurses make with the tool.
Final two: B beats D because only a realistic trial shows how nurses act on wrong suggestions; training shows what they know, not what they do.
Exam cue: when a person decides with AI advice, test the person and the model together in realistic conditions.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration)

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A lender's five fairness measures
questions.question: A Slovak mortgage lender's approval model passes two of five fairness measures across age groups and fails three; no record says which measures apply. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the model owner choose measures that fit the harm, with reasons
options.B: Require the model to pass the five measures before it is used
options.C: Report the model as fair, since it passes two of the measures
options.D: Report the model as unfair, since it fails most of the measures

questions.key_concept: When groups' base rates differ, fairness measures cannot all be met; the model owner chooses those that fit the harm and records why.
questions.pre_read: Ask who decided which fairness measures matter here, and on what basis.
questions.correct_explanation: Fairness measures can conflict: when groups' repayment rates differ, a model usually cannot meet them all at once. So the model owner, with legal and ethics input, must choose which measures fit the harm at stake, such as creditworthy older applicants wrongly declined, and record why before results are judged. Requiring all five sounds strict, but it may be impossible to meet and still leaves the harm undefined.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it sounds strictest. But fairness measures can conflict when groups differ, so no model may pass all five, and the harm that matters stays undefined.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because some measures pass. But counting passes means nothing until someone decides which measures fit the harm at stake.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because most measures fail. But a failed measure matters only if it fits the harm, and no one has yet chosen which measures do.

tips: Eliminate: C and D count passes and fails, which mean nothing until the model owner decides which measures fit the harm at stake.
Final two: A beats B because fairness measures can conflict, so passing all five may be impossible; the model owner chooses the measures that match the harm and records why.
Exam cue: when fairness results disagree, look for the owner's documented choice of measure tied to the harm, not a demand to pass every measure.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed)
