Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A job board's vacancy recommendations
questions.question: An Italian job board tested its vacancy-recommendation model for fairness by comparing click rates: women and men click recommended vacancies at equal rates. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the test, since women and men click at equal rates
options.B: Rerun the click-rate test on a larger, more recent sample
options.C: Compare pay levels of vacancies shown to women and men
options.D: Let users choose whether to see recommended vacancies

questions.key_concept: A recommender's fairness is tested on what it shows each group; click rates reflect responses to what was shown and can hide unequal exposure.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the model chose to show each group, not how users responded.
questions.correct_explanation: Click rates show how users respond to what they were shown, not what the model chose to show them. If women are shown fewer higher-paid vacancies, they can click at the same rate as men and still see worse jobs. Comparing the pay levels of vacancies shown to each group, against criteria the model owner set, tests the model's own decisions. A larger, newer click-rate sample repeats the measure that hides the gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because equal click rates look like equal treatment. But users can only click what they are shown, so the test misses differences in what each group sees.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a bigger, fresher sample makes a test more reliable. But it repeats a measure of user response, so differences in what the model shows each group stay hidden.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because choice respects users. But it says nothing about whether women and men are shown different vacancies.

tips: Eliminate: A reads equal click rates as equal treatment, and D offers users a choice, which shows nothing about who is shown which vacancies.
Final two: C beats B because the model's decision is what it shows; a larger click-rate sample measures user response more precisely, not what each group is shown.
Exam cue: for recommenders, test fairness on what the model shows each group, not on how users respond to what they were shown.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.1 (Test sets, metrics and TEVV tools documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.2 Fairness Testing Across Groups (a recommender's fairness is tested on what it shows each group, not on user click rates). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Validators rerunning the builders' code
questions.question: A Moroccan auto-finance company's validation unit, independent of the builders, reran the builders' code on the builders' test set for a car-loan model and matched every score. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the validation, as the unit is independent of the builders
options.B: Have IS audit rerun the code to confirm the validators' scores
options.C: Have validators also rerun training to confirm it is reproducible
options.D: Have validators challenge design choices using data they select

questions.key_concept: Independent validation challenges the builders' data, design and tests; rerunning their code on their test set only replicates their work.
questions.pre_read: List what in this validation came from the builders, not the validators.
questions.correct_explanation: Rerunning the builders' code on the builders' test set shows the code produces the reported scores, not that the model is sound. Any flaw in the data, design or test set is repeated faithfully. Independent validation must challenge those choices, with data and tests the validators select. Rerunning the training as well confirms reproducibility, which is useful, but it is still replication of the builders' own work.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the unit's independence is genuine. But independent people add little when every input to the work came from the builders.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reperformance is an audit technique. But it repeats the same replication and moves IS audit toward doing the validation.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reproducible training is good evidence. But it still replays the builders' choices instead of challenging them.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts work whose every input came from the builders, and B has IS audit repeat the replication, edging into validating the model itself.
Final two: D beats C because validation must challenge the builders' data and design; reproducing their training confirms it runs, not that it is sound.
Exam cue: validators using only the builders' code and test set give replication, not challenge; look for the validators' own data and tests.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.3 (Independent assessors not on the front-line development team); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.13 (Effectiveness of TEVV metrics and processes evaluated)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.3 Independent Validation, Robustness and Red Teaming (independent validation challenges, not replicates). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Open findings at launch
questions.question: A Jamaican lottery operator's red team found three high-severity jailbreaks in its player chatbot that remain open; the red team lead says it passes for launch anyway. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the red team lead's view, as they know the findings best
options.B: Have the model owner decide on launch with the open findings
options.C: Have the IS auditor judge whether the open findings are acceptable
options.D: Launch once a filter blocks the three jailbreak prompts

questions.key_concept: Red teams report findings; the model owner decides on launch within tolerance, since blocking known jailbreak prompts does not remove the weakness.
questions.pre_read: Ask who in this story is allowed to accept the remaining risk.
questions.correct_explanation: A red team tests and reports; it does not decide whether residual risk is acceptable. The model owner, within senior management's tolerance, decides on launch with the three open findings in view and can require fixes or limits first; management formally accepts any findings left open. Blocking the three known prompts looks like closure, but reworded jailbreaks often pass such filters, and the launch decision would still have no owner.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the red team knows the findings best. But testers assess and report; the model owner decides on launch, and management accepts any findings left open.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because IS auditors are independent. But deciding whether the risk is acceptable is the model owner's call; the IS auditor reports and follows up.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it closes the three findings quickly. But reworded jailbreaks often pass a filter built on known prompts, and no one has decided whether the remaining risk is acceptable.

tips: Eliminate: A lets the testers accept the risk they found, and C has the IS auditor judge acceptability, which is a management decision.
Final two: B beats D because a filter on three known prompts leaves reworded jailbreaks open; the model owner decides on launch, within tolerance, with that risk in view.
Exam cue: testers and IS auditors report findings; the accountable owner decides whether residual AI risk is acceptable.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.1 (Decide whether the system meets its purpose and should proceed); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.4 (Negative residual risks documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.3 Independent Validation, Robustness and Red Teaming (red teams report; the owner decides on residual risk). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A tiny share of bot clicks
questions.question: A Vietnamese used-car listings site's search-ranking model trains on 5 million clicks; analysts found 2,000 from bot accounts favoring one seller, and the team says 0.04% cannot matter. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: A small targeted share can still lift that seller's ranking
options.B: Overall ranking accuracy may fall below the team's tolerance
options.C: The bot accounts may be copying the ranking model through queries
options.D: Bot clicks may inflate that seller's reported engagement figures

questions.key_concept: Targeted poisoning can shift outcomes for chosen items with a tiny share of training data while overall accuracy stays normal.
questions.pre_read: When a figure is offered as reassurance, ask what it measures and what it leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: Targeted poisoning does not need a large share of the data. Clicks concentrated on one seller can move that seller's ranking for the queries attacked, while the model's overall accuracy barely changes. That is why a falling overall score is the wrong thing to watch. The team's 0.04% figure measures the attack against all clicks, not against the clicks for the queries it targets.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because accuracy is the usual health check. But targeted poisoning leaves overall accuracy almost unchanged while shifting results for chosen items.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because bots that query a model can help copy it. But these clicks were fed into training; the risk is what the model learned from them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because bot traffic distorts the seller's listing statistics. But reported engagement figures do not move rankings; the risk is the ranking lift the poisoned training clicks give.

tips: Eliminate: C mistakes the attack for model copying, though these clicks fed the model's training, and D worries about engagement reports, which do not set rankings.
Final two: A beats B because targeted poisoning moves chosen results while overall accuracy stays normal; a small share can be decisive for one seller.
Exam cue: judge poisoning by its share of the targeted slice, not of the whole dataset; overall metrics can hide it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.3.2 (Targeted Poisoning); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0020 (Poison Training Data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.1 Attacks on Data and Models (targeted poisoning needs only a small share of data). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. An offline model reading suppliers' invoices
questions.question: A Bahraini aluminum smelter's IT team says its invoice-approval model needs no AI threat model, having no internet access; suppliers' invoices reach it by email. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept IT's view, since no outsider can reach the model
options.B: Limit access to the model's files to its data scientists
options.C: Assess how crafted invoices could pass its checks
options.D: Require suppliers to submit invoices through a web portal

questions.key_concept: A model with no internet access can still be evaded through the inputs outsiders write; network position does not remove AI threats.
questions.pre_read: Ask who writes what this model reads.
questions.correct_explanation: Network isolation does not stop attacks that arrive as ordinary inputs. Suppliers write the invoices this model reads, so they can adjust wording, layout or amounts until it approves what it should not, and no network control sees it. Assessing how crafted invoices could pass the checks puts that path in the threat model. Limiting file access to data scientists guards against insider copying, but leaves the stated supplier path unassessed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because isolation blocks network attacks. But invoices reach the model by design, so suppliers can shape what it reads without any network access.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because insiders could copy the model. But nothing points to insiders, while suppliers write every invoice the model reads.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a portal seems more controlled than email. But the channel does not change what suppliers write, so crafted invoices still reach the model.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts network isolation though invoices reach the model by design, and D changes the delivery channel, not what suppliers write.
Final two: C beats B because the stated fact is that suppliers write the model's inputs; insider copying is real, but nothing here points to it.
Exam cue: an offline model still needs a threat model; ask who can shape the inputs it reads or the data it learns from.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.2 (Evasion Attacks and Mitigations); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0015 (Evade AI Model)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.1 Attacks on Data and Models (an internal model can be evaded through inputs outsiders write). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Data sent out in an image link
questions.question: A Danish software firm's support assistant can show web images in its replies; a tester's ticket made it send customers' details out inside an image link. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Tell the assistant in its prompt to disregard ticket instructions
options.B: Block replies from loading images or links from unapproved sites
options.C: Filter image links in replies to strip customer names
options.D: Scan incoming tickets for malware before the assistant reads them

questions.key_concept: Injected instructions can make an assistant leak data through links or images it renders; block untrusted outbound loads outside the model.
questions.pre_read: Trace how the data left the firm when the reply was displayed.
questions.correct_explanation: The attack hides instructions in a ticket, and the assistant obeys by building an image link that carries data; when the reply loads the image, the data leaves. Blocking replies from loading images or links from unapproved sites closes that channel whatever the injected text says. Filtering out customer names catches one kind of data, but addresses, order numbers or encoded text still pass.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it addresses the injected instructions. But text in a ticket can override a prompt rule; the model cannot be relied on to police itself.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it removes the most obvious personal data. But other details, or data encoded in the link, still leave; filtering outputs does not close the channel.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tickets are untrusted. But the instructions are plain text, which malware scanning does not flag.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a prompt rule that injected text can override, and D scans for malware, which plain-text instructions do not contain.
Final two: B beats C because closing the outbound channel stops any data leaving; a name filter catches one data type and misses encoded details.
Exam cue: when injected text can make an assistant send data out, look for limits on what replies can fetch or link to, enforced outside the model.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.4 (Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks and Mitigations); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0077 (LLM Response Rendering)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.2 Prompt Injection and Jailbreaks (injected text can exfiltrate data through rendered links). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Rights kept behind an injection filter
questions.question: A Portuguese energy retailer's customer agent can change customers' tariffs; IT says its new prompt-injection filter blocks 97% of known attacks, so the agent keeps those rights. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: New attack wording can slip past and change tariffs
options.B: The filter may block genuine requests to change tariffs
options.C: The filter adds a delay to every customer conversation
options.D: Blocked attacks may not be logged for the security team

questions.key_concept: Prompt-injection filters miss new attack wording, so an agent's powerful rights must be limited outside the model, not left behind a filter.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the missed 3%, and next month's new attacks, could do with the agent's rights.
questions.correct_explanation: Injection filters learn from attacks already seen, and attackers reword until one gets through, so 97% of known attacks says little about new ones. Because the agent keeps the right to change tariffs, any attack that slips past can change real customers' contracts. False blocks of genuine requests are a real cost, but they inconvenience customers, while a missed attack changes what they pay.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because false blocks frustrate customers. But a blocked request can be retried or escalated; an attack that gets through changes contracts.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because added delay affects service. But it is a performance cost, not a failure of the control protecting tariffs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because blocked attempts help spot campaigns. But logging gaps weaken detection; the greater risk is an attack the filter misses changing real tariffs.

tips: Eliminate: C is a latency cost and D a logging gap for attacks already stopped; neither concerns whether a missed attack can change tariffs.
Final two: A beats B because a missed attack changes what customers pay, while a false block is an inconvenience; the agent's standing rights make the misses costly.
Exam cue: a detection filter is probabilistic; when an agent keeps powerful rights behind it, ask what happens on the attack it misses.
questions.framework_ref: MITRE ATLAS AML.T0051 (LLM Prompt Injection); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.5 (Security of Agents)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.2 Prompt Injection and Jailbreaks (a probabilistic filter does not bound an agent's rights). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. An agent acting for any employee
questions.question: A Philippine outsourcing firm's HR agent, running under an administrator account, updates bank details for any employee who asks, on whichever record they name. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Tell the agent in its prompt to change just the asker's record
options.B: Review a log of the agent's bank-detail changes each month
options.C: Move the agent to a dedicated service account with HR rights
options.D: Limit each request to the rights of the employee asking

questions.key_concept: An agent acting for users should carry the requesting user's rights; a broad account lets anyone act through it on others' records.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose permissions the agent uses when an employee names someone else's record.
questions.correct_explanation: The agent uses an administrator's rights for whoever asks, so any employee can redirect a colleague's pay by naming their record. Limiting each request to the asking employee's own rights means the system, not the model, refuses changes to other records. A monthly review of bank-detail changes would detect misuse, but only after a salary has gone to the wrong account.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it states the rule clearly. But a prompt instruction can be talked around; the administrator rights still allow any change.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it creates oversight. But review comes after payday, so diverted salaries may already be lost.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because agents should have their own identity. But a dedicated account with the same HR rights still changes anyone's record on request.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a prompt rule the agent can be talked out of, and C gives the agent its own identity while keeping rights to change anyone's record.
Final two: D beats B because enforcing the asker's own rights prevents the change; a monthly review finds it after the money moves.
Exam cue: an agent acting for users should carry each user's rights, not a broad account that lets any user act through it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM06 (Excessive Agency)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.3 Excessive Agency and Access Management for AI (an agent acts with the requesting user's rights). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Approvals clicked by reflex
questions.question: A Romanian software house's coding agent asks developers to approve each command; logs show 99.8% approved within two seconds, including one that deleted a production database. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Train developers to read each command before approving it
options.B: Block destructive commands by policy, outside the approval prompt
options.C: Remove the approval step, since developers approve almost everything
options.D: Ask the agent to explain each command before it is approved

questions.key_concept: High-volume approval prompts for agent actions breed approval fatigue; destructive actions need hard limits enforced outside the model and the click.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the approval step actually checks at 99.8% within two seconds.
questions.correct_explanation: Approving hundreds of prompts a day trains people to click yes, so the approval step no longer checks anything; the deleted production database shows it. Blocking destructive commands by a policy the agent cannot override holds even when approval becomes a reflex. Training developers to read commands raises awareness, but the volume that caused the fatigue remains, so reflexive approvals continue.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because careful reading would catch bad commands. But the volume of prompts drives the fatigue, and training does not reduce it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the step adds little now. But removing it lets the agent run any command with no check.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because explanations seem to aid review. But they add more text to skim and come from the same model issuing the command.

tips: Eliminate: C removes the only check on the agent's commands, and D asks the same model to explain itself, adding text to an approval already given by reflex.
Final two: B beats A because a policy block holds when approvals become reflexive; training leaves the prompt volume that caused the fatigue.
Exam cue: when people approve agent actions at high volume, expect rubber-stamping; put hard limits on high-impact actions outside the approval click.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.5 (Security of Agents); OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM06 (Excessive Agency)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.3 Excessive Agency and Access Management for AI (approval prompts at volume become rubber stamps). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A merchant's report about a chatbot
questions.question: A Mexican payment processor's chatbot told a merchant to email card numbers; staff asked it the same question ten times, got safe answers and closed the report. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep it closed, as ten retries could not reproduce the reply
options.B: Add a prompt rule barring the chatbot from asking for card data
options.C: Reopen it, pull the logged chat and triage it by harm
options.D: Ask the merchant for proof that the reply was not altered

questions.key_concept: Generated replies vary run to run, so a failed retry does not disprove a reported AI failure; check the logged conversation and triage by harm.
questions.pre_read: Ask what record shows what the merchant was actually told.
questions.correct_explanation: A chatbot's replies vary from run to run, so ten safe retries show only that the unsafe reply is not the usual one, not that it never happened. The logged conversation shows what the merchant was actually told, and triage by harm sets the response: emailed card numbers expose customers to fraud. Asking the merchant for proof puts the burden on the reporter when the processor's own log can settle it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a fault that cannot be repeated looks like a false report. But generated replies vary, so ten safe retries cannot show the unsafe one never happened.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it targets the unsafe advice. But a prompt rule may not hold, and fixing without triage leaves the harm to this merchant unassessed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because screenshots can be edited. But the processor's own chat log shows what was said; the burden should not fall on the reporter.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a failed retry as proof, though generated replies vary, and B adds a prompt rule without assessing the harm already done.
Final two: C beats D because the processor's own log shows what the chatbot said; asking the merchant for proof delays triage of a possible fraud exposure.
Exam cue: generated output varies run to run, so 'could not reproduce' does not close an AI incident; check the logs and triage by harm.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.3 (Incidents and errors communicated and tracked); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2G.1 Recognizing and Triaging AI Incidents (generated replies vary run to run, so a failed retry does not close a reported AI failure; check the logs and triage by harm). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Records sent by a writing extension
questions.question: A Jordanian dental group's receptionist ran 300 patients' records through a free AI writing extension whose provider trains on inputs; IT says uninstalling it ended the exposure. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Handle it as a data-leak incident, triaged by harm
options.B: Get the provider's written confirmation it deleted the records
options.C: Block the extension on the clinic's computers
options.D: Accept IT's view, since the extension is now uninstalled

questions.key_concept: Data sent to an outside AI service outlives uninstalling the tool that sent it, so the upload is a data-leak incident to triage by harm.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the 300 records are now, and who can use them.
questions.correct_explanation: Uninstalling the extension stops new uploads, not what the provider already received; because it trains on inputs, the records may already be in its model. Handling it as an incident, triaged by harm to the 300 patients, drives a privacy review, any notifications and a deletion request. A deletion confirmation covers stored copies, not what the provider's model may already have learned from them.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because confirmation seems to prove the data is gone. But the provider trains on inputs, so deleting stored copies may not remove what its model learned.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it stops repeats. But the 300 records have already left, and blocking does nothing to assess or reduce harm to those patients.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the extension is gone. But the provider may still hold the records, so the patients' exposure is unassessed.

tips: Eliminate: C blocks future use but does nothing for the 300 records already sent, and D trusts the uninstall, though the provider may still hold the records.
Final two: A beats B because the provider trains on what it receives; a deletion confirmation covers stored copies, not what its model may already have learned.
Exam cue: removing an AI tool does not recall data it already sent to its provider; treat the upload as a data-leak incident and triage it by harm.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy)

Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A self-updating model after rollback
questions.question: A Kazakh grain elevator rolled back its grain-drying model, which updates itself from live humidity readings, after faulty sensors skewed its settings; the sensors are still faulty. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Let the rolled-back model run, as it was known to be good
options.B: Retrain tonight on clean data from the previous month
options.C: Replace the faulty sensors as soon as parts arrive
options.D: Stop the model's learning until the readings are checked

questions.key_concept: A model that learns from live data relearns a fault after rollback unless its learning is stopped; containment covers learning, not just the version.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the rolled-back model keeps learning from while the sensors stay faulty.
questions.correct_explanation: Rollback restored a good version, but this model keeps learning from live readings, so the restored version will relearn the fault from the same faulty sensors. Stopping its learning is the first containment step, and keeping the suspect readings intact supports root cause analysis. Replacing the sensors fixes the source, but until parts arrive the model keeps learning from bad readings.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the live model is good again. But it keeps learning from the faulty readings, so it will drift back to the fault.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because clean data avoids the bad readings. But an unplanned retrain before root cause is an untested change made under pressure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it fixes the cause. But until the sensors are replaced, the self-updating model keeps learning from bad readings.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts a rollback while the model keeps learning from faulty readings, and B rushes an untested retrain before the cause is known.
Final two: D beats C because the model learns from faulty readings until the sensors are replaced; stopping its learning contains the fault now.
Exam cue: a model that learns in production is not contained by rollback alone; stop its learning until its inputs are trusted.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2G.2 Containment: Disengage, Roll Back and Preserve Evidence (containment covers the retraining pipeline). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Loss-making bids from a live model
questions.question: A German energy trader's power-bidding model began placing loss-making bids, each live within seconds; its team wants it kept running a week to study the fault. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep it live, with traders checking each bid before it applies
options.B: Disengage it and study it in shadow mode on live inputs
options.C: Keep it live for the week under a daily loss limit
options.D: Retrain it tonight on last month's bids and redeploy

questions.key_concept: Studying an AI fault does not require leaving it live; shadow mode on real inputs shows the fault while a fallback stops the harm.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the team needs the bids to take effect to learn why they are wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: Each faulty bid becomes a real loss within seconds, so harm continues as long as the model is live. Disengaging it, with the previous version or traders bidding, stops the losses, while running it in shadow mode on live inputs still shows the team exactly how the fault behaves. A daily loss limit caps the damage, but it still accepts a week of real losses to learn what shadow mode shows without them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it keeps a person in the loop. But bids take effect within seconds, too fast for traders to check each one.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it bounds the harm. But it still accepts a week of real losses to learn what shadow mode shows without them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it acts quickly. But retraining before root cause is an untested change and may repeat the fault.

tips: Eliminate: A asks traders to check bids that take effect in seconds, and D retrains before the cause is known, an untested change under pressure.
Final two: B beats C because shadow mode stops the harm and still shows the fault; a loss limit keeps the harm running, only capped.
Exam cue: a harmful AI rarely needs to stay live to be studied; disengage it and observe it in shadow mode on real inputs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.3 (Procedures to respond to and recover from previously unknown risks)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2G.2 Containment: Disengage, Roll Back and Preserve Evidence (disengage first; study the fault in shadow mode). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Porter ratings and a route model
questions.question: Belgian hospital managers rate porters by a route-planning model's time estimates, a purpose never assessed; after porters complained of bias, the data team plans a retrain. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain the model as planned to reduce bias in its estimates
options.B: Add a disclaimer that estimates are not for rating staff
options.C: Have managers adjust ratings for porters on slower routes
options.D: Record the unapproved use as the root cause and halt it

questions.key_concept: When a model fails in a use it was never built or validated for, the root cause is the unapproved use, not the model.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the model was built and validated to do.
questions.correct_explanation: The model was built and validated to plan routes, not to judge people, so the failure began when managers used it for a purpose never assessed or approved. The root cause is that unapproved use, and the fix is to halt it and route any new use through assessment. A disclaimer states the limit but leaves managers able to keep rating porters with the model, so the cause stays in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because porters complained of bias. But the model was never built to rate people; retraining it treats a misuse as a model defect.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it states the limit. But a disclaimer does not stop managers rating porters with the model; the cause stays.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it softens the harm to porters. But it patches each rating while keeping a use no one validated.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains a model whose fault is how it was used, and C patches ratings while keeping the unvalidated use.
Final two: D beats B because the cause is a use no one approved; a disclaimer leaves that use running.
Exam cue: before treating a complaint as a model defect, check whether the model was being used for its validated purpose.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 RS.AN-03 (Root cause of the incident established); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.3 (Targeted application scope specified)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2G.3 Root Cause, Problem Management and Reporting (use beyond the validated purpose is the root cause). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A jailbreak fixed and forgotten
questions.question: An Ecuadorian bank closed the problem record for its chatbot's loan-fraud jailbreak after root cause was found and the fix held against reworded attacks in production. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Reopen the record until the model itself is retrained
options.B: Publish the jailbreak prompts so staff can recognize them
options.C: Add the attack prompts to tests rerun after every change
options.D: Pin the model version so the fix cannot be undone

questions.key_concept: AI incident fixes can be undone by later prompt, filter or model changes, so the incident's cases belong in regression tests.
questions.pre_read: Ask what would show, after next month's update, that the fix still holds.
questions.correct_explanation: The verified fix stops this attack today, but later prompt edits, filter changes or vendor model updates can quietly undo it. Adding the attack prompts to the tests rerun after every change turns the incident into lasting protection, catching a reopened gap before release. Pinning the model version blocks one source of change, but the bank's own prompt and filter edits can still reopen the gap, and a pin tests nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because deliberate attacks stay open until the cause is removed. But the fix removed the cause and held against reworded attacks in production; retraining is a larger, riskier change.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because awareness helps staff. But publishing working jailbreaks spreads the attack and does not protect future versions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendor updates can undo fixes. But the bank's own prompt and filter edits, and vendor-side changes behind a pin, can still reopen the gap; a pin tests nothing.

tips: Eliminate: A holds the record open for a retrain the verified fix does not need, and B spreads working jailbreak prompts more widely.
Final two: C beats D because a pin freezes only the model's weights; the bank's own prompt and filter edits can still reopen the gap, and only rerun tests show it.
Exam cue: lessons from AI incidents should become regression tests, because later prompt, filter or model changes can reopen the same gap.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.2 (Continual improvement integrated into AI system updates); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.IM-01 (Improvements identified from evaluations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2G.3 Root Cause, Problem Management and Reporting (incident cases become regression tests). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. A vendor score used as an input
questions.question: A Peruvian car insurer prices policies partly on a vendor's driving-risk score, which the vendor retrains at will without saying what data it uses. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Premiums may absorb the score's unknown biases and silent changes
options.B: Drivers may not know a vendor score helps set their premiums
options.C: The vendor may raise the score's price at contract renewal
options.D: The score may duplicate inputs the pricing model already uses

questions.key_concept: A feature produced by another organization's model brings that model's data, bias and changes into every decision it feeds.
questions.pre_read: Ask what you would need to know about an input before trusting decisions built on it.
questions.correct_explanation: The score is itself a model's output, so its errors, biases and retraining flow straight into premiums, and the insurer cannot see or test them without lineage and notice of changes. Unknown inputs also make premiums hard to explain. Telling drivers about the score matters, but disclosure does not reveal what the score contains or when it changes.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because people should know what sets their price. But disclosure does not show what drives the score or when the vendor changes it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because cost matters in vendor deals. But a price rise is a commercial issue, not a risk to the fairness or accuracy of premiums.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because redundant inputs add little. But duplication wastes effort; it does not carry hidden bias or unannounced changes into prices.

tips: Eliminate: C is a commercial matter for procurement, and D is an efficiency point; neither touches how premiums are set.
Final two: A beats B because a score made by another model carries that model's data, bias and retraining into each premium; telling drivers reveals none of it.
Exam cue: when one model's output feeds another, treat it as a data source needing lineage, an owner and notice of changes, like any training feed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 4.1 (Legal and technology risks of components including third-party data mapped); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SR-4 (Provenance)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A.1 Data Provenance, Lineage and Rights to Use (a feature produced by another organization's model needs lineage and notice of changes). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Copied partner web pages
questions.question: A Tanzanian tour operator's assistant quotes lodge rates from partner web pages saved at unknown times; lodges change rates often. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Fine-tune the assistant on the lodges' current rate sheets
options.B: Add a notice that copied pages may show outdated rates
options.C: Recopy pages on a schedule, recording each copy's source and date
options.D: Have staff confirm each quoted rate with the lodge before every booking

questions.key_concept: Retrieval content needs lineage: the source and capture date of each item, with scheduled refresh, so answers stay current and traceable.
questions.pre_read: Ask what decides how current each answer can be.
questions.correct_explanation: Answers are only as current as the saved pages, and without capture dates no one can tell which rates are stale or trace a wrong quote to its source. Recopying on a schedule and recording each copy's source and date keeps the library current and traceable. Staff checks of each quote catch stale rates, but only as a manual step on every booking, while the undated library keeps feeding stale rates into every other answer.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tuning teaches the model the rates. But tuned-in rates go stale just as copies do, and are harder to update or trace.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it warns customers. But a notice leaves wrong rates in every answer and does nothing to refresh the stale pages.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a call to the lodge confirms each rate. But it is a manual check on every booking, while the library stays stale, undated and untraceable for other answers.

tips: Eliminate: A tunes rates into the model, where they also go stale, and B warns customers while the stale pages stay in use.
Final two: C beats D because refreshing dated copies fixes the source for every answer; checking each quote by hand catches staleness case by case and leaves the library untraceable.
Exam cue: a retrieval library is data. Ask where each item came from, when it was captured and who keeps it current.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 4.1 (Legal and technology risks of components including third-party data mapped); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-07 (Inventories of data and metadata maintained)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A.1 Data Provenance, Lineage and Rights to Use (retrieval content needs a recorded source and capture date, and scheduled refresh). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. A quality filter tested only on English
questions.question: A Welsh broadcaster will clean its moderation model's training posts, a third of them in Welsh, with a vendor's quality filter validated only on English text. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Use the filter as supplied, since the vendor validated it
options.B: Test what the filter removes from Welsh and English posts first
options.C: Translate the Welsh posts into English before filtering them
options.D: Skip the filter for Welsh posts and keep every one of them

questions.key_concept: An AI filter used to clean training data is itself a model; test what it removes, by group, before relying on it.
questions.pre_read: Ask who the cleaning step could leave out, not just how clean the data looks.
questions.correct_explanation: A quality filter learns what good text looks like from its own training data, so one validated only on English may score Welsh posts as poor and strip them out, leaving the model weak on a third of its comments. Testing what it removes from each language first shows whether it can be trusted. Keeping every Welsh post unfiltered avoids that loss but leaves Welsh spam in the data and the filter untested.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor validated its filter. But that validation covered English only; its effect on Welsh posts is unknown.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the filter was validated on English. But translations lose how Welsh speakers really write, and the model must moderate real Welsh comments.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it protects Welsh posts. But Welsh spam and junk then stay in the training data, and the filter's behavior stays untested.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on validation that never covered Welsh, and C trains on translations instead of real Welsh comments.
Final two: B beats D because testing removals by language shows whether the filter can be trusted on both; skipping it for Welsh keeps the posts but leaves Welsh junk in and the filter untested.
Exam cue: an AI filter used to clean training data is itself a model. Check what it removes, by group, before relying on it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.6 (Harmful Bias and Homogenization)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A.2 Data Quality, Labeling and Representativeness (an AI quality filter can strip out a language group; test what it removes by group before use). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Labels that wait for chargebacks
questions.question: A Hungarian online electronics store retrains its payment-fraud model weekly; orders are labeled genuine unless a chargeback arrives, which can take up to 90 days. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Weekly retraining may be too frequent for proper change review
options.B: Chargeback data may arrive in formats the pipeline cannot read
options.C: Fraudsters may pose as genuine buyers to learn the model's limits
options.D: The model may learn to treat recent fraud as genuine

questions.key_concept: Labels that mature late make recent records look like the default class, so frequent retraining can teach the model to miss new fraud.
questions.pre_read: Ask how true each label is on the day the model trains on it.
questions.correct_explanation: Labels for recent orders are not final: any fraud still waiting for its chargeback is recorded as genuine, and weekly retraining teaches the model that pattern, so it learns to pass the newest fraud. Probing by fraudsters is a real threat to fraud models, but nothing in the facts points to it, while the labeling rule mislabels recent fraud every week.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because frequent retrains need control. But cadence is a process question; the labels feeding each retrain are the risk the facts point to.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because data feeds can break. But nothing suggests a format problem; the issue is what the labels say, not whether they load.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fraud models do get probed. But nothing in the facts suggests probing; the labeling rule mislabels recent fraud in every retrain.

tips: Eliminate: A is about change-review cadence and B about data formats; the facts point to neither, only to how labels are set.
Final two: D beats C because the labeling rule marks unconfirmed fraud as genuine in every weekly retrain; probing is a real risk, but the facts never point to it.
Exam cue: when labels arrive late, recent records look like the default class. Ask whether training waits for labels to mature.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A.2 Data Quality, Labeling and Representativeness (labels that mature late teach a frequently retrained model the wrong class). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Weights corrected after the sale
questions.question: A Faroese fish auction's price model was trained and tested on landing weights corrected weeks after each sale; live predictions use the uncorrected weights. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The corrected weights may themselves contain errors no one reviewed
options.B: Test results may overstate how well it predicts at sale time
options.C: Delayed corrections may make the model too slow to retrain
options.D: Predictions may drift as fish stocks and buyer demand change

questions.key_concept: A model tested on cleaner data than it receives live, such as values corrected later, shows scores that overstate live performance.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the model saw in testing with what it will see when it predicts.
questions.correct_explanation: The model was tested on information that did not exist when a price is predicted, so its test score reflects corrected data and overstates how it performs on the rougher weights it sees live. Testing must use data as known at prediction time. Drift is a real ongoing risk, but nothing here suggests it; the mismatch between test and live inputs exists from day one.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because corrections can be wrong. But nothing suggests the corrections are poor; the issue is that live predictions never see them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because data delays slow pipelines. But retraining speed is not the risk; the test measured inputs the live model does not get.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because markets change. But no shift is described; the test overstates performance from the first live prediction.

tips: Eliminate: A doubts corrections nothing suggests are poor, and C worries about retraining speed rather than what the test measured.
Final two: B beats D because the test used weights known only later, so its score overstates live accuracy from day one; drift is a real risk the facts never raise.
Exam cue: test with data as it is known at prediction time; test data cleaner than live inputs overstates live accuracy.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A.3 Training, Validation and Test Separation (testing on data corrected after prediction time overstates live performance). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Prompt examples from the test set
questions.question: A Uruguayan beef exporter's export-rules assistant scored 94% on its 300-question test set; the 40 worked examples in its prompt were copied from that set. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The score partly reflects answers it already holds in its prompt
options.B: The test questions may not match what staff really ask
options.C: The long prompt may slow answers during busy shipping weeks
options.D: Forty examples may be too few to teach it the rules

questions.key_concept: Test questions copied into a prompt as worked examples are no longer unseen, so scores on them overstate performance on new questions.
questions.pre_read: Ask what must be true of a test set for its score to predict live use.
questions.correct_explanation: Forty of the 300 test questions sit in the prompt with their answers, so the assistant can repeat them, and the 94% partly measures recall, not performance on new questions. Scores must come from questions kept out of the prompt. Whether the questions reflect what staff really ask matters too, but nothing suggests they do not; the copying inflates the score now.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because test sets should mirror real use. But nothing suggests the questions are unrealistic; the copied examples inflate the score whatever the questions are.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because long prompts add delay. But speed is an operations matter; the risk is a score that overstates how well the assistant answers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because more examples can help. But prompt examples mainly shape answers; the issue is that test answers sit in the prompt.

tips: Eliminate: C is a speed issue, and D treats prompt examples as how the assistant learns rules; neither touches what the score measures.
Final two: A beats B because 40 test answers sit in the prompt and inflate the score now; whether the questions are realistic is a real issue the facts never raise.
Exam cue: anything a model is shown before testing, prompt examples included, must stay out of the test set, or the score measures recall.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.1 (Test sets, metrics and TEVV tools documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A.3 Training, Validation and Test Separation (test questions copied into a prompt as examples are no longer unseen). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A model that updates itself
questions.question: A Moroccan solar plant's panel-cleaning model updates itself daily from live output data; its lifecycle has one validation gate, passed at launch two years ago. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Daily updates may overload the plant's change advisory board
options.B: Live output data may hold personal data about plant staff
options.C: Today's model may no longer behave like the validated one
options.D: The launch validation may not have covered the sandstorm seasons

questions.key_concept: A self-updating model moves away from what was validated; the lifecycle must bound its updates and revalidate it periodically.
questions.pre_read: Ask what evidence exists for each stage of this model's life since launch.
questions.correct_explanation: A model that retrains itself daily is a different model each day, so a gate passed two years ago says little about today's version. The lifecycle needs limits on self-updates, monitoring and periodic revalidation. Gaps in launch coverage matter, but they describe a model that no longer runs; even complete launch testing would not cover today's behavior.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI changes need control. But the facts point to a model that changes daily with no fresh validation, not to the change advisory board's workload.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because data protection matters. But solar output readings are equipment data; nothing suggests personal data in them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because launch tests can miss seasons. But even complete launch testing covered a model that has since rewritten itself hundreds of times.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about the change advisory board's workload, which the facts never raise, and B finds personal data in equipment readings.
Final two: C beats D because after two years of daily self-updates the validated model no longer exists; better launch coverage would still describe an old version.
Exam cue: a model that learns in production needs bounded updates, monitoring and revalidation, not just a launch gate.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.1 (Post-deployment monitoring including appeal, override, incident response and change management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B.1 The AI Lifecycle and Stage Gates (a model that updates itself in production needs bounded updates and revalidation). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A pilot that grew into production
questions.question: A Croatian national park's visitor-numbers model, piloted at one entrance one summer, now sets ranger shifts at all nine entrances year-round, with no code change or review since. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The unchanged code was not retested before the wider rollout
options.B: Rangers may stop questioning the shift plans the model produces
options.C: The pilot's approval was not extended in writing to the other entrances
options.D: Its forecasts for other entrances and seasons are untested

questions.key_concept: A pilot's results cover only the places and seasons it ran in; an unchanged model facing new conditions still has no evidence there.
questions.pre_read: For each option, ask what it would do to the shift plans rangers actually work.
questions.correct_explanation: The pilot showed how the model forecasts at one entrance in one summer; other entrances and the winter months can bring different visitor patterns, so ranger shifts now rest on forecasts nobody has checked. Unchanged code proves nothing here, because a model's behavior depends on the data it meets. A written approval would record the wider rollout, but it would add no evidence that the forecasts hold beyond the pilot.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retesting is a normal release step. But the code is unchanged; what nobody has checked is how the model forecasts in places and seasons the pilot never covered.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because automation bias is a real AI risk. But nothing shows rangers defer to the plans; the known gap is forecasts never checked beyond one summer entrance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because extending an approval is a normal control. But a signature on the wider use adds no evidence that the model forecasts well beyond the pilot.

tips: Eliminate: A retests code that never changed, and B worries about deference to the plans when nothing shows rangers defer to them.
Final two: D beats C because the shifts rest on forecasts never checked beyond one summer entrance; a written approval records the rollout but adds no evidence.
Exam cue: an unchanged model in new places or seasons is untested there. Ask which conditions its pilot actually covered.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.1 (Intended purposes, context and laws documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B.1 The AI Lifecycle and Stage Gates (a pilot's evidence covers only the places and seasons it ran in, even with the code unchanged). Completeness round 1, 5 Nov 2026: re-angled from a recommend-the-deployment-gate frame (too close to aaia_d2_026) to the GREATEST concern, where the pilot's data coverage decides. Completeness round 2, 5 Nov 2026: stem states no review since the pilot; explanations claim only the pilot's coverage, not its training data. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Contract terms for a bought scoring model
questions.question: A Lithuanian export-control agency's draft contract for a vendor's hosted export-risk model, retrained monthly, covers uptime and data security; refused exporters may appeal within a year. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add a right to audit the vendor's data centers and access controls
options.B: Require version logs and vendor analysis for challenged results
options.C: Require the vendor to insure the agency against wrong scores
options.D: Have the IS auditor draft the contract's AI clauses

questions.key_concept: A contract for a bought model must let the buyer trace and explain past scores, since the vendor holds the version and settings.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each contract term would let the agency do in practice.
questions.correct_explanation: An exporter may appeal a refusal months later, after monthly retraining has replaced the model that scored it. Only the vendor holds that version and its settings, so terms requiring version logs and vendor analysis for challenged results make each past score traceable. A right to audit data centers and access controls checks security, which the contract already covers; it cannot show why one score was given.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because audit rights are a standard vendor term. But the contract already covers security, and data centers cannot show why a since-retrained model scored one exporter as it did.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it covers losses from wrong scores. But insurance moves cost, not accountability; the agency still cannot explain a disputed score.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IS auditor knows the risks. But drafting contract terms is management's job; the IS auditor recommends and later assesses them.

tips: Eliminate: C moves the cost of wrong scores but explains none, and D has the IS auditor drafting terms that management owns.

Final two: B beats A because monthly retraining replaces the model that scored an appealed case, so only vendor version records can trace it; data center audits check security the contract already covers.
Exam cue: for a bought model that is retrained, check that the contract lets you trace and explain a past decision, not only that the service is up and secure.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.9 (Model explained, validated and documented, output interpreted in context)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B.2 Model Documentation and Build, Buy or Tune (contracts for bought models should require documentation and cooperation, so past scores can be traced). Final review round: stem gives monthly retraining and a one-year appeal window instead of naming the gap. Final fix round: stem says the model is vendor-hosted, supporting that only the vendor holds past versions, inputs and settings. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Safety results copied from the base model
questions.question: A Thai airline fine-tuned a vendor's chat model on 8,000 baggage-claim chats; its model card copies the vendor's safety test results for the base model. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Safety-test the tuned model itself before releasing it
options.B: Ask the vendor to confirm its safety results still apply after tuning
options.C: Rely on the vendor's results, since the claim chats were harmless
options.D: Record the base model's version beside the copied results

questions.key_concept: Fine-tuning can weaken a base model's safety behavior, so a tuned model needs its own safety testing before release.
questions.pre_read: Ask which model each result in the card was actually measured on.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning changes the model's weights, and studies show even harmless tuning data can weaken a base model's safety behavior. The copied results describe a model the airline does not run, so the tuned model needs its own safety testing before release. Recording the base model's version makes the card accurate about where results came from, but adds no evidence about the tuned model.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor knows its model. But the vendor never tested the airline's tuned version, so its confirmation is a claim, not evidence.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because claim chats look harmless. But tuning on harmless data can still weaken safety behavior; only testing the tuned model shows the effect.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because accurate cards matter. But naming the base version only says where the copied results came from; it does not test the tuned model.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts a vendor claim about a model the vendor never tested, and C assumes harmless tuning data cannot weaken safety.
Final two: A beats D because only testing the tuned model shows whether it kept its safety behavior; a version note makes the card accurate but adds no evidence.
Exam cue: a tuned model is a new model. Inherited test results describe the base model, not what you deploy.
