questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Partial retirement of a shared model
questions.question: An Estonian insurer shares most models across lines; car claims dropped a triage model still serving boat claims, and the inventory marked it retired, ending drift checks. Which IS auditor recommendation BEST prevents a recurrence?

options.A: Require drift checks on every model the inventory lists as live
options.B: Retire the model for boat claims too, so it matches the inventory
options.C: Have the IS auditor run drift checks until the inventory is fixed
options.D: Record each use of a model as its own inventory entry

questions.key_concept: Inventory and monitoring should follow each use of a model, so retiring one use does not end oversight of another.
questions.pre_read: Ask what else depends on the inventory status being right.
questions.correct_explanation: Marking the whole model retired when only car claims dropped it shows the inventory tracks models, not uses, so one line's retirement ended drift checks on a live use. With most models shared, the gap can recur anywhere. An entry per use puts boat claims back on the live list and keeps other uses monitored. Checking every model listed as live keeps the per-model status that caused the gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it covers every model. But status is kept per model, so one line dropping a shared model still marks it retired and ends checks for the others.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it makes the record true. But whether to retire a working use is the owner's business decision, not a fix for a record.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it fills the gap. But running the monitoring would make the IS auditor part of the control they must assess.

tips: Eliminate: B ends a working use just to fit a record, and C has the IS auditor operating the monitoring.
Final two: D beats A because drift checks keyed to a model's status lapse once one line drops a shared model; only per-use entries keep boat claims and every other live use monitored.
Exam cue: one model can serve several uses. Inventory, ownership and monitoring belong to each use, so retiring one must not silence the others.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.6 (Mechanisms to inventory AI systems); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.7 (Decommissioning AI systems safely)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B.3 Decommissioning AI Systems (inventory and monitoring follow each use, so retiring one use keeps the others watched). Final review round: stem now states that many models are shared across lines, so the per-use inventory fix is needed beyond this one model. Re-audit round: runner-up A is now a model-level standing rule, so the per-use fact, not root-cause wording, decides the final two; stem says 'still serving' so it no longer echoes the key. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Returning to manual checks
questions.question: A Nepali bank will retire its trade-document checking model next month and return to manual checks, which its staff have not done unaided for four years. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Keep the model running for staff to consult after its retirement
options.B: Retire on schedule and let staff relearn the checks on the job
options.C: Confirm staff can check documents accurately before switch-off
options.D: Update the written manual checking procedure staff will follow

questions.key_concept: Long reliance on AI can erode staff skills, so a manual fallback must be shown to work before the model is retired.
questions.pre_read: Ask who will do the work once the model is gone, and how well.
questions.correct_explanation: Four years of relying on the model can erode the skills the manual process needs, so the fallback may fail on day one. Confirming that staff can check documents accurately, for example on sample cases, shows whether retirement is safe or what training is needed first. An updated procedure tells staff what to do, but not whether they can still do it well.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it keeps help on hand. But a retired model has no owner or monitoring, so staff would rely on an unsupported tool.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because skills return with practice. But errors made while relearning reach customers' trade payments first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because written steps support staff. But a procedure shows what to do, not that staff can still do it accurately.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps staff relying on a model no one will monitor, and B lets relearning errors reach customers.
Final two: C beats D because long reliance on AI erodes manual skill, so proficiency must be shown before switch-off; a procedure shows the steps, not the skill.
Exam cue: retiring or disengaging AI moves work back to people. Check that the fallback still works, including staff skills.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.7 (Decommissioning AI systems safely); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.4 (Operator and practitioner proficiency defined and assessed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B.3 Decommissioning AI Systems (long reliance on AI erodes skills, so the manual fallback is proven before retirement). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Four unlogged edits
questions.question: Reviewing a Costa Rican social-security fund's member assistant, the IS auditor finds four edits made last month outside change management. Which edit should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Renewing the TLS certificate on the assistant's web page
options.B: Changing how many document passages it retrieves per answer
options.C: Adding server memory to the host of its document index
options.D: Rewording the greeting shown when a member opens the chat

questions.key_concept: Retrieval settings decide what a generative model reads, so changing them changes answers and needs change control.
questions.pre_read: For each edit, ask whether it could change what the assistant tells someone.
questions.correct_explanation: The number of passages retrieved decides what the model reads before it answers, so changing it can shift answers on benefits for every member without any code change. That makes it an AI change needing testing and approval. Certificate renewal matters for availability and trust, but it is routine operations that leaves every answer unchanged.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because certificates protect connections. But renewal is a routine operational task that does not change what the assistant tells members.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because infrastructure changes need control. But added memory changes capacity, not which passages the model reads or what it says.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because members see the greeting. But fixed greeting text does not change how the assistant answers benefit questions.

tips: Eliminate: C adds capacity without changing answers, and D rewords fixed text that steers nothing the model says.
Final two: B beats A because retrieval settings change what the model reads and so what it tells members; certificate renewal is routine and leaves answers untouched.
Exam cue: in generative systems, retrieval settings, prompts and thresholds steer outputs. Treat them as changes even when no code moves.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.1 (Post-deployment monitoring including appeal, override, incident response and change management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2C.1 What Counts as an AI Change (retrieval settings steer a generative system's answers, so editing them is a change). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A broader labeling guide
questions.question: A Chilean telecom widened its formal-complaint definition and relabeled past emails, under an approved change, to retrain its triage model; the release test set keeps old labels. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Correct routings under the new definition will count as errors
options.B: More emails will reach the complaints team than it can handle
options.C: Relabeling past emails by hand may introduce labeling errors
options.D: The complaints team, not data science, now owns the definition

questions.key_concept: When a label definition changes, the test set must follow it; otherwise release tests score the new model against the old meaning.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern by how much of the release decision it could make wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: The model is retrained to call more emails formal complaints, but the release test set still records them under the narrower definition. Each newly covered email the model routes correctly will be scored as an error, and real errors can hide among the same cases, so the test cannot show whether the model is fit to release. Hand-labeling errors are a real risk, but sampling checks can catch them.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a wider definition sends more emails to complaints. But that is the intended effect of the policy, for the business to plan, not a flaw in the release.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because hand labeling can go wrong. But sampling checks can catch label errors; the test-set mismatch misjudges every case the new definition changed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because label ownership matters. But the business should define what a complaint is; data science then labels and tests to that definition.

tips: Eliminate: B is the intended effect of the wider definition, and D objects to the business defining its own complaint category.
Final two: A beats C because a test set labeled under the old definition misjudges every changed case, so the release rests on wrong evidence; label errors can be sampled and caught.
Exam cue: when what a label means changes, the test set must change with it, or release tests measure the wrong thing.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-4 (Impact Analyses); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.1 (Test sets, metrics and TEVV tools documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2C.1 What Counts as an AI Change (a change to labeling rules changes what the model learns, so its release tests must follow the new labels). Completeness round 1, 5 Nov 2026: re-angled from 'treat the guide change as an AI change' (same frame as aaia_d2_063) to the GREATEST concern when the release test set keeps the old labels. Completeness round 2, 5 Nov 2026: option A reworded to drop the stem echo 'release'. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Versions kept versus late outcomes
questions.question: A Paraguayan soybean exporter retrains its export-volume model weekly and keeps the last two versions; actual volumes, which reveal its errors, arrive about six weeks later. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the IS auditor approve each deletion of an old model version
options.B: Rebuild old versions from archived code and data when needed
options.C: Retrain daily so that errors are corrected before outcomes arrive
options.D: Keep versions long enough to roll back past the outcome delay

questions.key_concept: When outcomes reveal errors late, keep model versions long enough to roll back past that delay; rebuilt models may differ.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the team would have on hand on the day an error is found.
questions.correct_explanation: Errors in this model show up only when shipments are known, about six weeks on, by which time the faulty version and every earlier one have been deleted. Keeping versions past that delay keeps a known rollback target. Rebuilding from archived code and data takes time and, because training is not fully repeatable, may not produce the model that once worked.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because deletions need control. But approving them would make the IS auditor part of the control; the owner sets retention to fit the delay.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because code and data were archived. But retraining rarely reproduces the exact model, and rebuilding takes time during a failure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because faster retraining reacts sooner. But it adds more versions and still cannot see errors before outcomes arrive.

tips: Eliminate: A puts the IS auditor in the control, and C retrains faster without seeing errors any sooner.
Final two: D beats B because a kept version is ready and known; retraining rarely reproduces the exact model that worked, and rebuilding takes time mid-failure.
Exam cue: set model retention by how long errors take to appear, not by how often you retrain.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-2 (Baseline Configuration); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2C.2 Model Versioning, Configuration Baselines and Rollback (keep model versions past the delay before outcomes reveal errors). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Staged releases of delivery-time models
questions.question: A Mongolian courier's new delivery-time model matched rural and city accuracy on past deliveries; staging covers 5% of customers, all in Ulaanbaatar; 40% of parcels go rural. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the plan, since rural accuracy already matched city accuracy
options.B: Raise the staged share from 5% to 20% of Ulaanbaatar customers
options.C: Include rural routes in the staged share before full release
options.D: Release to everyone, then roll back if rural complaints rise

questions.key_concept: A staged release is the live check of a model, so its share must include each segment the model will serve, whatever past-data tests covered.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each check here tells the courier about live deliveries.
questions.correct_explanation: Testing on past deliveries shows how the model did on history, even where rural and city accuracy matched. Live rural deliveries can differ from that history, through new roads, seasons or patchy location data, in ways only live use reveals, and a city-only stage gives no live evidence for 40% of parcels. Including rural routes in the staged share checks the model where it will run before everyone relies on it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because rural accuracy matched in testing. But those were past deliveries; live rural conditions can differ, and the staged release is the only live check before full use.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a larger share gives steadier results. But 20% of city customers still says nothing about rural routes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because rollback limits the damage. But every rural customer is exposed first, and complaints arrive only after wrong estimates have reached them.

tips: Eliminate: B enlarges a stage that is still all city, and D exposes every rural customer and waits for complaints before acting.
Final two: C beats A because matching accuracy on past deliveries cannot show how the model handles live rural conditions; only a stage that includes rural routes gives that evidence.
Exam cue: past-data tests and staged releases answer different questions. Check that a staged release covers every segment the model will serve.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2C.2 Model Versioning, Configuration Baselines and Rollback (a staged release is evidence only for the segments it covers). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A platform's new AI provider
questions.question: A Swedish retailer ranks job applicants with its HR platform's AI; the platform's sub-processor notice shows it switched AI model providers, with data kept in the EU. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Applicants may not be told a new provider's model now ranks them
options.B: Applicant groups' rankings may have shifted without any testing
options.C: The platform may raise its fees to cover the new provider
options.D: The notice may not include the new provider's security certifications

questions.key_concept: When a vendor swaps the model provider behind its product, the customer faces an untested model change that affects people.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changed for the people being ranked, not only for the supplier list.
questions.correct_explanation: A new model provider means a new model behind the rankings, so outcomes for applicants can shift, including for particular groups, without any change the retailer tested. In hiring, that untested effect on people is the greatest concern. The new provider's security certifications are worth requesting, but they say nothing about how its model ranks applicants.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because applicants should know who processes their data. But a notice changes nothing about the rankings; untested shifts in them are what could harm applicants.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because supplier changes affect cost. But fees are a commercial matter, not a risk to how applicants are ranked.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendor reviews often start with certifications. But certifications cover security controls, not how a different model ranks applicants; untested shifts in rankings are the harm.

tips: Eliminate: A is a notice issue that leaves rankings untouched, and C is a commercial matter rather than a risk to applicants.
Final two: B beats D because a new provider changes the model behind each ranking, and the untested effect on applicants is the harm; security certifications say nothing about rankings.
Exam cue: a vendor's change of its own AI supplier is a model change for you. Look for it in sub-processor and release notices.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2C.3 Vendor Model Updates (a vendor's switch of model provider is an untested model change for its customers). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. An endpoint that picks the model
questions.question: A Slovenian newsroom's headline assistant calls its vendor's 'auto' endpoint, which sends each request to one of several models depending on load. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Run weekly regression tests against the vendor's auto endpoint
options.B: Ask the vendor to publish its routing rules every month
options.C: Have editors rate a sample of the published headlines each month
options.D: Call a named model version and log it with each headline

questions.key_concept: Load-based routing across models makes outputs untraceable and tests unrepresentative; call a named version and log it with each output.
questions.pre_read: Ask which model wrote a given output, and how anyone would know.
questions.correct_explanation: With load-based routing, the model behind any headline can change from one request to the next, so tests cover whichever mix happened to answer and no output can be traced to its model. Calling a named version and logging it fixes what is being tested and makes each headline traceable. Weekly regression tests on the auto endpoint measure a moving target.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because regression tests catch changes. But the endpoint may route test prompts to different models than live ones, so results may not describe live use.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because transparency helps. But knowing the rules does not fix which model answers, or record which one did.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because review catches poor headlines. But a monthly sample cannot show which model wrote each headline or keep behavior stable.

tips: Eliminate: B learns the routing without controlling it, and C samples headlines without knowing which model wrote them.
Final two: D beats A because a named, logged version fixes what is tested and traces each output; tests on a load-routed endpoint measure whatever mix answered.
Exam cue: you can only test, compare and explain outputs from a known model version. Pin it and log it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-2 (Baseline Configuration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2C.3 Vendor Model Updates (a load-routed endpoint hides which model answered; pin and log the version). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Recommendations that apply by default
questions.question: A Polish hospital's model recommends moving intensive-care patients to general wards; each recommendation takes effect if no doctor responds within two hours, as happens for 40%. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Hold each transfer until a doctor decides, and escalate late ones
options.B: Send doctors a reminder one hour before the response deadline
options.C: Report how many recommendations apply by default each month
options.D: Extend the response window from two hours to four hours

questions.key_concept: If an AI recommendation takes effect when no one responds, silence becomes approval and oversight exists only on paper.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens to the patient when nobody answers.
questions.correct_explanation: When silence counts as approval, 40% of recommended transfers happen with no doctor's decision at all, so oversight exists only on paper. Holding each recommendation until a doctor decides, and escalating late ones, makes a person decide every transfer. A reminder may cut timeouts, but any recommendation still unanswered at two hours moves the patient by default.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reminders prompt action. But when the deadline passes, silence still moves the patient; the default stays automatic.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reporting shows the scale. But a monthly figure arrives after patients were moved without any doctor's decision.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because doctors get more time. But unanswered recommendations still take effect, only later; silence remains approval.

tips: Eliminate: C reports transfers after they happen, and D lengthens the window while silence still counts as approval.
Final two: A beats B because only holding the recommendation makes a doctor decide each transfer; a reminder helps, but silence still moves patients by default.
Exam cue: check what happens when the human does nothing. If the AI's choice applies by default, oversight is not real.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 3.2 (Roles defined for human-AI configurations and oversight)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.1 Human Oversight and Automation Bias (an AI decision that applies when no one responds is not under human oversight). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Cross-domain fixes 5 Nov 2026 (batch 6): AI use moved from discharges to intensive-care transfers (discharge setting already used in CRISC d3_044, notes 3A.2 and principles.json).

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. A 98% catch rate on seeded flags
questions.question: A Philippine overseas-employment agency tests reviewers of its model's fake-contract flags with seeded wrong flags, all copied from one 2022 batch; reviewers catch 98%. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The 98% rate may set too high a bar for new reviewers
options.B: Seeded flags may delay real workers' departures by mistake
options.C: Reviewers may spot seeds by their old details, not by judgment
options.D: Reviewers' override rate on live flags is not yet reported

questions.key_concept: Seeded cases measure reviewer vigilance only if they look like live flags; seeds reviewers can recognize measure seed-spotting.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each piece of oversight evidence here actually measures.
questions.correct_explanation: Seeds measure whether reviewers catch model errors only if reviewers cannot tell them from live flags. Seeds copied from one 2022 batch share dates, employers and formats reviewers can learn, so a 98% catch rate may show seed-spotting while real model errors pass unchallenged. Seeds should resemble current live flags and change over time. An override rate on live flags is worth having, but on its own it cannot separate vigilance from deference.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fair targets matter. But the issue is not how high the bar is; the test may not measure vigilance at all.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because seeds must not touch real workers. But nothing suggests seeds reach real cases; the doubt is what the 98% really measures.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because overrides show disagreement. But a low override rate alone fits deference and an accurate model alike; it cannot repair a flawed seed test.

tips: Eliminate: A debates a bar rather than what the test measures, and B worries about real cases nothing links to the seeds.
Final two: C beats D because seeds reviewers can recognize turn a vigilance test into a memory test; an override rate alone cannot tell vigilance from deference either.
Exam cue: a seeded test of oversight works only if seeds look like live cases. Check how seeds are drawn and refreshed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.1 Human Oversight and Automation Bias (seeded cases test vigilance only if reviewers cannot recognize them). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Drift alerts every winter
questions.question: A Kazakh gas distributor's demand model raises input-drift alerts every winter as heating use climbs, and staff now close them unread. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Raise the drift limits until the winter readings stop triggering alerts
options.B: Base drift limits on past winters so alerts flag unusual change
options.C: Retrain the model each autumn before heating demand rises
options.D: Switch off the drift alerts during the winter months

questions.key_concept: Drift alerts that fire on normal seasonal change get ignored; baselines should reflect known patterns so real drift stands out.
questions.pre_read: Ask what staff learn from an alert that fires every winter.
questions.correct_explanation: Alerts that fire every winter for expected change teach staff to ignore them, so a real shift would also be closed unread. Basing limits on past winters lets alerts flag only unusual change, which staff can then be required to act on. Retraining each autumn refreshes the model but leaves the alerts meaningless and gives no evidence it performs well.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fewer alerts would be read. But wider limits hide real drift all year, not only the expected winter rise.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a fresh model suits the season. But scheduled retraining is not monitoring; ignored alerts would still miss unusual change.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because winter alerts are noise. But it leaves the model unwatched in the season when demand, and harm from errors, peaks.

tips: Eliminate: A widens limits so real drift goes unseen all year, and D leaves the model unwatched in its busiest season.
Final two: B beats C because seasonal baselines make alerts meaningful again; autumn retraining refreshes the model but leaves alerts that staff still ignore.
Exam cue: a monitoring alert that fires on expected change is noise. Look for baselines that reflect known patterns, so alerts get acted on.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-4 (System Monitoring)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.2 Monitoring Drift, Performance and Impacts (drift baselines should reflect known seasonal patterns so alerts get acted on). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Chats never handed to staff
questions.question: A Slovak parcel-locker company measures its support chatbot by the share of chats never handed to staff, now 85% and rising each month. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The rising share may breach the vendor's fair-use chat limits
options.B: Support staff may lose their skills as fewer chats reach them
options.C: Customers' questions may be drifting from the chatbot's training data
options.D: Customers who need a person may be kept from reaching one

questions.key_concept: A chatbot measured on keeping chats from staff can look better while customers go unhelped; pair it with outcome measures.
questions.pre_read: Ask what this measure rewards, and what it never counts.
questions.correct_explanation: Counting chats never handed to staff rewards the chatbot for holding on to customers, whether or not their problem was solved, so a rising figure can mean more people stuck without help. The measure needs a partner, such as unresolved issues or repeat contacts. Staff skill loss is a real long-run effect, but the measure's direct harm falls on customers now.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because volume affects contracts. But fair-use limits are commercial; the measure's risk is customers' problems going unsolved.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because skills fade without practice. But it is a slower, indirect effect; customers kept from help are harmed now.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rising figures can signal change. But nothing suggests drift; the measure itself rewards keeping customers from staff.

tips: Eliminate: A is a commercial limit, and C reads drift into a figure the measure's design already explains.
Final two: D beats B because the measure rewards keeping customers from staff, harming them now; skill loss among staff is real but slower and indirect.
Exam cue: an AI measure that improves when people get less help is a warning sign. Pair it with a measure of harm.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.2 (Metrics and control effectiveness regularly assessed); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.2 Monitoring Drift, Performance and Impacts (a chatbot KPI that rises when people get less help needs a harm measure beside it). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Appeals that overturn by age
questions.question: A Malaysian state's flood-relief model rejects claims; appeals overturn 35% of its rejections for applicants aged over 65, against 7% for others. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner investigate the model's errors for this age group
options.B: Add appeal staff so older applicants' appeals are decided sooner
options.C: Lower the model's rejection threshold for applicants aged over 65
options.D: Add age as a model input so it learns older applicants better

questions.key_concept: Appeal reversal rates by group are a warning signal of model error; investigate the cause, not just the appeals backlog.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the gap between the two reversal rates measures.
questions.correct_explanation: Appeals overturn older applicants' rejections at five times the rate for others, which signals that the model makes more errors for that group, and wrongly rejected people who do not appeal are never counted. The model owner should investigate the cause so fewer wrong rejections happen. Faster appeals help those who appeal, but leave the model rejecting older applicants wrongly in the first place.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it helps older applicants sooner. But it treats each wrong rejection after the fact while the model keeps making them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it would cut rejections for that group. But changing a threshold before knowing the cause may trade one error for another, untested.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it targets the group. But it changes the model before the cause is known, and using age directly may itself be unlawful.

tips: Eliminate: C and D both change the model before the cause is known, and adding age as an input may itself be unlawful.
Final two: A beats B because the reversal gap signals model errors for older applicants; faster appeals help those who appeal while wrong rejections continue.
Exam cue: appeal outcomes are monitoring data. A group whose rejections are overturned more often points to model error for that group.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.3 (Feedback and appeal processes for end users and affected communities); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.3 Decision Logs, Appeals and Feedback (appeal reversal rates by group signal model error for that group). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Transcripts without actions
questions.question: An Indian bus-ticketing platform's AI support agent can rebook trips, waive fees and issue refunds; its log keeps each chat transcript but not the actions it took. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep chat transcripts until the refund dispute period ends
options.B: Have the agent summarize its actions at the end of each chat
options.C: Log each tool call the agent makes, with its result
options.D: Review a monthly sample of transcripts for unusual refunds

questions.key_concept: An agent's chat transcript shows what it said, not what it did; its tool calls and their results must be logged.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a dispute about a refund would need to show.
questions.correct_explanation: A transcript shows what the agent said, not what it did; an agent can state one thing and call a refund tool with different values. Logging each tool call with its result records the actions themselves, so refunds and waivers can be traced and disputes settled. Keeping transcripts longer only preserves more of the same incomplete record.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because disputes need records. But transcripts kept longer still omit the refunds and waivers the agent actually made.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because summaries are readable. But they are generated text, a lead to verify, not a record of the calls the agent made.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because review can catch abuse. But transcripts do not show the refunds made, so the sample cannot see them.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts the agent's own account of its actions, and D samples records that do not contain the actions.
Final two: C beats A because only tool-call logs record what the agent did; transcripts kept longer preserve the same record of words, not actions.
Exam cue: for AI agents, log actions as well as conversations. What the agent said and what it did can differ.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-2 (Event Logging); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.5 (Security of Agents)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.3 Decision Logs, Appeals and Feedback (an agent's tool calls, not only its chats, belong in the decision log). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A hosted grader updated without notice
questions.question: A Panamanian health insurer compares each member-assistant release with the last using pass rates from a hosted grading model, which its vendor updates without notice. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Pass rates may fall below the level needed for release approval
options.B: Pass-rate changes may come from the grader, not the assistant
options.C: The grader may favor answers written in its own vendor's style
options.D: The assistant's own answers may vary from one run to the next

questions.key_concept: A grading model is a measuring instrument; if it changes silently, results across releases are not comparable, so its version must be pinned and recorded.
questions.pre_read: Ask what must stay fixed for two pass rates to be comparable.
questions.correct_explanation: A grading model is a measuring instrument, and each silent vendor update can make it stricter or more lenient, so a rise or fall in pass rates between releases may reflect the grader, not the assistant. Release decisions then rest on comparisons that mean little. The assistant's answers do vary run to run, but repeated runs measure that spread so it can be allowed for; a silently updated grader moves every score.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because release gates use pass rates. But a falling rate is what testing should reveal; the doubt is whether the rate measures the assistant at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI graders can favor familiar styles. But nothing suggests such bias here, while the silent updates are a stated fact that shifts every score.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because generated answers vary. But repeated runs measure that variation so it can be allowed for; a grader that changes silently shifts every score.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a lower pass rate as the risk rather than asking whether it is valid, and C assumes a style bias the facts never raise.
Final two: B beats D because repeated runs measure run-to-run variation so it can be allowed for, but a silently updated grader moves every score; compare releases only with a fixed, recorded grader.
Exam cue: when AI grades AI, the grader is a measuring instrument. Pin and record its version, or score changes between releases cannot be trusted.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.13 (Effectiveness of TEVV metrics and processes evaluated); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.1 TEVV and Acceptance Criteria (a grading model is a test instrument; silent updates make release-to-release scores incomparable). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Summaries accepted on word overlap
questions.question: A Bangladeshi news agency accepted its article-summary model because summaries shared 60% of their words with editors' own summaries, above the target. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The vendor, not the agency, may have set the target
options.B: Editors' summaries may differ in length from the model's
options.C: Sharing 60% of words may be too low a bar for news
options.D: Summaries can share many words yet misstate the facts

questions.key_concept: Word-overlap scores for generated text measure shared wording, not factual accuracy, so they cannot show alone that a summary is correct.
questions.pre_read: Ask what kind of wrong summary would still pass this test.
questions.correct_explanation: Word overlap rewards summaries that reuse the editors' words, but a summary can share most of them and still reverse a figure, a name or who did what. The acceptance measure does not test what matters for news: factual accuracy. Raising the overlap target would demand more shared words while still never checking whether the facts are right.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because owners should set targets. But nothing says the vendor set it, and any target on this measure still ignores accuracy.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because length affects overlap. But length differences are minor next to a measure that never checks facts.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because higher bars seem safer. But more shared words still says nothing about whether the summary's facts are right.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a fact the question never gives, and B is a minor effect on the score, not a gap in what it tests.
Final two: D beats C because overlap measures shared words, not facts; a higher target asks for more of the wrong evidence.
Exam cue: check that an acceptance measure tests what harms people if wrong. For generated text, fluency and overlap are not accuracy.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.13 (Effectiveness of TEVV metrics and processes evaluated); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.1 TEVV and Acceptance Criteria (word-overlap scores do not test the facts in generated text). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Synthetic voices for older callers
questions.question: An Icelandic health line's speech-recognition menu had too few recordings of callers aged over 80, so its fairness test used synthetic voices made to sound older. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Synthetic voices may not show how older callers really speak
options.B: The test may hold too few cases to give reliable results
options.C: The synthetic voices may infringe the rights of a voice actor
options.D: Older callers may prefer to speak with staff in any case

questions.key_concept: Fairness results on synthetic data reflect the generator's idea of a group, not the real group, until checked on real cases.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose voices the test really measured.
questions.correct_explanation: Synthetic voices come from a model's idea of older speech, which may miss real features such as tremor, breathing or slower pace, so good results may not hold for real callers aged over 80. The test answers a question about the generator, not the group. Sample size is a common limit, but synthetic voices can be made in any number; their realism is the gap.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because group tests are often too small. But synthetic voices can be produced in any number; their realism, not their count, is in doubt.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because voice cloning raises rights questions. But nothing suggests a real person's voice was copied, and it would not affect the test's validity.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because some callers prefer people. But preferences do not excuse a menu that may fail the older callers who use it.

tips: Eliminate: C raises a rights issue the facts never suggest, and D excuses a possible failure by assuming callers' preferences.
Final two: A beats B because synthetic voices can be made in any number, so count is not the problem; whether they sound like real callers aged over 80 is.
Exam cue: synthetic test data shows how a model handles the generator's idea of a group. Ask for real cases before trusting results for that group.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.2 Fairness Testing Across Groups (fairness results on synthetic data may not hold for the real group). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Equal error rates in a farm-credit model
questions.question: A Brazilian development agency's farm-credit model shows equal error rates for women and men farmers, but credit officers, who decide, overturn its approvals more often for women. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retest the model's error rates by sex on recent applications
options.B: Remove the officers' power to overturn the model's approvals
options.C: Test final decisions by sex, including the officers' overrides
options.D: Train officers on the model's validated equal error rates

questions.key_concept: Fairness testing must cover final human-plus-AI decisions; overrides can create a gap the model alone does not show.
questions.pre_read: Ask where in the process the women's applications are actually decided.
questions.correct_explanation: Farmers live with the final decision, not the model's suggestion, and here the officers' overrides could create the gap the model avoids. Testing final outcomes by sex, overrides included, shows whether the whole decision process is fair and where any gap arises. Retesting the model again measures only the part already shown to be even.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fairness tests usually target the model. But the model already shows equal errors; the possible gap arises after officers act.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it stops biased overrides. But it removes human oversight, including overrides that correct real model errors.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it builds confidence in the model. But it nudges officers to defer, and does not test whether their overrides are fair.

tips: Eliminate: B removes oversight to fix it, and D pushes officers toward deference without testing their decisions.
Final two: C beats A because farmers live with final decisions, and the overrides may create the gap; retesting the model measures a part already shown even.
Exam cue: test fairness where the decision is made. If people can change AI outputs, the human-plus-AI outcome is what needs testing.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.2 Fairness Testing Across Groups (fairness tests cover final human-plus-AI decisions, overrides included). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Reasons shown to underwriters
questions.question: A South African life insurer's underwriters see the top three reasons an explanation tool gives for each risk score; validation tested the scores but not the reasons. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Show underwriters the top ten reasons for each score instead
options.B: Test whether changing a cited factor moves the score as claimed
options.C: Ask underwriters whether the reasons match their own judgment
options.D: Add a notice that the reasons shown are estimates, not exact causes

questions.key_concept: Explanations need validating for faithfulness: a cited reason should move the score when it changes, not merely look plausible.
questions.pre_read: Ask how you would know the reasons are the model's, not just believable.
questions.correct_explanation: An explanation tool approximates the model, and its reasons can look sensible while not reflecting what actually drives a score. Testing whether a cited factor really moves the score checks that the reasons are faithful. Underwriters' sense that reasons look right tests plausibility, and plausible but wrong reasons are exactly what could mislead their decisions.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more detail seems more transparent. But ten untested reasons are no more reliable than three.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because experts know underwriting. But reasons that match expectations can still misstate what drives the model; plausible is not faithful.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is honest about limits. But it leaves underwriters relying on reasons nobody has tested.

tips: Eliminate: A adds more untested reasons, and D labels the reasons without testing them.
Final two: B beats C because only changing a cited factor shows whether it really drives the score; underwriters' agreement tests plausibility, not faithfulness.
Exam cue: explanations are outputs too. Validate that they reflect the model's behavior, not just that people find them convincing.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.9 (Model explained, validated and documented, output interpreted in context); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.5 (Explainable and Interpretable)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.3 Independent Validation, Robustness and Red Teaming (validation should test that explanations are faithful to the model). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Red-teaming a paying agent
questions.question: A Colombian insurer plans to red-team its AI claims agent, which can approve and pay claims, by attacking the live agent through real customers' accounts. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Cap each claim payment during the test at a small fixed amount
options.B: Skip red teaming, as the vendor red-teamed the model
options.C: Red-team the model alone, with its payment tools detached
options.D: Red-team an identical copy wired only to test systems

questions.key_concept: Red-teaming an AI agent that can act should use an identical copy whose tools touch only test systems.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a successful attack would actually do during the test.
questions.correct_explanation: Attacks that succeed against the live agent cause real payments and touch real customers' claims. An identical copy wired only to test systems lets testers push the agent, with the same model, prompts and tools, as hard as needed without real harm. Testing the model with its tools detached is safe, but it misses the attacks that matter most: tricking the agent into paying.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it limits losses. But successful attacks still move real money and change real customers' claims during the test.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors test their models. But the vendor tested the model alone, not this agent with its payment tools.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it removes the risk of real payments. But without its tools the agent cannot be tricked into paying, so the riskiest attacks go untested.

tips: Eliminate: A still lets successful attacks move real money, and B relies on the vendor's tests of the bare model.
Final two: D beats C because an identical copy keeps the payment tools attacks target without touching real accounts; detaching the tools makes testing safe but misses the main risk.
Exam cue: agents act in the real world. Red-team them in an identically configured copy with tools pointed at test systems.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.5 (Security of Agents); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.7 (Security and resilience evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.3 Independent Validation, Robustness and Red Teaming (red-team an acting agent on an identical copy wired to test systems). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Varied attempts until a payment passed
questions.question: A Nigerian card issuer's fraud model refused thousands of slightly varied attempts at the same large purchase, made on many cards, before variants began to pass. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Detect and throttle repeated declined attempts across cards
options.B: Retrain the fraud model every week on the latest fraud cases
options.C: Lower the decline threshold so more payments are refused
options.D: Cancel and reissue every card used in the attempts

questions.key_concept: Attackers can probe a model with many varied inputs to learn what passes; detecting and limiting repeated attempts blocks that feedback.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each failed attempt taught the attacker.
questions.correct_explanation: Thousands of slightly varied attempts at one purchase look like probing: fraudsters use the model's declines as feedback to learn what passes, then send the variants that fit. Detecting and throttling repeated declined attempts, across cards as well as within each, cuts off that feedback. Weekly retraining on new fraud helps, but attackers can probe each new version the same way, so the gap reopens after every release.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because fresh fraud data improves models. But probing works against any version; without limits, attackers relearn what passes after each retrain.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it blocks more fraud. But it refuses more genuine payments, and probing simply finds the new cutoff.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the cards were used for fraud. But the attackers learned what the model passes, not just card numbers; they can reuse that lesson with other cards.

tips: Eliminate: C moves a cutoff that probing will find again, and D cancels cards while the attackers keep what they learned about the model.
Final two: A beats B because throttling repeated declines across cards denies attackers the feedback they learn from; retraining helps, but each new version can be probed the same way.
Exam cue: many slightly varied queries before an attack suggest probing. Limit and watch query patterns, not just the model.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.2 (Evasion Attacks and Mitigations); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0043 (Craft Adversarial Data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.1 Attacks on Data and Models (probing teaches attackers what a model passes; limit repeated attempts). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A classifier kept secret
questions.question: A Czech bank's IT team says its phishing-email classifier is safe from evasion because its design is secret and no outsider can query it. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Insiders may leak the classifier's design to attackers
options.B: The classifier may slow email delivery at peak times
options.C: Emails crafted against similar public models often fool it too
options.D: Classifier updates may bypass the bank's change management

questions.key_concept: Attacks crafted on similar models often transfer, so keeping a model's design secret does not protect it from evasion.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether an attacker really needs to see this model to fool it.
questions.correct_explanation: Evasion does not need the design or direct access: attackers can craft emails against similar public models, and such adversarial examples often transfer to other models trained for the same task. Secrecy therefore gives weak protection, and the bank should test robustness itself. An insider leak would help attackers, but the defense fails even if the design never leaks.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because leaks defeat secrecy. But attackers do not need the design; emails crafted against similar models often work anyway.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because filters add delay. But speed is an operations matter, unrelated to the claim that secrecy prevents evasion.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because AI updates are changes. But nothing suggests updates bypass change control; the claim in question is about evasion.

tips: Eliminate: B is an operations issue, and D raises a change-control gap the facts never suggest.
Final two: C beats A because crafted emails often transfer from similar models, so the defense fails without any leak; an insider leak only adds another route.
Exam cue: secrecy is not robustness. Expect attackers to practice on similar models, and test the real one for evasion.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.2 (Evasion Attacks and Mitigations); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0015 (Evade AI Model)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.1 Attacks on Data and Models (evasion attacks transfer between similar models, so secrecy is weak protection). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A gradual conversation
questions.question: A Spanish chemical distributor's product assistant refused every harmful single prompt its testers tried, but staff later got dangerous mixing instructions over a long, gradual conversation. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add the staff's prompts to the assistant's blocked-prompt list
options.B: Rerun the single-prompt tests after each assistant update
options.C: Limit each conversation with the assistant to ten turns
options.D: Test and screen whole conversations, not single prompts alone

questions.key_concept: Multi-turn jailbreaks spread a harmful request across harmless-looking steps, so tests and filters must assess whole conversations.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the testers' single prompts could never reveal.
questions.correct_explanation: Multi-turn jailbreaks build a harmful request step by step, so each message looks safe on its own, and single-prompt tests and filters pass them. Testing and screening whole conversations catches the pattern the attack depends on. Blocking the prompts staff used stops that exact path, but the same gradual approach can be reworded endlessly.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it blocks the known attack. But gradual attacks can be reworded endlessly; a list of past prompts misses the next one.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because regression tests are useful. But these tests never caught the attack, so rerunning them proves nothing about it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because shorter chats limit build-up. But attacks can work in a few turns, and genuine long product questions get cut off.

tips: Eliminate: B reruns the tests that already missed the attack, and C caps turns that a gradual attack can fit within.
Final two: D beats A because the attack lives in the conversation's build-up, which only whole-conversation testing sees; a blocked list stops one wording of it.
Exam cue: if harmful output came from a sequence of harmless-looking steps, test and monitor the sequence, not each step.
questions.framework_ref: MITRE ATLAS AML.T0054 (LLM Jailbreak); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.3 (Direct Prompting Attacks and Mitigations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.2 Prompt Injection and Jailbreaks (multi-turn jailbreaks need whole-conversation testing and screening). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. An instruction saved to memory
questions.question: A Jersey trust company's staff assistant saves lasting 'memories' from chats; a tester's pasted document planted one telling it to copy future drafts to an outside address. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Wipe every user's saved memories at the end of each week
options.B: Block memory writes from documents and let users review memories
options.C: Tell the assistant in its prompt to ignore instructions in documents
options.D: Scan pasted documents for malware before the assistant reads them

questions.key_concept: Assistant memory can turn a one-time prompt injection into a lasting instruction; control writes to memory and let users review it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what makes this injection different from one inside a single chat.
questions.correct_explanation: Memory turns a one-time injection into a lasting instruction that steers every later session, so the risk sits in what may be written to memory. Blocking writes that come from document content, and letting users see and remove entries, stops planted instructions and exposes any that slip in. A weekly wipe still lets a planted memory act for days and erases useful ones.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it limits how long memories last. But a planted instruction still acts until the wipe, and the next document can plant it again.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it states the rule clearly. But injected text can override prompt instructions; a prompt rule is not a control.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because scanning catches harmful files. But the planted instruction is plain text, which a malware scan passes.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on a prompt instruction that injection can override, and D scans for malware when the attack is plain text.
Final two: B beats A because controlling what reaches memory stops planted instructions persisting; a weekly wipe lets them act for days and returns with the next document.
Exam cue: an assistant's memory is a stored input. Control what can write to it, as you would any data that steers outputs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.4 (Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks and Mitigations); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0051.001 (LLM Prompt Injection: Indirect)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.2 Prompt Injection and Jailbreaks (assistant memory can make an injection last; control what writes to memory). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Steps added after approval
questions.question: A Ghanaian data-center operator's AI operations agent asks an engineer to approve its plan, then carries out every step, including steps it adds after approval. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the tool layer block actions outside the approved plan
options.B: Have the agent explain each added step in its final report
options.C: Tell the agent in its prompt to keep strictly to approved plans
options.D: Have the engineer review each plan in more detail before approving

questions.key_concept: Approving an agent's plan does not control steps it adds later; the tool layer must block actions outside what was approved.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the engineer actually approved, and what the agent can do beyond it.
questions.correct_explanation: Approval of a plan means little if the agent can add steps afterward; added steps run with no one having seen them. Having the tool layer block actions outside the approved plan, and seek fresh approval for them, enforces the boundary whatever the agent decides. A more careful review of the plan improves the approval but cannot cover steps the agent invents later.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it records what happened. But the report comes after the added steps ran, and it is the agent's own account.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it states the rule. But a prompt instruction can be ignored, misread or overridden; it does not enforce limits.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because better review catches bad plans. But it cannot cover steps the agent adds after approval.

tips: Eliminate: B reports added steps only after they run, and C relies on a prompt rule the agent may not follow.
Final two: A beats D because blocking unapproved actions enforces the plan's limits; a closer review of the plan cannot see steps added after it.
Exam cue: approving an agent's plan is not approving its actions. Enforce the approved scope where the tools are called.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.5 (Security of Agents); OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM06 (Excessive Agency)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.3 Excessive Agency and Access Management for AI (plan approval does not bound an agent's later steps; enforce scope at the tools). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. An agent that makes its own accounts
questions.question: A Finnish software firm's AI deployment agent acts on tickets any employee can file, under an account that can create service accounts and access keys. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: New accounts may break the firm's naming standard for accounts
options.B: Ticket text could steer it into creating unreviewed access
options.C: Access keys the agent creates may lack an expiry date
options.D: Ticketed deployments may take longer while new accounts are created

questions.key_concept: An agent acting on text others write can be steered into creating access; identity creation should stay outside its reach.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can influence what the agent does.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent that acts on text anyone can write can be steered by that text, so a crafted ticket could make it create accounts and keys for an attacker, outside the approval and review applied to people. That steerable power to grant access is the greatest concern. Keys that never expire make the problem last longer, but the gap is that the access was never approved at all.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because standards aid reviews. But naming is cosmetic next to an agent that can be steered into creating access.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because old keys are a known risk. But expiry limits how long access lasts; the larger gap is that anyone filing a ticket can steer its creation.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because speed matters in deployment. But delay is an efficiency issue, not a risk to the firm's systems.

tips: Eliminate: A is a naming standard and D is a speed issue; neither touches who can steer the agent into granting access.
Final two: B beats C because a crafted ticket can steer the agent into creating any access, unreviewed; key expiry only limits how long that access lasts.
Exam cue: an AI agent that reads text others write can be steered by it. Keep powers such as creating accounts out of its reach.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM06 (Excessive Agency)

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Deposits set out of sight
questions.question: A Romanian utility's model sets new households' security deposits; customers are not told a model is involved, and its AI incident process starts only from complaints. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Complaint handlers may route AI-related complaints to the wrong team
options.B: The deposit model may breach the utility's pricing policy
options.C: The model may set higher deposits for some groups of households
options.D: Households unaware of the model may never report a wrong deposit

questions.key_concept: When people cannot tell AI made a decision, few report its errors, so incident detection cannot rely on complaints alone.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the incident process would first hear of a problem.
questions.correct_explanation: When people do not know a model set their deposit, they have little reason to suspect a systematic error, and many will simply pay. The incident process waits for complaints, so the deciding gap is detection: harm of any kind, unequal deposits included, can go unnoticed. Detection needs monitoring of the decisions themselves, not only a complaint channel.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because misrouting delays response. But it affects only complaints that arrive; the bigger gap is harm no one reports.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because pricing rules matter. But nothing suggests a breach; the issue is how errors would ever be noticed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because deposit models can treat groups unequally. But nothing suggests that here, and a process that waits for complaints would miss such harm too.

tips: Eliminate: A matters only for complaints that arrive, and B assumes a pricing breach nothing suggests.
Final two: D beats C because a complaint-only process misses any harm customers cannot see, unequal deposits included; C guesses at one harm the facts never show.
Exam cue: complaints detect AI harm only when people can see it. Opaque AI needs monitoring of its decisions, not just a complaint channel.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.3 (Incidents and errors communicated and tracked); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 4.3 (Practices enable AI testing, incident identification and information sharing)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2G.1 Recognizing and Triaging AI Incidents (hidden AI decisions draw few complaints, so detection cannot rely on them). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A cloned voice passes verification
questions.question: A Kenyan mobile-money operator's voice-verification model accepted a cloned voice that emptied a customer's wallet; the fraud team refunded the customer and closed the case. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Retrain the model on cloned voices before reopening the case
options.B: Add a second factor for that customer's future transactions
options.C: Treat it as a model attack and review other recent voice matches
options.D: Keep the case closed, since the customer was fully refunded

questions.key_concept: A cloned voice passing verification is an attack on the model, so the incident covers every account the model protects.
questions.pre_read: Ask what exactly the attacker defeated.
questions.correct_explanation: A cloned voice passing verification is an attack on the model itself, and the same technique can be used on any account it protects. Handling it as an AI incident and reviewing other recent voice matches finds other victims and shows whether the model can be fooled at scale. A second factor protects one customer while the weakness stays open for everyone else.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model needs to resist clones. But retraining before the attack is understood may not fix it, and it delays finding other victims.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it stops a repeat for this customer. But the model can be fooled for every account, not just this one.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the customer is made whole. But a refund closes the loss, not the weakness that every account faces.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains before the attack is understood, and D treats a refund as closing a weakness every account shares.
Final two: C beats B because the cloned voice defeated the model, which guards every account; a second factor protects one customer while others stay exposed.
Exam cue: when an attack fools the model, the incident is the model's weakness, not one victim's loss. Triage it across everyone the model protects.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0015 (Evade AI Model)

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A library overwritten each night
questions.question: A Dutch tax-advice firm disengaged its client assistant after harmful advice and saved the chat logs; the tax-guidance library the assistant retrieves from is overwritten every night. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Move the saved chat logs to restricted, locked storage
options.B: Preserve the guidance library and its earlier versions now
options.C: Rerun the clients' questions to recreate the harmful advice
options.D: Correct the faulty guidance in the library before tonight

questions.key_concept: Retrieval content is evidence: the library an assistant read from can be overwritten, so preserve it before it changes.
questions.pre_read: List every input that shaped the advice, and when each could change.
questions.correct_explanation: The advice came from what the assistant retrieved, and the nightly overwrite will replace the guidance it read, leaving root cause work with logs but no source. Preserving the library, with any earlier versions still held, comes first. Moving the saved logs to restricted storage is good custody, but they are already kept, while the library changes tonight.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because logs need protection. But the logs are already saved; the library is the evidence about to be lost.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems to rebuild events. But answers vary run to run, and the library will have changed, so reruns cannot show what clients were told.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because faulty guidance should be fixed. But correcting it now changes the evidence before anyone knows what the assistant read.

tips: Eliminate: C reruns a model whose answers vary, against a library that has changed, and D edits the evidence before it is preserved.
Final two: B beats A because the library is overwritten tonight while the logs are already kept; secure first what is about to disappear.
Exam cue: for retrieval-based AI, the documents it read are evidence. Preserve the index or library version before it refreshes.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI)

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A switch only the vendor holds
questions.question: During an AI incident, a Bulgarian ministry found that only its procurement-software vendor could turn off the software's AI supplier ratings, which took four days. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Secure a tested way for the ministry to switch the ratings off
options.B: Agree with the vendor a four-hour response time for AI incidents
options.C: Ask the vendor to roll the ratings back to last month's model
options.D: Give the IS auditor authority to stop the ministry's AI ratings

questions.key_concept: Owners need a tested way to disengage AI features in bought software themselves, without waiting for the vendor.
questions.pre_read: Ask what containment depended on in this setup.
questions.correct_explanation: Disengaging AI quickly is the first containment step, and here it depended entirely on the vendor's speed. A tested way for the ministry itself to switch the ratings off puts that step in the owner's hands. A four-hour response time shortens the wait but still leaves containment depending on the vendor answering, possibly at night or under its own pressures.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it cuts the delay. But containment still waits on the vendor, and four hours of harmful ratings may still be too long.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rollback is a standard AI containment step. But the rollback still waits on the vendor, the same dependence that took four days.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because someone must hold the authority. But stopping systems is the owner's call; the IS auditor assesses whether that ability exists.

tips: Eliminate: C still waits on the vendor to act, and D gives the IS auditor an operating power that belongs to the owner.
Final two: A beats B because the ministry's own tested switch lets the owner disengage at once; a faster vendor response still makes containment wait on another party.
Exam cue: for AI inside bought software, check the owner can disengage it without waiting for the vendor.
