questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A flaw in a shared template
questions.question: A Greek museum group traced its chatbot's wrong ticket prices to a prompt template four assistants on other models share; the problem record covers the chatbot alone. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Fix the template, retest the chatbot, then close the problem record
options.B: Have each assistant tell visitors to check prices on the website
options.C: Retrain the chatbot's model on the correct ticket prices
options.D: Extend the problem record to every assistant using the template

questions.key_concept: When an AI root cause sits in a shared component, the problem record must cover every system that uses it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what else the template's flaw could have touched.
questions.correct_explanation: The cause sits in a shared template, so the same flaw may already be giving wrong prices in four other assistants, and because a prompt behaves differently on each model, a fix proven on the chatbot proves nothing for them. Extending the problem record to every assistant using the template makes the fix, retesting and closure cover all of them. Retesting only the chatbot leaves four unchecked.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the fix reaches the shared template. But a prompt acts differently on each model, so the four other assistants stay unproven after the change.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it warns visitors. But a notice leaves wrong prices in place across five assistants.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the model gave wrong prices. But the cause is the template, and retraining changes the wrong component.

tips: Eliminate: B warns visitors instead of fixing the cause, and C retrains a model when the cause is in the template.
Final two: D beats A because a prompt acts differently on each model, so a fix proven on the chatbot says nothing about the other four; the problem record must cover all five.
Exam cue: when an AI root cause is a shared component, such as a template, base model or index, widen the problem to every system using it and retest each.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 RS.AN-03 (Root cause of the incident established); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.3 (Incidents and errors communicated and tracked)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2G.3 Root Cause, Problem Management and Reporting (a root cause in a shared component widens the problem to every system using it). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Closed as staff error
questions.question: An Egyptian elevator-safety agency closed a problem record as staff error: an inspector shown the model's 'low risk' rating passed a faulty elevator, using a checklist judged sound. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Show inspectors the model's confidence score beside each rating
options.B: Retrain the model on the faulty elevator's inspection records
options.C: Test if the model's ratings change how closely inspectors look
options.D: Accept the closure, as the checklist was judged sound

questions.key_concept: People anchor on AI ratings and check less, so 'staff error' is not a root cause until the review is tested beside the rating.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether another inspector, in the same seat, would have done the same.
questions.correct_explanation: A checklist that is sound on paper can still fail once a model's rating sits beside it: people predictably anchor on AI output and check less. One inspector's miss may be a symptom of that design. Testing whether ratings change how closely inspectors look, across all inspectors, finds a cause that would trip anyone. Accepting the closure because the checklist is sound never tests how it is used beside the rating.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it gives inspectors more to judge by. But it is a fix chosen before the cause is known, and a confident wrong rating may be trusted even more.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the model was wrong. But one record changes little, and it leaves the review that missed the error unexamined.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the checklist passed review. But a sound checklist can be applied less carefully once a model's rating is shown; the closure never tests that.

tips: Eliminate: A adds a confidence score before the cause is known, and B tweaks the model with one record.
Final two: C beats D because AI ratings predictably change how closely people check; a checklist judged sound says nothing about how it is used beside a rating.
Exam cue: 'staff error' is rarely a full root cause for AI failures. Ask what in the human-AI design made the error likely.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 RS.AN-03 (Root cause of the incident established); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2G.3 Root Cause, Problem Management and Reporting (accepting a wrong AI output is a design effect, so staff error is not a root cause). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Round 2: stem states the inspector was shown the rating, so the explanations rest on a given fact.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Pooling clients' data for one model
questions.question: A Luxembourg payroll-software firm plans to train one salary-benchmarking model on every client company's payroll data; client contracts allow processing only to run each client's own payroll. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Train by federated learning so no client's data leaves its system
options.B: Have management obtain clients' agreement to shared model training
options.C: Proceed, since the firm already holds every client's data
options.D: Pilot the model on one client's data to measure accuracy

questions.key_concept: Holding data for one purpose does not grant the right to train a shared model on it; settle rights before any technical safeguard.
questions.pre_read: Note every limit the stem states before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The contracts allow each client's data to be processed only to run that client's payroll. A pooled model learns from every client's records and then serves all of them, a new purpose the contracts do not cover, so clients' agreement comes first. Federated training keeps each client's records in place, but the shared model still learns from all of them, so the use is still one the contracts do not cover.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because client data never leaves each client's system. But every client's data still trains a model that serves all clients, a purpose the contracts never allowed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the firm lawfully holds the data. But holding it to run payroll does not permit using it to train a shared model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it tests value early. But testing on a client's data is itself a use the contracts may not allow; rights come first.

tips: Eliminate: C treats holding data as permission for any use, and D tests on data before the right to use it is settled.
Final two: B beats A because a shared model is a new purpose wherever it trains; federated learning keeps data in place but still uses it for that purpose.
Exam cue: when data will train a model it was not collected for, rights to use come before any technical safeguard or test.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 4.1 (Legal and technology risks of components including third-party data mapped); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PT-3 (Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A.1 Data Provenance, Lineage and Rights to Use (rights to use come before training; a pooled model is a new purpose that security measures cannot authorize). Review round 1: runner-up changed from pseudonymizing to federated learning so an AI fact decides, and the model from anomaly detection to salary benchmarking (notes payroll anomaly example). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Retrieval rights that lag the source
questions.question: A Qatari sovereign wealth fund's research assistant indexes deal files with their access rights, refreshed weekly, so a deal restricted on Monday stays retrievable fund-wide until Sunday. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Instruct the assistant not to quote restricted deals
options.B: Refresh the index's copy of access rights every night
options.C: Remove restricted deals from the index each quarter
options.D: Check each user's current rights at the moment of retrieval

questions.key_concept: A retrieval index holds copies of documents and their permissions; checking rights at query time keeps answers in step with the source.
questions.pre_read: Trace when the index learns that a deal was restricted.
questions.correct_explanation: The index holds its own copy of each file's access rights, so for up to a week after a deal is restricted, anyone at the fund can retrieve it through the assistant. Checking the user's current rights at the source each time the assistant retrieves closes that gap. Nightly refreshes shrink the window to a day, but a restricted deal can still reach the wrong staff within that day.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it targets the restricted deals. But a prompt instruction is not an access control, and rephrased questions can still draw them out.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it shortens the gap from a week to a day. But a restricted deal can still reach the wrong staff within that day.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it removes restricted files. But quarterly removal leaves them retrievable for months after a restriction.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a prompt instruction, which is not access control, and C leaves restricted deals retrievable for months.
Final two: D beats B because rights checked at retrieval are always current; a nightly copy still lags the source by up to a day.
Exam cue: in retrieval systems, the index is a copy. Ask whether its access rights can fall out of step with the source.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.9 (Information Security)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A.1 Data Provenance, Lineage and Rights to Use (retrieval must apply each user's current access rights; an index's copied rights lag changes at the source). Review round 1: setting moved from an investment bank (aaia_d2_065; aaia_d3_034). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Live readings no one checks
questions.question: A Uruguayan sawmill cleaned its log-grading model's training data once, at build; live readings from its 12 scanners now feed daily grades and weekly retraining. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Check live readings against ranges and patterns seen in training
options.B: Have the vendor recalibrate the 12 scanners once a year
options.C: Repeat the original cleaning checks before each weekly retraining
options.D: Rely on the model to discount readings that look faulty

questions.key_concept: Cleaning data once at build does not protect live use; inputs need checks wherever they reach the model, including for predictions.
questions.pre_read: Trace each path the data takes into the model.
questions.correct_explanation: A model gives confident grades even on faulty readings; it raises no error. Here the live readings feed both today's grades and each week's retraining, so checking them as they arrive, against what the model saw in training, protects both paths. Repeating the cleaning checks before retraining protects the next model but leaves every grade until then resting on unchecked readings.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because scanners drift. But yearly calibration leaves faults between visits unchecked, and readings still reach the model untested.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it restores the build-time checks. But it covers only retraining; faulty readings still drive the grades issued every day in between.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because models seem to learn what normal looks like. But a model scores whatever it receives and rarely signals that an input is wrong.

tips: Eliminate: D expects the model to spot bad inputs, which models rarely do, and B fixes scanners yearly while readings go unchecked between visits.
Final two: A beats C because the readings drive daily grades as well as retraining; checking only before retraining leaves every grade exposed.
Exam cue: data checked once at build is not checked in production. Look for every path by which live data reaches the model.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-10 (Information Input Validation); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A.2 Data Quality, Labeling and Representativeness (data quality is checked where data enters use, in production as well as at build). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Labelers who agree
questions.question: A Nigerian music-streaming app's comment filter learns from toxicity labels made by six overseas contractors, who agree on 96% of comments; a third are in Nigerian Pidgin. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Sending users' comments to overseas contractors may breach privacy rules
options.B: Agreement below 100% shows the labels cannot be trusted
options.C: The contractors' agreement may reflect a shared misreading of Pidgin
options.D: Users may dodge the filter by writing abuse in Pidgin slang

questions.key_concept: High labeler agreement shows consistency, not accuracy; labelers who share a gap, such as a language, agree on the same wrong labels.
questions.pre_read: Ask who produced the labels and what they were able to judge.
questions.correct_explanation: Agreement shows labelers are consistent, not that they are right. Six contractors outside Nigeria may all misread Pidgin slang or banter the same way, so 96% agreement can hide systematic errors on a third of the comments, and the filter would learn to treat Pidgin speakers' posts as toxic. Sending comments abroad raises a privacy question to manage, but it does not corrupt what the model learns.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because comments carry personal data. But that is a privacy question to manage; it does not corrupt the labels the filter learns from.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because labels should be reliable. But no labeling reaches full agreement; 96% is high, and the issue is what the agreement measures.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because evasion through slang is real. But nothing here points to it; the stated facts concern how the labels were made.

tips: Eliminate: B demands perfect agreement, which no labeling reaches, and D raises evasion, which nothing in the facts points to.
Final two: C beats A because shared misreadings corrupt the labels for a third of comments and bias the filter against Pidgin speakers; data access is a separate, manageable risk.
Exam cue: agreement among labelers is not accuracy. Ask whether the labelers could judge every kind of data they labeled.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Near-identical questions on both sides
questions.question: A Bruneian courier fine-tuned its delivery assistant on 6,000 emails and tested on 600 others from the same months as unseen questions; customers often send near-identical questions. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add 600 more test emails drawn from those same months, then retest
options.B: Remove test emails that closely reword a tuning email, then retest
options.C: Remove test emails that exactly match a tuning email, then retest
options.D: Accept the score, as no test email was used in tuning

questions.key_concept: Separate test data must also differ in substance; reworded copies of training questions let a tuned model score from memory.
questions.pre_read: Consider how alike the training and test records are.
questions.correct_explanation: Customers often send near-identical questions, so many test emails are likely rewordings of tuning emails whose answers the model already learned. Its score then partly measures recall, not how it handles new questions. Screening out close rewordings leaves a test the model has not effectively seen. Removing exact matches catches copies but misses the rewordings, which a tuned model can often answer from what it learned.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a bigger test seems stronger. But emails drawn the same way carry the same overlap, so the score stays inflated.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it targets duplicates directly. But customers rarely repeat a question word for word, so exact matching leaves most rewordings in the test.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the test emails are separate records. But near-identical questions let the model answer from what it learned in tuning.

tips: Eliminate: A enlarges a test drawn the same way, keeping its overlap, and D treats separate records as unseen ones.
Final two: B beats C because a tuned model can answer a reworded question from what it learned; exact matching misses most near-duplicates.
Exam cue: for language models, leakage includes paraphrases. Ask whether test items are new in substance, not just new in wording.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.1 (Test sets, metrics and TEVV tools documented); NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.11-001 (Document benchmark assumptions and limitations including possible training/test data cross contamination)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A.3 Training, Validation and Test Separation (test data must be unseen in substance; reworded near-duplicates of training items leak answers). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Photos removed from both sets
questions.question: A Latvian teledermatology clinic removed blurry and poorly lit photos from both training and test sets for its mole-checking model; patients will upload home phone photos. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Test on photos left unfiltered, like those patients will send
options.B: Add blurry and dim photos to the training set, then retrain
options.C: Test separately on moles photographed on darker skin
options.D: Remove faces and backgrounds from patients' uploaded photos

questions.key_concept: Cleaning training data can be sound; filtering the test set the same way hides how the model handles the inputs it will really get.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each cleaning step changes about the results.
questions.correct_explanation: Removing blurry and dim photos from the test set means its results describe clean images only, yet patients' home photos will often be blurry or dim. Testing on an unfiltered set like the photos patients send shows how the model really performs on them. Adding such photos to training may help the model, but without an unfiltered test no one knows whether it does.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the model never learned from poor photos. But retraining is the owner's choice, and without an unfiltered test no one can tell whether it helped.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because skin-tone gaps are a known risk. But nothing here points to it; the stated fact is what the filtering removed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because home photos are sensitive. But that is a privacy step; it says nothing about how the model handles poor photos.

tips: Eliminate: C tests a risk the facts never raise, and D is a privacy step that leaves performance unknown.
Final two: A beats B because only a test that looks like real uploads shows how the model performs; retraining without one is a fix nobody can check.
Exam cue: cleaning training data can be fine; cleaning the test set hides the cases the model will meet. Test on inputs like those in use.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. An impact trigger tied to data type
questions.question: A Norwegian county's AI lifecycle requires an impact assessment only for models using personal data, so its snowplow routing model, which uses only road sensors, skipped it. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add a privacy review of the sensor data the routing model reads
options.B: Accept the exemption, since no personal data means low risk
options.C: Assess the model's impacts after its first full winter
options.D: Base the impact-assessment trigger on effects on people

questions.key_concept: AI can harm people without using their data; impact assessment follows who the decisions affect, not what data the model reads.
questions.pre_read: Read what the lifecycle rule measures and what the model does.
questions.correct_explanation: Plowing routes decide which roads are cleared first, so they can affect ambulance access, school travel and remote households, whatever data the model reads. A trigger tied to personal data misses AI that harms people through its decisions. Setting the trigger on effects on people brings this model, and others like it, into assessment. A privacy review of sensor data examines a risk the model barely has.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because data reviews are familiar. But road sensors hold little personal data; the risk lies in which roads, and so which people, wait.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because privacy risk is low. But low privacy risk is not low impact; routing decides who gets cleared roads first.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because real use shows effects. But assessing after a winter lets any harm to residents happen before anyone looks.

tips: Eliminate: B equates no personal data with low risk, and C assesses impacts only after a winter of use.
Final two: D beats A because the model affects people through its routes, not its data; a privacy review studies the wrong risk.
Exam cue: AI impact follows decisions, not data type. A model reading only sensors can still decide who waits and who gets served.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.1 (Intended purposes, context and laws documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B.1 The AI Lifecycle and Stage Gates (impact assessment is triggered by effects on people, not by whether personal data is used). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Teams choosing their own risk tier
questions.question: A Montenegrin health insurance fund's lifecycle lets each project team set its own model's risk tier, which decides whether independent validation is needed; most teams choose 'low'. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Let teams keep choosing, as they know their models best
options.B: Require independent validation for every model, whatever its tier
options.C: Have the AI governance committee confirm each model's risk tier
options.D: Have internal audit approve each project team's chosen tier

questions.key_concept: Risk tiers set how deep the lifecycle gates go, so someone outside the build team must confirm them; validating every model alike wastes scarce effort.
questions.pre_read: Follow how a tier choice changes the work a model must pass.
questions.correct_explanation: Teams that pick their own tier can avoid independent validation by choosing 'low', which most do. Having the AI governance committee confirm each tier keeps the decision with a body that approves high-impact uses and has no stake in an easy gate. Validating every model, whatever its tier, removes the incentive but spends scarce validation effort on low-impact models instead of the risky ones.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because teams know their models. But they also gain from a lighter gate, so their tier choice needs confirming.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it closes the loophole. But it treats a low-impact model like a high-impact one and spreads validators thin.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because audit is independent. But approving tiers is a management decision; internal audit would then assess its own decision.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves tiering with those who gain from a low tier, and D has internal audit take a management decision it must later assess.
Final two: C beats B because confirmed tiers send validation where risk is; validating everything treats low-impact models like high-impact ones.
Exam cue: when a tier decides how deep the gates go, check who sets it. Builders choosing their own tier is the gap.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.3 (Level of risk management activity set by risk tolerance); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.3 (Independent assessors not on the front-line development team)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B.1 The AI Lifecycle and Stage Gates (gate depth follows risk tiers, so tiers are confirmed outside the build team; validating every model equally wastes effort). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A code license taken for the weights' license
questions.question: An Armenian chess-coaching app's engineers chose an open-weight model for its game-review helper, since the model's code repository carries an Apache 2.0 license. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have counsel check the weights' own license against the planned use
options.B: Confirm the Apache 2.0 license covers the planned commercial use
options.C: Test the model's reviews on real players' games
options.D: Proceed, since an open license permits any commercial use

questions.key_concept: Open-weight models' weights often carry their own license, separate from the code's, that may restrict uses or users; check it before building.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the team assumes from what is written down.
questions.correct_explanation: Open weights mean the model files can be downloaded, not that any use is allowed. The code that runs a model and its weights are often licensed separately, and many weight licenses restrict some uses, require separate terms above a number of users or set an acceptable-use policy. Checking the weights' license against the planned use comes first, because testing effort is wasted if the app may not use the model this way.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because Apache 2.0 allows commercial use. But that license covers the repository's code; the weights often carry separate terms that can limit uses or users.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fitness must be shown. But it comes second: tests are wasted if the weights' license bars this use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because 'open' sounds unrestricted. But open-weight licenses can limit uses and users; only the terms say what is allowed.

tips: Eliminate: D reads 'open' as unrestricted, and C tests the model before anyone knows the app may use it.
Final two: A beats B because the Apache 2.0 license covers the repository's code, not necessarily the weights; only the weights' own terms say what use is allowed.
Exam cue: open weights are not open permission. Before building on a downloaded model, check what the weights' own license allows.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.10 (Intellectual Property)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B.2 Model Documentation and Build, Buy or Tune (open-weight models come with licenses that can limit use; settle the terms before investing in testing). Review round 1: setting moved from a tutoring platform's student helper (aaia_d1_124, aaia_d3_028); the trap is now a code license read as covering the weights, so an AI fact decides. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. A model card's assumed review
questions.question: A vendor's model card for a Cambodian eye clinic's retinal-scan model says results assume an ophthalmologist reviews every scan; the clinic now clears scans rated normal without one. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The model's accuracy may drift as cameras and patient groups change
options.B: The vendor's evidence no longer covers how the model is used
options.C: The model card may be too technical for clinicians to use
options.D: The vendor becomes accountable for every scan cleared

questions.key_concept: A model card's conditions of use are part of its evidence; using the model outside them leaves its results unsupported.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changed after the model was bought.
questions.correct_explanation: The vendor's results assume an ophthalmologist reviews every scan, so misses the model makes were expected to be caught. Clearing 'normal' scans without that review removes the safety net the results depend on, and patients with missed eye disease get no follow-up. Drift is a real risk for any model, but nothing here points to it; the stated change in use does.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because drift affects every model. But nothing here points to it; the stated fact is that the assumed review was removed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because documentation must be usable. But readability is minor beside using the model outside its stated conditions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor built the model. But the clinic that clears scans stays accountable for that decision.

tips: Eliminate: C is a documentation style issue, and D wrongly moves accountability for the clinic's decisions to the vendor.
Final two: B beats A because the stated change removes the review the card's results depend on; drift is a real risk the facts never raise.
Exam cue: model cards state conditions as well as scores. Using a model outside its stated conditions leaves its evidence behind.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.9 (Model explained, validated and documented, output interpreted in context)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B.2 Model Documentation and Build, Buy or Tune (a model card's conditions of use, such as human review, are part of what its results rest on). Re-audit: key option reworded so the stem's 'results' no longer echoes only in the key. Re-audit 2: setting moved from a hospital chest X-ray model (aaia_d2_153; CISA d1_108) to an eye clinic's retinal-scan model. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Offline copies that outlive the server
questions.question: Bolivia's health ministry retired its faulty child-malnutrition screening model and shut its server, yet health workers screen children daily with offline copies on tablets the ministry manages remotely. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Take down the download link so no further tablets receive the model
options.B: Mark the model and its offline copies retired in the AI inventory
options.C: Retrain the model to fix the errors, then reissue it
options.D: Disable the model on every device that already holds it

questions.key_concept: A model retired on the server still acts wherever copies run; retirement must disable every copy, including offline ones on devices.
questions.pre_read: Ask where else the model could still be running.
questions.correct_explanation: Shutting the server stopped one copy, but the offline copies on tablets keep screening children with the faulty model, so wrong results still reach families. Because the ministry manages the tablets remotely, it can disable the model on every one now. Removing the download link prevents new copies but leaves every tablet that already has the model screening children with it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it stops the model spreading. But every tablet that already holds it keeps screening children with the faulty version.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the inventory should show every copy as retired. But a record changes nothing on the tablets still using the model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the errors need fixing. But a retrained model is a new model needing validation, and the faulty copies keep running meanwhile.

tips: Eliminate: B updates a record while copies keep running, and C builds a new model that needs validation while the faulty copies stay in use.
Final two: D beats A because existing copies keep screening children; blocking new downloads protects only tablets that never had the model.
Exam cue: retiring a model means stopping every copy, including offline and on-device ones, not just the server.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.7 (Decommissioning AI systems safely); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B.3 Decommissioning AI Systems (retirement must reach every copy of a model, including offline copies on devices). Review round 2: the stem now says the offline copies are in daily use, so stopping current screening outranks blocking new downloads. Review round 3: the stem now says the ministry manages the tablets remotely, so disabling existing copies is feasible now and outranks blocking new downloads. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Promises an agent left behind
questions.question: A Taiwanese logistics firm retired its customer chat agent; no refund system records the refunds it promised 180 customers in chats, some coaxed past its rules. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Restore the agent so it can complete the refunds it promised
options.B: Have the IS auditor decide which promises the firm honors
options.C: Have a service manager review each promise the agent made
options.D: Honor the promises the agent logged as within its rules

questions.key_concept: Agents make commitments in conversations that systems may not record; retirement includes finding and settling them under a named owner.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the agent left unfinished when it was switched off.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent's promises in chats can bind or mislead customers even when no system recorded them, and retiring the agent leaves nobody tracking them. A service manager reviewing each promise against the firm's refund rules decides which to honor, correct or explain, so every commitment has a named person accountable. Honoring the promises the agent logged as within its rules, option D, trusts the agent's own judgment, which the coaxing manipulated.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the agent made the promises. But a retired agent settling its own promises decides again with no person accountable, including on promises it was coaxed into.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the auditor is independent of the agent. But deciding which promises to honor is management's call; the auditor assesses and recommends, never settles them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the agent's logs look like system evidence. But coaxing that got the agent past its rules can skew its own record too, so the log cannot sort them.

tips: Eliminate: A brings back a retired agent to settle its own promises, and B puts the auditor in management's seat, deciding which promises the firm honors.
Final two: C beats D because coaxing that got the agent past its rules can skew its own log too; only a person's review sorts the promises on their merits.
Exam cue: when an agent retires, look for what it left open: promises, bookings and tasks in progress. Each needs a named owner to settle it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.7 (Decommissioning AI systems safely); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B.3 Decommissioning AI Systems (retiring an agent includes settling the commitments it made in conversations, each under a named owner). Cross-domain gate fix, 12 Nov 2026: re-angled because the earlier version reused the frame of aaia_d2_145 (an agent retired by removing its account while something it left keeps acting). Re-audit 12 Nov 2026: stem now states some promises were coaxed past the agent's rules, so the manipulation the explanations relied on is given and decides C over D. Re-audit 3, 12 Nov 2026: wrong explanation A no longer claims a reason for the retirement the stem does not give. Final fix, 12 Nov 2026: option B changed from disowning the promises (a blunt action that left C the only review option, and whose explanation claimed reliance the stem never states) to the IS auditor deciding which promises to honor, a lens trap. Final fix 2, 12 Nov 2026: runner-up D now honors every promise the transcripts prove (evidence-based, a CISA instinct), so only the coaxing fact defeats it; key C names a service manager instead of the repeated 'named owner' wording. Final fix 3, 12 Nov 2026: runner-up D now honors the promises the agent logged as within its rules (system-log evidence, a CISA instinct), so knowing that coaxing can skew an agent's own record decides C over D. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A change board that reads only code
questions.question: An Ethiopian telecom's change board approves each retrained airtime-loan model by reviewing its code differences, usually none, and the builders' accuracy summary. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Base approval on independent tests of how each version decides
options.B: Have the IS auditor sign off each retrained release
options.C: Ask the builders to explain each release's code changes in more detail
options.D: Fast-track retrained releases that show no code changes

questions.key_concept: Retraining changes a model's behavior with no code change, so change approval must rest on independent tests of how each version decides.
questions.pre_read: Ask what actually changes when a model is retrained.
questions.correct_explanation: A retrain changes the model's weights through new data, usually with no code change, so a board reading code differences sees almost nothing, and the builders' own summary is not independent evidence. Basing approval on independent tests of how the new version decides shows what actually changed. More detail on code changes still describes the code, not the decisions the retrained model makes.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because auditors are independent. But approving releases is a management decision; the IS auditor would later audit their own sign-off.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it deepens the board's existing review. But a retrain changes weights, not code, so more code detail still shows nothing about how the model now decides.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because nothing in the code changed. But a retrain changes the model's weights, so a release with no code change can still decide very differently.

tips: Eliminate: B has the IS auditor take a release decision that belongs to management, and D waves retrains through because their code is unchanged.
Final two: A beats C because a retrained model changes through its data, not its code; more code detail cannot show how it now decides.
Exam cue: if a change process only sees code, retraining slips past it. Ask who approves a retrained model, and on what evidence.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.3 (Independent assessors not on the front-line development team)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2C.1 What Counts as an AI Change (a retrained model changes without any code change, so a change process that reviews code never sees it). Review round 1: re-angled from builders self-approving (CISA d3_136; aaia_d2_063, 147) to a change board whose evidence cannot see a retrain. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. An emergency prompt fix
questions.question: A Kuwaiti cinema chain's assistant answers cancellation and exchange questions; spot checks show an emergency system-prompt line, 'never discuss refunds', stopped wrong fee quotes. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST next?

options.A: Check that users cannot prompt the assistant past the new line
options.B: Confirm with a sample of fee questions that quoting has stopped
options.C: Retrain the model so the new prompt line can be removed
options.D: Regression-test answers on every topic the assistant covers

questions.key_concept: A system prompt shapes every answer, so a one-line fix can change unrelated behavior; test across topics, not just the target.
questions.pre_read: Ask what else a change could affect besides what it was meant to fix.
questions.correct_explanation: A system prompt shapes every answer, and 'never discuss refunds' can also stop the assistant explaining the cancellations and exchanges it handles. Regression tests across every topic show what else the emergency change altered. Checking that users cannot argue past the line tests resistance to attack, but the line was added for accuracy, and its effect on every customer's ordinary answers is the untested risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because prompt rules can be argued around. But the line was added for accuracy, not security; its untested effect on every customer's other answers is the larger risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it confirms the fix worked. But the spot checks already show that; the new line can change answers on other topics too.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems a lasting fix. But retraining is a bigger change needing its own tests, and it leaves this edit untested.

tips: Eliminate: B repeats the spot checks already done, and C answers an untested change with a bigger one.
Final two: D beats A because a prompt line acts on every answer; bypass testing probes attackers, not what the line changed for every customer.
Exam cue: emergency AI changes still need testing afterward, and for prompts that means the whole range of answers, not just the target.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-4 (Impact Analyses); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2C.1 What Counts as an AI Change (a prompt edit changes behavior across all answers, so even an emergency fix needs regression testing beyond its target). Review round 1: setting moved from a bank's customer assistant (aaia_d2_065, 176, 234); distractor A recast from a strawman to an AI-plausible attack test. Review round 2: the stem now gives the broad prompt line and the spot-check result, so the fix is confirmed and side effects decide (runner-up now A, bypass testing); key option reworded without its contrast clause. Review round 3: the stem now says the assistant also answers cancellation and exchange questions, the fact that points to side effects over bypass; distractor A's explanation no longer calls bypass one user's choice. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A baseline for a hosted assistant
questions.question: A Bahraini insurer's configuration baseline for its hosted claims assistant covers network, identity and encryption settings, which a monthly scan checks. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Run the baseline scan weekly instead of monthly
options.B: Add the settings that shape answers, such as prompt and filters
options.C: Rely on the hosting vendor to keep the assistant's settings stable
options.D: Encrypt the assistant's chat logs at rest as well

questions.key_concept: For AI services, the prompt, model version, filters and retrieval sources are configuration items and belong in the baseline.
questions.pre_read: Think about what makes this system different from an ordinary server.
questions.correct_explanation: An assistant's answers depend on its system prompt, model version, safety filters and retrieval sources. None of these are in a baseline built for servers, so they can change without detection while every scan passes. Adding them lets the baseline catch changes that alter claims answers. Scanning weekly checks the same infrastructure settings more often and still misses every change to the assistant's behavior.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more frequent checks catch drift sooner. But the scan still covers only infrastructure, so changes to prompts or filters stay invisible.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor hosts it. But the insurer sets its own prompt and filters, and vendors change settings too.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logs hold personal data. But encryption protects stored chats; it does not track the settings that shape answers.

tips: Eliminate: C hands the insurer's own settings to the vendor, and D adds a security control that tracks no configuration.
Final two: B beats A because the gap is what the baseline covers; scanning infrastructure more often still misses prompt and filter changes.
Exam cue: an AI baseline lists what shapes outputs: model version, prompt, settings, filters and retrieval sources.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-2 (Baseline Configuration); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-6 (Configuration Settings)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2C.2 Model Versioning, Configuration Baselines and Rollback (an AI service's baseline includes the settings that shape its answers, not only infrastructure settings). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Cached answers after a rollback
questions.question: A Zambian agro-dealer chain rolled its farmer assistant back after wrong pesticide-mixing answers, but its response cache keeps serving stored answers to repeated questions for 30 days. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Shorten the cache's expiry from 30 days to one day
options.B: Retest the restored version on pesticide-mixing questions
options.C: Stop serving answers cached under the withdrawn version
options.D: Add a notice that cached answers may be out of date

questions.key_concept: A rollback is complete only when nothing produced by the withdrawn version keeps reaching users, including cached generated answers.
questions.pre_read: Trace every path by which an answer reaches a customer.
questions.correct_explanation: The rollback restored the model, but the cache still hands farmers answers the faulty version wrote, so wrong mixing instructions keep going out for up to 30 days. Stopping those cached answers, while keeping a copy for the investigation, completes the rollback. A one-day expiry shortens future exposure but still serves today's wrong answers until they expire.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because shorter caching limits staleness. But wrong mixing answers already stored keep going out until they expire.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a rollback should be confirmed. But retesting the restored model checks fresh answers; the cache keeps serving the withdrawn version's answers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it warns farmers. But wrong mixing instructions still reach them, and a notice does not withdraw them.

tips: Eliminate: D warns instead of withdrawing wrong answers, and B retests the restored model while the cache keeps serving old answers.
Final two: C beats A because answers already cached keep going out until purged; a shorter expiry limits future exposure, not today's.
Exam cue: after an AI rollback, look for what the bad version left in service: caches, stored outputs and downstream copies.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2C.2 Model Versioning, Configuration Baselines and Rollback (rollback must cover everything a withdrawn version left in service, including cached generated answers). Review round 1: setting moved from a bank's customer assistant (aaia_d2_065, 176, 232); strawman distractors B and D replaced. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. A feature the vendor switched on
questions.question: An Austrian notary office's hosted staff assistant gained a 'memory' feature in a vendor update, switched on by default, that keeps client details across chats. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept it, since vendor updates fall under the vendor's testing
options.B: Pin the model version so that new vendor updates cannot apply
options.C: Review a sample of stored memories each quarter
options.D: Turn it off office-wide until assessed and approved as a change

questions.key_concept: Vendor updates can add capabilities, such as memory or tools, that change data flows and risks; treat them as changes before use.
questions.pre_read: Ask what kind of change the update made to the service.
questions.correct_explanation: A memory that keeps client details across chats changes what the assistant stores, who may see it later and how long it lasts, so it is a change for the office to assess and approve, with the feature off office-wide until then. Pinning the model version only stops future model changes; it does not switch off a feature already running.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor tests its releases. But vendor testing covers the vendor's product, not this office's client data or duties.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because pinning is a standard control for vendor model updates. But it stops future model changes; the memory feature has already arrived and stays on.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it looks at what is stored. But quarterly review finds client details only after they have been kept and reused.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on the vendor's testing for the office's own risks, and C reviews stored client details months after the fact.
Final two: D beats B because the memory is a service feature already running; pinning the model version stops future model changes but leaves it on and unassessed.
Exam cue: vendor updates can add features as well as change models. A new capability is a change for the deployer to assess.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2C.3 Vendor Model Updates (a vendor update can add capabilities as well as change the model; new features are changes to assess before use).
