Review round 2: runner-up B changed from a staff opt-out to model-version pinning, so the AI fact (an update can add a service feature, not only change the model) decides the item; pre_read made neutral. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Same replies, different actions
questions.question: A vendor model update made an Indonesian theme park's booking agent grant twice as many free fast-track passes, each within limits; replies read the same. Which control should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Test the agent's actions, not only its replies, before updates apply
options.B: Rely on vendor release notes to flag behavior changes
options.C: Compare samples of replies before and after each update applies
options.D: Lower the agent's pass limit after each vendor update

questions.key_concept: For AI agents, an update can change what they do while their words look the same; regression tests must cover actions.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the agent says from what it does.
questions.correct_explanation: The update changed the agent's decisions, granting twice as many free passes, while its replies read the same, so a test that compares text would pass it. Running test cases that check the agent's tool actions, such as when it grants passes, before an update applies catches that kind of change. Comparing sample replies is useful, but it measures words, not the actions that cost the park money.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors describe changes. But release notes rarely predict how one customer's agent will behave with its own tools.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is a regression check. But the replies here read the same; only the actions changed, and text comparisons would pass them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it limits cost. But it caps each grant after the fact and does not test what the next update changes.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts vendor notes to predict this agent's behavior, and D trims a limit without testing the update.
Final two: A beats C because the update changed actions, not words; comparing replies would have passed it.
Exam cue: for agents, test what they do as well as what they say. An update can change tool use while the text looks the same.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.2 (Pre-trained models monitored as part of regular maintenance); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-4 (Impact Analyses)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2C.3 Vendor Model Updates (a vendor model update can change an agent's actions while its text looks the same; update tests must cover tool use). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Review only when the model is unsure
questions.question: A Tunisian social-security fund's model sends disability claims it scores below 80% confidence to assessors and decides the rest itself; its confidence was never checked against outcomes. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Assessors may be overloaded by the low-confidence claims
options.B: Confident but wrong decisions take effect with no one seeing them
options.C: Assessors may defer to the model on the low-confidence claims they see
options.D: Claimants may word claims to raise the model's confidence

questions.key_concept: A model's confidence is its own estimate; if it is not checked against outcomes, confident errors reach people with no review.
questions.pre_read: Trace one claim through each route the process allows.
questions.correct_explanation: Only claims scored below 80% confidence reach an assessor, so confidently wrong decisions take effect with no person seeing them. Because the confidence was never checked against outcomes, nobody knows how many such errors there are, and a disability claimant wrongly refused has no reviewer at all. Automation bias among assessors is a real risk, but it affects claims that at least reach a person.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because workload affects review quality. But nothing points to overload, and it concerns the reviewed claims, not the unreviewed ones.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because automation bias is a classic oversight risk. But those claims at least reach a person; confident errors reach no one.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because claimants could game the score. But nothing points to gaming, and errors need no gaming to slip through.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes an overload nothing points to, and D assumes gaming the facts never raise.
Final two: B beats C because confident errors bypass review entirely while the cutoff rests on unchecked confidence; deference affects only claims a person sees.
Exam cue: when only uncertain cases reach people, ask whether the model's confidence has been shown to track correctness.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.1 Human Oversight and Automation Bias (routing only low-confidence cases to people leaves confident errors unreviewed; confidence must be shown to track correctness). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. The customer as the reviewer
questions.question: A South Korean card issuer says its app assistant, which recommends debt-consolidation loans, has human oversight because every customer must confirm a recommendation before it proceeds. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Customers may tap to confirm without reading the recommendation
options.B: Customers may not know an AI made the recommendation
options.C: No one able to judge suitability reviews its recommendations
options.D: The assistant's recommendations may not be logged for review

questions.key_concept: Human oversight needs a person who can judge the output; the affected customer confirming a recommendation is consent, not oversight.
questions.pre_read: Ask who stands between the model and the harm.
questions.correct_explanation: Oversight needs a person able to judge whether the output is right and to stop it. Here the only 'reviewer' is the customer the loan affects, who usually cannot judge whether consolidation suits them and may trust the issuer's recommendation. Confirming taps without reading is a symptom of the same problem; even a careful reader lacks the knowledge to catch an unsuitable loan.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because quick taps show inattention. But even a careful customer is the person affected, not an overseer able to judge suitability.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because people should know when AI advises them. But disclosure tells customers who advised them; it puts no capable reviewer before an unsuitable loan.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logs support later review. But logging records recommendations after the fact; it does not stop an unsuitable loan before the customer takes it.

tips: Eliminate: B adds disclosure and D adds logging; neither puts anyone able to judge suitability between the model and the loan.
Final two: C beats A because even a careful customer cannot act as the overseer; skipped reading is a symptom of having no qualified reviewer.
Exam cue: check who the overseer is. An affected person accepting an AI recommendation is consent, not oversight.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 3.2 (Roles defined for human-AI configurations and oversight); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.1 Human Oversight and Automation Bias (oversight needs someone able to judge the output; an affected customer confirming a recommendation is not oversight). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Retention calls and false alarms
questions.question: A Spanish newspaper calls subscribers its churn model flags; monitoring counts flagged subscribers who stay as false alarms, and that rate doubled after callers began offering discounts. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Calls that kept subscribers are being counted as model errors
options.B: The model may be drifting as subscribers' reading habits change
options.C: The monitoring dashboard may be refreshed too rarely
options.D: Subscribers may find the retention calls intrusive

questions.key_concept: Interventions triggered by a model change the outcomes used to monitor it; a rise in 'errors' may be the intervention working.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens between a flag and the recorded outcome.
questions.correct_explanation: Flagged subscribers get a call, and since callers began offering discounts more of them stay. Monitoring scores each one who stays as a false alarm, so the doubled rate may show the discounts working, not the model failing, and could trigger a needless retrain. Drift is always possible, but the timing points to the discounts, which change outcomes after every flag.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a doubled error rate often signals drift. But the rise followed the discounts, which change what happens after each flag.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because stale dashboards mislead. But the figure itself is current; what it counts is the problem.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because calls affect people. But nothing suggests complaints, and it does not explain the monitoring figure.

tips: Eliminate: D raises intrusiveness the facts never show, and C doubts timeliness when the problem is what the figure counts.
Final two: A beats B because the rise followed the discounts, which keep flagged subscribers; drift is possible but the facts point to the intervention.
Exam cue: if a model's flags trigger action, outcomes reflect the action too. Check how monitoring treats cases where the action worked.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.2 (Metrics and control effectiveness regularly assessed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.2 Monitoring Drift, Performance and Impacts (when a model's flags trigger action, the action changes outcomes; monitoring must separate model errors from interventions that worked). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Privacy rules and drift checks
questions.question: A Tanzanian HIV-care network's missed-visit model has no drift monitoring, because privacy rules forbid keeping patients' model inputs after scoring. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Skip drift monitoring, since privacy rules take priority
options.B: Keep patients' raw model inputs for 30 days under restricted access
options.C: Retrain monthly so drift monitoring is no longer needed
options.D: Monitor drift from summary statistics that hold no patient details

questions.key_concept: Drift monitoring needs distributions, not individual records; summary statistics can track drift without keeping personal data.
questions.pre_read: Read exactly what the privacy rule forbids before judging what it rules out.
questions.correct_explanation: Drift checks compare distributions, such as the share of patients by age band or visit gap, with the training data. Those summaries can be computed at scoring time and kept without any patient's details, so the privacy rule and monitoring can both be met. Keeping raw inputs for 30 days would enable monitoring but breaks the privacy rule that bars keeping them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because privacy matters most here. But skipping monitoring leaves patients exposed to a model that may be failing unseen.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because raw data makes monitoring easy. But it breaks the privacy rule for HIV patients when summaries would do.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because retraining refreshes the model. But scheduled retraining is not monitoring; it can learn the same shift without anyone noticing.

tips: Eliminate: A treats privacy and monitoring as either-or, and C replaces monitoring with scheduled retraining, which detects nothing.
Final two: D beats B because summaries meet both needs; keeping raw HIV-care records breaks the privacy rule when it is not needed.
Exam cue: drift monitoring needs distributions, not people's records. Look for the option that meets both privacy and oversight.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.2 Monitoring Drift, Performance and Impacts (drift can be monitored from summary statistics, so privacy limits on raw records are not a reason to skip monitoring). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Broker records in eligibility scores
questions.question: A Polish mobile operator's contract-eligibility model scores applicants partly on data-broker records matched by name and birth date; refused applicants receive only their main score factors. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain the model without the data-broker records
options.B: Let applicants see and correct the records the model used
options.C: Give each applicant a fuller list of their own score factors
options.D: Publish how the model weighs each kind of record

questions.key_concept: To contest an AI decision, people need to see and correct the data it used; factor explanations cannot reveal wrong records.
questions.pre_read: Ask what could be wrong in this decision besides the model.
questions.correct_explanation: Records matched only by name and birth date can belong to someone else, so some refusals may rest on another person's debts. Factors such as 'payment history' cannot show a refused applicant that the history is not theirs. Letting applicants see and correct the records used gives them a real way to contest. A fuller factor list explains the score better but still hides a wrongly matched record.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the matched records cause errors. But it leaves past refusals resting on wrong records, and refused applicants still cannot see or challenge what was used.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more explanation helps. But factors describe how the score used the data, not whether the data is the applicant's own.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because transparency helps. But a general description lets no applicant find or fix a wrong record in their own case.

tips: Eliminate: D explains the model in general, not each case, and A redesigns the model and leaves past refusals unremedied.
Final two: B beats C because a wrongly matched record looks like a normal factor; only seeing the records lets an applicant prove it is not theirs.
Exam cue: contestability covers inputs as well as reasons. Ask whether affected people can see and correct the data an AI decision used.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.3 (Feedback and appeal processes for end users and affected communities); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.4 (Accountable and Transparent)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.3 Decision Logs, Appeals and Feedback (contesting an AI decision needs access to the input data used, not only the factors behind the score). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2D AI supervision. Error reports sent straight to retraining
questions.question: A Laotian electricity utility's customer assistant gets 1,500 'wrong answer' reports monthly through a button; the team plans to retrain it on every reported answer, marked wrong. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain on the reports, as customers saw the errors firsthand
options.B: Report the monthly count to the AI governance committee
options.C: Have the model owner triage reports and fix causes before retraining
options.D: Turn off the report button, as there are too many to read

questions.key_concept: User reports of wrong answers need an owner to judge them and fix causes; unreviewed reports fed into retraining can teach errors.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a single report can and cannot tell you.
questions.correct_explanation: Customer reports signal wrong answers, but some are mistaken or malicious, and causes can sit outside the model, such as an outdated tariff document or a prompt gap that retraining never touches. Having the model owner triage the reports and fix each cause before any retraining turns them into real oversight. Retraining on every report skips that judgment, so the model can learn from wrong labels while the real causes stay in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because customers saw the errors. But unjudged reports include mistaken and malicious ones, and causes outside the model, such as documents or prompts, are untouched by retraining.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because governance should see trends. But a count informs the committee while no one fixes the wrong answers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because volume is high. But removing the button loses the main signal that customers are getting wrong answers.

tips: Eliminate: B reports a count that fixes nothing, and D removes the main way customers flag wrong answers.
Final two: C beats A because reports must be judged before they become training labels; some are wrong, and causes can sit outside the model.
Exam cue: user feedback is a lead, not a label. Look for an owner who adjudicates it before it reaches retraining.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 5.2 (Adjudicated feedback incorporated into design); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.3 (Feedback and appeal processes for end users and affected communities)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2D.3 Decision Logs, Appeals and Feedback (user feedback is an oversight signal only if an owner adjudicates it; feeding it straight into retraining skips that judgment). Review round 1: the unadjudicated-retraining plan moved into the stem so the AI fact decides (frame of aaia_d2_035). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Criteria and test set from the vendor
questions.question: A Zimbabwean revenue authority accepted a bought document classifier on the vendor's pass mark and benchmark, documents the vendor had tuned the model against. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the model owner set pass marks and test on in-house files
options.B: Have the model owner set pass marks and rerun the benchmark in-house
options.C: Accept the result, as the vendor knows its classifier best
options.D: Have the vendor retrain it on the authority's own documents

questions.key_concept: A model tuned against a test set scores well on it; acceptance needs the owner's criteria and unseen data from the deployer's own use.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the model relates to the test it passed.
questions.correct_explanation: A model tuned against a test set learns its quirks, so any score on that benchmark overstates how it will classify documents it has never seen. The model owner should set pass marks from the authority's risk tolerance and test on unseen in-house files. An in-house rerun of the benchmark, option B, is real reperformance but still measures the model on data it was tuned to pass.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because rerunning the test in-house is reperformance. But the model was tuned against that benchmark, so any rerun measures data it learned to pass.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor knows its product. But it does not know the authority's documents or tolerance, and it has a stake in passing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because local data should improve the fit. But a retrain is a change that needs its own acceptance test, and it sets no owner criteria.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts the seller's own test, and D orders a retrain, a change that itself needs acceptance testing, before any unseen test.
Final two: A beats B because a benchmark the model was tuned against measures what it learned, wherever it is rerun; only unseen in-house files show how it handles new documents.
Exam cue: a score on data the model was tuned against is not assurance. Acceptance needs the owner's criteria and unseen data from the actual use.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.5 (Organizational risk tolerances determined and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.1 TEVV and Acceptance Criteria (acceptance criteria come from the owner's use and tolerance; rerunning the vendor's own test on its own criteria adds no assurance). Re-audit: the stem now states the vendor's test set came from other countries' tax forms, so a training-versus-deployment data mismatch decides rather than the general acceptance-testing rule. Re-audit 2: deciding fact changed from other countries' forms (frame of aaia_d2_118 and aaia_d1_064) to a vendor benchmark the model was tuned against, not a public one (aaia_d2_056 covers public-benchmark contamination). Cross-domain gate fix, 12 Nov 2026: runner-up B changed from an independent rerun of the vendor's set, which repeated aaia_d2_163's final two. Re-audit 12 Nov 2026: runner-up B changed from a fresh vendor benchmark, which left the final two to general audit sense, to in-house files judged against the vendor's pass mark, so who sets the criteria decides. Re-audit 3, 12 Nov 2026: runner-up B now pairs owner-set marks with the tuned benchmark, so the tuning fact decides A over B; D changed to a vendor retrain so it does not fall for the same reason as B. Final fix, 12 Nov 2026: runner-up B now offers an in-house rerun of the benchmark (reperformance, a CISA instinct), so only the tuning fact defeats it. Final fix 2, 12 Nov 2026: stem no longer says 'test set' (echoed only in key A) and names the vendor as the one who tuned the model. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Tested at one temperature, run at another
questions.question: A Serbian tax authority's assistant passed acceptance tests run at temperature 0, which makes answers nearly repeatable; production runs at 0.8 for more natural replies. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rerun the acceptance tests at temperature 0 with more questions
options.B: Accept the results, as temperature affects wording, not content
options.C: Have taxpayers rate the answers during the first month
options.D: Rerun the acceptance tests at 0.8, several runs per question

questions.key_concept: Generation settings are part of the system under test; results at one temperature do not show behavior at another.
questions.pre_read: Compare the system that was tested with the one that runs.
questions.correct_explanation: Temperature controls how much a generative model varies its answers; at 0.8 the assistant samples less likely wording and can produce errors that never appear at 0. Acceptance results from temperature 0 describe a different configuration from the one taxpayers use. Rerunning the tests at 0.8, several times per question, tests the system as deployed and shows how often it errs. Adding questions at 0 enlarges a test of the wrong configuration.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a bigger test seems stronger. But it still tests a setting production does not use, so it shows nothing about answers at 0.8.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because replies may look similar. But higher temperature can change content, including figures and rules, not just wording.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because user feedback is real-world. But taxpayers cannot rate accuracy reliably, and errors reach them before any rating.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes temperature affects only style, and C relies on taxpayers to spot wrong tax answers after launch.
Final two: D beats A because the test must match the deployed setting; more questions at temperature 0 still test a configuration nobody uses.
Exam cue: for generative AI, test with the deployed model, prompt and generation settings. A different setting is a different system.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.1 TEVV and Acceptance Criteria (test the configuration that runs in production; generation settings such as temperature change behavior). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. No sex or age inputs
questions.question: A Rwandan correctional service's team says its model recommending inmates for vocational training needs no fairness testing because it uses no sex or age inputs. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Also remove inputs that closely track sex or age
options.B: Compare selection and error rates by sex and age
options.C: Treat the model as fair because those traits are excluded
options.D: Publish the list of inputs the model uses

questions.key_concept: Fairness is judged by outcomes; other inputs can stand in for missing traits, so leaving traits out proves nothing.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the team claims from what has been tested.
questions.correct_explanation: Inputs such as sentence length, education level or prison wing can track sex and age, so a model can treat groups differently without seeing those traits. Only testing selections and error rates by sex and age shows whether it does. Removing correlated inputs too still leaves the outcomes untested, may weaken the model, and other proxies can remain.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it targets proxies. But proxies are hard to find completely, and without testing outcomes no one knows whether unfairness remains.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the traits are absent. But other inputs can stand in for them, so absence proves nothing about outcomes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because transparency builds trust. But an input list does not show how outcomes fall across groups.

tips: Eliminate: C treats absent traits as proof of fairness, and D publishes inputs, which shows nothing about outcomes.
Final two: B beats A because only outcome testing shows whether groups are treated differently; removing proxies is a design change still left untested.
Exam cue: 'we don't use the protected trait' is never fairness evidence. Look for outcomes and errors tested by group.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.2 Fairness Testing Across Groups (leaving protected traits out of the inputs does not make a model fair; outcomes must be tested by group). Completeness round 1: setting moved from a cooperative bank's credit model to a correctional service's training-place model (lending settings already used in aaia_d1_138, aaia_d1_123 and aaia_d3_031). Review round 2: key reworded to drop the emphasis word and the stem echo. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A shortlist and a workforce benchmark
questions.question: Of 2,000 applicants to an Australian miner, half women, its résumé-screening model shortlisted 400; women are 30% of the shortlist, which the vendor says matches the mining workforce. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The shortlist of 400 is too small to judge fairness
options.B: The shortlist matches the mining workforce, so it shows no bias
options.C: Women applicants are shortlisted at under half the men's rate
options.D: Women applicants are shortlisted at the same rate as men

questions.key_concept: Selection fairness compares rates within the applicant pool; matching an outside population, such as the current workforce, can carry past imbalance forward.
questions.pre_read: Recompute each group's rate from the numbers given before reading the claims.
questions.correct_explanation: Of 1,000 women, 120 were shortlisted (30% of 400), a 12% rate; of 1,000 men, 280 were, a 28% rate. Women are shortlisted at about 0.43 times the men's rate, under half. The vendor compares with the current mining workforce, which reflects past hiring; the fair comparison is with the people who actually applied, so matching the workforce can carry an old imbalance forward.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because samples can be too small. But 400 shortlisted from 2,000 applicants is enough to show a gap this large.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it cites a real benchmark. But the workforce reflects past hiring; selection fairness compares rates among those who applied.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because both groups are half the applicants. But women are 30% of those shortlisted, so their rate is 12% against men's 28%.

tips: Eliminate: D miscomputes the rates, 12% for women against 28% for men, and A calls 400 of 2,000 too small.
Final two: C beats B because fairness compares rates within the applicant pool; the workforce benchmark carries past hiring forward.
Exam cue: check the comparison group. Selection rates are compared across applicants, not with a population shaped by past decisions.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.6 (Harmful Bias and Homogenization)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.2 Fairness Testing Across Groups (selection rates are compared within the applicant pool, not with an outside population shaped by past decisions). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. Explanations offered as validation
questions.question: A Guatemalan airline's validators, refused its vendor's code and training data, plan to validate its loyalty-fraud model by running an explanation tool on its scores. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the vendor's own validation report in place of review
options.B: Run the explanation tool on a larger sample of the model's scores
options.C: Require the vendor to disclose its code before further use
options.D: Test its alerts on past cases whose outcomes are already known

questions.key_concept: Explanations show what drives a score, not whether it is right; a closed model is validated by testing its outputs against known outcomes.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each method could prove about a single score.
questions.correct_explanation: Testing the model's alerts on past loyalty cases with known outcomes, including confirmed frauds, shows how well it performs on the airline's own members, without needing the vendor's code. That is independent evidence even when code is refused. An explanation tool shows which inputs drive each score, not whether the score is right, so running it on more scores still validates nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor tested it. But builders' own validation is not independent, and it covers the vendor's data, not this airline's members.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because explanations open up a closed model. But they show what drives a score, not whether it is correct; a bigger sample repeats the same gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because code access aids review. But vendors often refuse, and code alone does not show how the model performs on the airline's own accounts.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the vendor's own validation as independent, and C makes validation wait on code the vendor has refused.
Final two: D beats B because an explanation shows why the model scored an account, not whether it was right; only known outcomes show accuracy.
Exam cue: a closed vendor model can still be validated from outside, by testing its outputs against known outcomes. Explanations are not validation.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.3 (Independent assessors not on the front-line development team); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.3 Independent Validation, Robustness and Red Teaming (a vendor model can be validated through its outputs on the organization's own cases, even without its code or data). Review round 1: setting moved from a bank AML model (CISA d3_137; aaia_d1_115); runner-up is now an explanation tool, as output testing on own data alone repeats CISA d1_162 and d2_117; the code-access claim now matches notes 2E.3 and aaia_d2_079. Re-audit: setting moved from a retail chain's return-fraud model (aaia_d3_048; CISA d1 returns-fraud) to an airline's loyalty-fraud model. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2E AI testing. A 1% change that flips decisions
questions.question: A Mauritian housing agency's validators found that changing an applicant's declared income by 1% flips 15% of its grant model's decisions. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Small input errors may decide which families receive a grant
options.B: The model may be overfitted to quirks in its training data
options.C: Income may act as a proxy for applicants' ethnicity
options.D: Refused families may not understand why the model refused them

questions.key_concept: A robustness test that shows decisions flipping on tiny input changes means ordinary data errors can decide outcomes for people.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a 1% change means in everyday data entry.
questions.correct_explanation: A 1% change in declared income is within ordinary rounding or entry error, yet it flips 15% of decisions, so whether a family gets a grant can turn on a typing slip rather than its need. That harm to applicants is what the robustness test exposes. Overfitting may explain why the model is so sensitive, but it is a cause to investigate, not the risk to people.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because brittle models are often overfitted. But that is a possible cause to investigate; the concern is families' grants turning on entry errors.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because income can track protected groups. But nothing here points to it; the stated result is about sensitivity to small changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because grant refusals need reasons. But the result is about sensitivity: even a clear reason would rest on a figure a typing slip can flip.

tips: Eliminate: D raises explainability, which the result does not test, and C raises a proxy risk the facts never point to.
Final two: A beats B because the concern is the effect on families now; overfitting is one possible cause to investigate.
Exam cue: read robustness results for their effect on people. If tiny input changes flip decisions, ordinary data errors decide outcomes.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2E.3 Independent Validation, Robustness and Red Teaming (robustness results are read for their effect on people; decisions that flip on tiny input changes let entry errors decide outcomes). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A signed model from a partner
questions.question: A Swiss university hospital will load a model file, signed by a research partner, straight onto a server holding patient records. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Test its accuracy on a sample of patient records first
options.B: Rely on the partner's signature as proof the file is safe
options.C: Open it first in an isolated environment with no patient data
options.D: Scan the model file with the hospital's antivirus software

questions.key_concept: Some model formats execute code on load; untrusted model files are opened only in isolation and converted there to data-only formats.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens at the moment the file is opened.
questions.correct_explanation: Many common model file formats can run code when loaded, so a model file can carry instructions that execute the moment it is opened, whoever signed it. Opening it first in an isolated environment with no patient data, and converting it there to a format that stores only weights, keeps patient records out of reach. Antivirus tools often miss code hidden inside model files, so a clean scan, option D, is weak assurance.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fitness must be tested. But loading the file to test it may run hidden code beside patient records.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a valid signature proves who sent the file and that it is unaltered. But it cannot show any code inside is safe; the partner may have been compromised.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because scanning is the usual control for downloads. But code hidden in model files often passes antivirus tools, and loading it beside patient data risks them.

tips: Eliminate: A loads the file beside patient records to test it, and B treats a signature, which proves only origin and integrity, as proof the code is safe.
Final two: C beats D because code hidden in a model file can run on load and often passes antivirus; isolation keeps patient data out of its reach.
Exam cue: a model file is software. Some formats run code when opened, so isolate any outside model before it touches real data, whoever sent it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.2 (Supply Chain Attacks and Mitigations); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0011.000 (Unsafe AI Artifacts)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.1 Attacks on Data and Models (some model file formats run code when loaded, so outside model files, even signed, are opened only in isolation). questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Partner-shop photos in retraining
questions.question: A Thai phone trade-in app retrains its screen-damage classifier monthly on photos from partner shops, after staff confirm each photo's label. Which added control should the IS auditor recommend as BEST against poisoning?

options.A: Retrain weekly so any poisoned photos are replaced sooner
options.B: Track each photo's shop and cap any one shop's share
options.C: Have a second staff member confirm every photo's label
options.D: Encrypt the partner shops' stored photos at rest

questions.key_concept: Poisoned training samples can carry correct labels; tracing each contributor's samples, and capping its share, works where label checks cannot.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the existing check can and cannot see.
questions.correct_explanation: In clean-label poisoning, attackers submit photos whose labels are correct but whose subtle changes teach the model a hidden weakness, so a second label check confirms them too. Tracking which shop supplied each photo lets suspect photos be traced and removed, and capping any one shop's share curbs bulk influence, though a targeted attack may need only a few photos. Double-checking labels repeats a check the attack is built to pass.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fresher data seems safer. But more frequent retraining takes in new poisoned photos sooner as well.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it doubles a familiar check. But clean-label poisoned photos are correctly labeled, so a second reviewer confirms them too.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it protects stored data. But the poisoned photos arrive through the normal upload path, not by tampering with storage.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains more often on the same untraced uploads, and D protects storage from a threat that enters through uploads.
Final two: B beats C because clean-label poison passes any label check; tracing each photo to its shop lets poison be found and removed, and a cap curbs bulk influence.
Exam cue: poisoned data can be correctly labeled. When outsiders supply training data, look for source tracking and limits on any one source's influence.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.3.2 (Targeted Poisoning); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0020 (Poison Training Data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.1 Attacks on Data and Models (clean-label poisoning keeps correct labels, so label review cannot catch it; limit and trace each contributor's influence). Review round 1: setting moved from a marketplace banned-item classifier (aaia_d2_008; notes 2F.1 example). Re-audit: distractor D now names the partner shops, so the stem's source noun no longer appears only in the key. Re-audit 2: explanation leads with provenance tracing and limits the share cap to bulk influence, matching NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.3.2 and aaia_d2_165. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A price floor written in the prompt
questions.question: A Dutch used-car dealer's chatbot books orders at prices it agrees to; its system prompt sets a floor, yet a tester talked it into a 90% discount. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the order system reject prices below the approved floor
options.B: Add an output filter blocking replies that quote prices under the floor
options.C: Add a website notice that chatbot prices are not binding
options.D: Add the tester's prompt to a blocklist of known attacks

questions.key_concept: Limits written into a prompt can be argued away by users; enforce price, refund and approval limits in the systems that carry them out.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens after the chatbot says yes.
questions.correct_explanation: A floor stated in the system prompt is an instruction the chatbot weighs against the user's arguments, and the tester's 90% discount shows it can be talked out of it. Having the order system reject any price below the approved floor enforces the limit whatever the chatbot agrees to. An output filter helps, but it judges wording, so a below-floor deal phrased another way can still reach the order.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it checks replies outside the model. But a filter reads words, and a deal phrased another way, such as 'ninety percent off', can still reach the order.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it limits liability. But a disclaimer leaves the chatbot offering prices, and customers may still hold the dealer to them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it stops this attack. But any customer can try a new wording; blocking one known prompt fixes nothing.

tips: Eliminate: C adds a disclaimer that leaves the chatbot agreeing to prices, and D blocks one known prompt among endless rewordings.
Final two: A beats B because the order system checks the actual price, whatever words led to it; a reply filter judges wording and can miss a deal phrased another way.
Exam cue: a limit stated only in a prompt is not a control. Look for limits enforced where the action takes effect.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.3 (Direct Prompting Attacks and Mitigations); MITRE ATLAS AML.T0054 (LLM Jailbreak)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.2 Prompt Injection and Jailbreaks (business limits stated in a prompt can be talked away; enforce them in the systems that act). Review round 1: runner-up changed from stronger prompt wording (aaia_d2_017, 046, 125) to an output filter; the stem now states that the chatbot books orders. Re-audit 2: distractor D recast from blocking the tester's account to blocklisting the known jailbreak prompt. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Replies the portal runs as code
questions.question: A Kosovar ministry's staff portal displays its citizen assistant's replies as web code; a tester got a reply carrying a script that ran in staff browsers. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Scan citizens' messages for malware before the assistant reads them
options.B: Train staff to close the portal when replies look odd
options.C: Instruct the assistant in its prompt to refuse writing code
options.D: Treat replies as untrusted and encode them before display

questions.key_concept: AI output can carry attacker-chosen content; systems that display or run it must treat it as untrusted input.
questions.pre_read: Follow the output to whatever uses it next.
questions.correct_explanation: Citizens control what the assistant reads, so they can steer it into writing a script, and the portal then runs that script in staff browsers. Treating every reply as untrusted input and encoding it before display stops any script from running, whatever the model writes. A prompt instruction to refuse writing code is something an attacker's wording can override, so it is not a control.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because inputs are often scanned. But the attack is plain text steering the model, which a malware scan does not detect.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because staff are the target. But a script runs when the page loads, before anyone can judge how a reply looks.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it targets the behavior. But prompt instructions can be overridden by crafted input, so scripts can still get through.

tips: Eliminate: A scans for malware when the attack is plain text, and B relies on staff reacting after the script has run.
Final two: D beats C because encoding at display stops scripts whatever the model writes; a prompt instruction can be overridden.
Exam cue: model output is untrusted input to the next system. Look for validation or encoding where the output is used.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-15 (Information Output Filtering); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.3 (Direct Prompting Attacks and Mitigations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.2 Prompt Injection and Jailbreaks (model output is untrusted input to whatever displays or runs it; encode or validate it there). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. A looping appointment agent
questions.question: A Barbadian dental chain's appointment agent, stuck in a loop on one booking, sent a patient 4,000 texts overnight before anyone noticed. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Alert on-call staff whenever message volume spikes
options.B: Enforce hard caps on the agent's actions and messages for each task
options.C: Retrain the agent's model on the looping conversation
options.D: Add a prompt rule telling the agent to stop repeating messages

questions.key_concept: Agents can loop or be steered into repeated actions; hard limits enforced outside the model bound the damage before anyone notices.
questions.pre_read: Ask what bounds the agent when no one is watching.
questions.correct_explanation: Agents can loop or be manipulated into repeating actions, and here nothing stopped one sending 4,000 texts. A hard cap on actions and messages per task, enforced by the systems the agent uses, stops a runaway at a set point whatever the model does. A volume alert helps, but overnight it depends on someone responding, and texts keep going until they do.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it detects the runaway. But it depends on a person responding, and overnight the texts continue until someone does.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the model misbehaved. But retraining on one loop changes little, and the agent stays unbounded meanwhile.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it addresses repetition. But a looping agent may not follow its prompt, and a rule inside the model is not a limit.

tips: Eliminate: D relies on a prompt rule the looping agent may not follow, and C retrains the model while the agent stays unbounded.
Final two: B beats A because an agent can loop faster than anyone responds; a cap outside the model stops it at a set point, while an alert waits for a person.
Exam cue: agents need system-enforced ceilings on actions, messages and spend per task, not only alerts or prompt rules.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.6 (Evaluated regularly for safety risks, fails safely); OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM06 (Excessive Agency)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.3 Excessive Agency and Access Management for AI (agents need hard, system-enforced limits on actions and cost per task, because they can loop or be steered). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2F AI threats. Tool descriptions that can change
questions.question: A Saudi engineering consultancy's research agent uses tools from an outside provider's server; it reads their descriptions as instructions, and the provider can change them without notice. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Tell the agent in its prompt to ignore odd tool descriptions
options.B: Accept tool providers that hold a recognized security certificate
options.C: Pin approved tool descriptions and review any change before use
options.D: Review the agent's tool calls in a monthly log check

questions.key_concept: Tool descriptions are prompt text the agent obeys; outside tool definitions are pinned, and any change is reviewed like a change to the agent.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the agent trusts that someone else can edit.
questions.correct_explanation: The agent treats each tool's description as instructions, so a provider, or an attacker who reaches the provider's server, can change the agent's behavior by editing that text without touching the consultancy's systems. Pinning the approved descriptions and reviewing any change before the agent uses it closes that path. A security certificate says the provider runs controls; it does not stop a changed description reaching the agent.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it warns the agent. But a prompt instruction is not a control, and a poisoned description is itself an instruction.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because certification signals good practice. But a certified provider can still change, or be made to change, the text the agent obeys.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logs show what happened. But a monthly check finds misuse weeks after a changed tool steered the agent.

tips: Eliminate: A answers injected text with more prompt text, and D reviews logs weeks after a changed tool acted.
Final two: C beats B because pinned, reviewed descriptions stop a changed tool reaching the agent; a provider's certificate does not.
Exam cue: for agents, outside tool definitions are part of the prompt. Treat changes to them like any other AI change.
questions.framework_ref: MITRE ATLAS AML.T0011.002 (Poisoned AI Agent Tool); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SR-3 (Supply Chain Controls and Processes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2F.3 Excessive Agency and Access Management for AI (an agent reads tool descriptions as instructions, so outside tool definitions are pinned and changes reviewed before use). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A flaw reported by another customer
questions.question: A Sri Lankan municipal council uses a vendor's complaint-routing model; another council publicly reported that the same model under-prioritizes Tamil-language complaints, though this council's monitoring shows no alerts. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Log it as a possible AI incident and test Tamil complaints
options.B: Rely on monitoring, since it has raised no alerts
options.C: Ask the vendor to confirm whether the report is accurate
options.D: Retrain the model on the council's own Tamil complaints

questions.key_concept: A flaw reported in a shared vendor model is an incident signal for every user; test your own use instead of waiting.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the monitoring could see this kind of flaw at all.
questions.correct_explanation: The same vendor model probably behaves the same way here, and monitoring that tracks overall results may never show a gap affecting one language group. Logging it as a possible incident starts triage, and testing the council's own Tamil complaints shows whether its residents are affected. Asking the vendor helps, but a vendor's word on its own model is a claim, and the wait leaves residents exposed.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because monitoring is in place. But monitoring of overall results can miss a gap in one language group entirely.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor knows the model. But its answer is a claim about its own product, and waiting leaves Tamil-speaking residents exposed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it targets the flaw. But the flaw is unconfirmed here, and retraining a vendor model is not the council's first step.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts monitoring that may not measure by language, and D retrains before the flaw is even confirmed here.
Final two: A beats C because the council's own test shows whether its residents are harmed; the vendor's confirmation is a claim and takes time.
Exam cue: a flaw reported in a shared model is an incident signal for every user. Triage and test your own use; do not wait.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.3 (Incidents and errors communicated and tracked); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2G.1 Recognizing and Triaging AI Incidents (an outside report of a flaw in a shared vendor model is an incident signal; test your own use rather than wait for monitoring or the vendor). Review round 1: setting moved from an insurer's claims-triage model (CISA d2_163; aaia_d2_187; crisc_d1_141). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Drift the auditor finds in fieldwork
questions.question: During fieldwork, an IS auditor finds an Albanian hospital's postpartum-hemorrhage alert model has run two months with input drift beyond its owner's tolerance, unnoticed; alert volumes look normal. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Confirm from patient outcomes that detection has fallen first
options.B: Notify the model owner of the drift at once
options.C: Recommend in the report that the owner add drift monitoring
options.D: Have the data team retrain the model on recent data

questions.key_concept: Drift beyond tolerance in a live model is an AI incident even before harm shows; the IS auditor alerts the model owner at once.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option does in the next few days.
questions.correct_explanation: Input drift beyond the owner's tolerance means the model now sees data unlike what it was validated on, so its detection rate can no longer be trusted, even though alert volumes look normal. That makes it a live AI incident, so the IS auditor tells the model owner at once to triage it, such as adding manual checks. Waiting for patient outcomes to confirm a fall could take weeks while hemorrhages are missed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because findings need sufficient evidence. But missed hemorrhages show up in outcomes only later; drift beyond tolerance is already the owner's trigger to act.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because missing drift monitoring is the control gap. But it belongs in the report later; a live model beyond tolerance needs the owner's action now.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retraining targets drift. But the IS auditor does not direct fixes, and an untested retrain is not containment.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves a live incident for the report, and D has the IS auditor direct a retrain, which is management's role.
Final two: B beats A because drift beyond tolerance is itself an incident trigger; outcomes reveal missed hemorrhages only later, while the model keeps running.
Exam cue: drift beyond tolerance in a live model is an incident even when outputs look normal. Alert the owner at once; report the control gap later.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.1 (Post-deployment monitoring including appeal, override, incident response and change management); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2G.1 Recognizing and Triaging AI Incidents (drift beyond tolerance in a live model is an AI incident; the auditor tells the owner at once rather than waiting for the report). Review round 1: setting moved from a sepsis-alert model (principles.json independence-of-ai-assurance example; crisc_d2_012). Review round 2: stem states the drift as a detection rate below tolerance, so the learner must see drift in a live model as an incident; key option lost its purpose clause. Review round 3: stem now gives input drift beyond tolerance with normal-looking alert volumes, and distractor A (switching the model off) became confirming the fall from patient outcomes first, so recognizing drift as an incident decides rather than general escalation sense. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Stopping one function of a model
questions.question: A Senegalese crafts marketplace's model removes protected-wildlife listings and suspends sellers; it began wrongly suspending Wolof-language sellers, though its removals show no such pattern. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Switch the whole model off until it is retrained and retested
options.B: Keep the model running and have staff review each suspension later
options.C: Have the IS auditor choose which of the model's functions to stop
options.D: Disengage its suspensions and keep the rest running

questions.key_concept: Containment disengages the AI action causing harm; stopping functions that show no fault can create new harm, such as banned listings going live.
questions.pre_read: List each thing the model does before choosing what to stop.
questions.correct_explanation: Containment stops the harmful action, and here the harm is confined to seller suspensions: removals show no such pattern, so stopping only suspensions protects Wolof-language sellers while protected-wildlife listings stay blocked. Switching the whole model off, option A, also stops the harm, but it ends removals that are working and lets banned listings go live for as long as retraining and retesting take.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a full stop is the surest containment. But the removals show no fault, so stopping them trades one harm for another.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because review catches wrongful suspensions. But they keep landing on Wolof-language sellers until each is reviewed after the fact.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because audit is independent. But choosing what to disengage is a management decision; the IS auditor would then assess its own decision.

tips: Eliminate: B lets wrongful suspensions continue until reviewed, and C gives the IS auditor a containment decision that belongs to management.
Final two: D beats A because only the suspensions are faulty; stopping the whole model also ends listing removals that still work.
Exam cue: contain the AI action that is causing harm; when other functions show no fault, keep them running and weigh the harm of stopping.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2G.2 Containment: Disengage, Roll Back and Preserve Evidence (containment disengages the AI action causing harm and weighs the harm of stopping functions that still work). Cross-domain gate fix, 12 Nov 2026: re-angled because the earlier version reused the frame of aaia_d2_108 and aaia_d2_088 (triggers or ratings built on outages, missing harm to people). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Planted pages in the index
questions.question: A Honduran university's assistant began telling students to pay fees into an outside account after planted pages entered its retrieval index; engineers want to roll back its model. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Retrain the model to ignore instructions found in pages
options.B: Delete the planted pages from the index and its backups
options.C: Pull the planted pages from the index, keeping copies as evidence
options.D: Roll the assistant's model back to last month's approved version

questions.key_concept: In retrieval systems the fault often sits in the index, not the model; contain it there and preserve what is removed.
questions.pre_read: Ask which component changed when the bad answers began.
questions.correct_explanation: The bad answers come from planted pages in the retrieval index, not from the model, so rolling the model back leaves the pages feeding every answer. Pulling them from the index stops students being sent to the outside account, and keeping copies preserves evidence of what was planted, when and by whom. Deleting them everywhere also contains the harm but destroys that evidence.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model obeyed the pages. But retraining is slow, untested, and leaves the pages live meanwhile.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it removes the harm completely. But deleting backups destroys the evidence needed to trace the attack and its victims.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because rollback is a standard containment step. But the model did not change; the planted pages keep feeding answers after it.

tips: Eliminate: B contains the harm but destroys evidence, and A starts a slow retrain while the pages stay live.
Final two: C beats D because the fault lives in the index, so a model rollback leaves the planted pages feeding answers.
Exam cue: contain an AI incident where the fault lives, often the index or prompt, not the model, and preserve what you remove.
questions.framework_ref: MITRE ATLAS AML.T0070 (RAG Poisoning); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI)

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Misses past page 40
questions.question: A Peruvian road agency's bid-review assistant misses commitments past about page 40 of proposals; evaluators now hand-check those pages, and the team plans retraining on longer bids. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Check how much of each long proposal the model receives
options.B: Add more long proposals with late commitments to the retraining data
options.C: Switch to a model advertising a larger input limit
options.D: Close the problem, as long proposals are a known limit

questions.key_concept: When AI failures follow input position or size, check what the integration passes to the model, such as truncated text, before retraining.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the pattern of failures says about where they start.
questions.correct_explanation: Misses that begin at a fixed point in long documents suggest the model never receives the later pages: the integration may cut text at a size or context limit. Checking how much of each proposal reaches the model tests that cause directly. Retraining on long proposals treats a model weakness that may not exist; if the text is cut before the model sees it, no training fixes that.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more examples often help. But if later pages never reach the model, no amount of training data fixes the misses.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a larger limit might fit long proposals. But the cause is unconfirmed, and the cut may sit in the agency's integration, not the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because limits exist. But the limit may sit in the integration and be fixable; closing without a cause leaves the misses.

tips: Eliminate: C swaps models before the cause is known, and D closes the problem with no root cause.
Final two: A beats B because misses past a fixed page point to truncated input; retraining cannot fix text the model never sees.
Exam cue: when AI failures follow input position or size, check the pipeline into the model before blaming or retraining the model.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 RS.AN-03 (Root cause of the incident established); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. A labeling guide with a gap
questions.question: A Belgian broadcaster traced its misinformation model's flagging of satire to a labeling guide with no satire rule; staff relabeled 900 posts, retrained and closed the problem. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have labelers reread the labeling guide before each batch
options.B: Reopen the problem until the labeling guide covers satire
options.C: Search the training data for satire posts staff missed
options.D: Accept the closure, as the retrained model now passes tests

questions.key_concept: If bad labels come from a gap in the labeling guide, fixing the found labels treats the symptom; the guide is the root cause.
questions.pre_read: Ask what will produce the next batch of labels.
questions.correct_explanation: The bad labels came from a guide with no rule for satire, so labelers will mislabel the next satire posts the same way and the next retrain will learn the error again. Reopening the problem until the guide covers satire fixes the cause. Searching for missed satire posts cleans more of today's data, but new labels made under the same guide repeat the flaw.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it targets how labels are made. But the guide has no satire rule, so rereading it leads labelers to the same wrong labels.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because some satire posts may remain mislabeled. But it cleans past data only; new labels made under the same guide repeat the error.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tests now pass. But the guide that produced the bad labels is unchanged, so the next labels bring the error back.

tips: Eliminate: A has labelers reread a guide that still lacks a satire rule, and D accepts closure while the guide is unchanged.
Final two: B beats C because the guide produces every future label; cleaning past posts fixes the data but not the process that made it wrong.
Exam cue: trace bad AI behavior to the process that made the data. A gap in labeling rules is a root cause; relabeling found cases is a symptom fix.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 RS.AN-03 (Root cause of the incident established); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.2 (Continual improvement integrated into AI system updates)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2G.3 Root Cause, Problem Management and Reporting (when bad labels trace to the labeling guide, the root cause is the guide; relabeling fixes only the cases found).
